studies.title: From A Single Soul
studies.meaning: The address here is to all people, not to believers only. The call to be mindful rests on a fact about where everyone came from. One soul, its mate from it, and out of that pair a scattering of many men and women. Early scholars differ over whether the single soul is Adam, or the shared beginning of us all stated broadly. Then the sentence joins being mindful of God to being mindful of the ties of blood, and closes by calling Him a watcher.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina, and this verse opens it. What follows deals with orphans, inheritance, marriage and the property of people who cannot protect it. Early scholars treat this verse as the doorway to all of it. That material is introduced by a statement about shared descent. Much of the surah belongs to the period after Uhud, when many households in Medina had lost men and the care of widows and orphans had become urgent.

keyTerms.note: The word for soul is grammatically feminine and is not tied to one sex. Its use here puts the origin of humanity in one undivided source, before any distinction between men and women appears.
The plural of the word for a womb, used of blood relatives generally. It shares its root with the divine names of mercy, so the same consonants carry both the organ and the compassion.
A sentry posted to keep watch, a word from the language of guarding rather than of judging. It closes a verse about family, where wrongs are usually invisible to anyone outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In seventh-century Arabia the kinship tie was the basic unit of safety. Your protection came from relatives who would answer for you. A traveller cut off from kin could be robbed with no consequence to anybody. Poets swore by the tie, and cutting it was among the gravest charges you could bring against a man. Naming kinship beside the name of God spoke straight into that arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: Two surahs open with exactly the same words of address, this one and surah 22, each beginning by telling all people to be mindful of their Lord. They carry on very differently. Here the reason given is a shared origin; there it is the shaking of the Hour. Surah 4 is the second longest in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Awareness of God is drawn out of biology here rather than simply commanded. The verse gives a reason before it gives an instruction, and the reason is one every listener shares, whatever they believe. Putting kinship beside the name of God in a single clause has been read as making the treatment of relatives part of what reverence means. It is not a separate duty. The last word keeps all of it under watch.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the account of the single soul and its mate, going on into the birth of children.
Draws the social conclusion, that peoples were made distinct for recognition rather than for ranking.
Turns straight to the property of orphans, showing what the appeal to kinship is about to require.

studies.applyIt: Call the relative you have not spoken to for the longest time, and do not make it an occasion. Ask about their week. This verse puts the ties of blood in the same breath as awareness of God. The tie it means is not the feeling but the contact, which is the part that lapses when nobody makes the call.
studies.explainEasier: God made all people from one soul, and from it made its partner. Everyone alive came from that pair. So keep God in mind, and take care of your family.

studies.title: What Belongs To The Orphan
studies.meaning: Three separate failures are named here, not one. Property held in trust has to actually reach the person who owns it. A guardian must not swap poor goods for sound ones out of the estate, and early scholars describe exactly that: a lean animal exchanged for a fat one, worn coin for good. And the wealth is not to be quietly folded into the guardian's own holdings, where the line between them disappears. The word chosen for the offence at the close is unusually heavy, and nothing is added to soften it.
studies.historicalContext: This comes early in a surah from Medina that gathers what the community owes to people who cannot protect themselves. Fighting had left many households without fathers, and the property of the dead passed to whoever stood near enough to hold it. Guardianship was a known arrangement, and already open to abuse. No single occasion is reported. The verse opens a run on orphans that reaches through the inheritance shares and past them.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for one left alone. In Arabic usage it names a child whose father died before the child grew up, and it carries the older sense of a solitary thing, a single pearl.
A word for what is spoiled rather than merely inferior. Setting it against the wholesome makes the swap a moral act and not a question of trade quality.
From a root meaning to lean or incline, since wealth is what leans towards a person and away again. The word for theirs is repeated twice in one short verse.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was countable and physical: date palms in a named grove, camels with known marks, silver kept in a household chest. A guardian could take an orphan's strong she-camel and leave a weaker one in its place in broad daylight. The herds grazed together and nobody kept a written ledger. Children had no standing to object, and years would pass before anyone thought to ask.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this verse uses for the offence occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Arabic has many terms for sin and the Quran uses several of them often. This one appears a single time, attached to the taking of an orphan's property. Surah 4 carries the name The Women, and yet it opens on the orphan rather than on marriage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being a trustee is first a matter between the guardian and God, and only after that between him and the child. The orphan cannot check the accounts or bring a claim. In most cases he will never learn what was taken. The passage answers that gap by making the reckoning belong to God rather than to the town. It also refuses the excuse of size. The swap of one animal is set beside eating up the whole estate.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the instruction not to approach an orphan's property except in the best way, until he grows up.
Names neglect of the orphan and greed for inheritance as signs of a whole society's disorder.
Addresses a prophet who was himself an orphan, and turns his own history into an instruction.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you hold that is not really yours: a shared account, a sibling's stored boxes, money someone left with you, a task somebody trusted you with. Check on it today, before anyone asks. This verse is less about theft than about the slow blurring of a boundary. Boundaries blur while nobody is looking at them.
studies.explainEasier: Give orphans the property that belongs to them. Do not swap your poor things for their good ones. Do not mix their money into yours and eat it up. Doing that is a very big wrong.

studies.title: The Fear Of Being Unfair
studies.meaning: The verse opens and closes on fairness, with marriage in between, stated as a condition. It begins by tying the subject to orphan girls in a guardian's care. That is how early scholars read the link, and a well attested early report describes guardians marrying their wards to keep hold of their property. The permission that follows is hemmed in twice, by a number and by the condition of dealing evenly. Then the reason is given plainly, which is that this makes unfairness less likely.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina. Early scholars connect the verse to guardians who married orphan girls in their charge, which kept control of the girls' inheritance while giving them less than a fair dowry. An early report describing exactly that is preserved as the occasion. The verse came to a community that had lost many men and had many dependants to place. The verses around it concern the property of those same orphans.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to give each side its due measure. It names fairness in dividing rather than affection, and the verse makes that the governing test at both ends of the sentence.
A second word for justice, from a root about balance and evenness. Using two different terms in one sentence keeps the standard from collapsing into a single claim easily met.
Scholars differ over its sense, reading it either as leaning away from justice or as having more dependants than you can support. Both readings make the closing words a warning against overreach.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An orphan girl in Medina came with a name, a share of palms, and no father to argue on her behalf. Her guardian controlled both her property and her marriage, and marrying her himself removed any outside party who might ask questions. Households were large and layered, with dependants attached to a head expected to house and feed them all. Fairness there was measured in food, cloth and nights.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for orphans here is masculine plural in the grammar. Early scholars read it as meaning orphan girls, because the sentence goes straight from them to marriage. This is also the only verse in the Quran that names a number of wives at all, and it does so while narrowing the possibility rather than opening it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A permission is set inside a condition, and the condition is then stated twice. That puts the weight of the sentence on the fairness rather than on the concession. Fear of your own unfairness is treated as a reason to act, not only a feeling to manage. And by starting with orphans, the passage frames the whole matter as care of people who cannot protect themselves, not as appetite.

crossReferences.why: Returns to these same orphan girls and their guardians, answering a later request for clarification.
States plainly that perfect evenness of feeling lies beyond human reach, and asks for restraint instead.
Carries on this surah's insistence that women in a household are not property passed between hands.

studies.applyIt: Notice the method of this verse rather than its subject. It asks you to consult your own fear of falling short. Take one responsibility you have taken on. Ask honestly whether you have room for it, or whether you took it because it was there. Then let the honest answer change one small thing this week.
studies.explainEasier: If you are afraid you cannot be fair to orphan girls in your care, then marry other women instead. And if you are afraid you will not treat them all fairly, marry only one. That way you are less likely to be unjust.

studies.title: A Gift, Not A Price
studies.meaning: Two instructions here, both about money and the people it passes between. The first sends the dowry to the bride herself, and calls it by a word meaning a free gift. Early scholars read that as setting aside an older practice in which the payment went to her guardians. If she hands part of it back, that is hers to decide. The second concerns wealth held for someone whose judgement is not formed yet. The property is not kept from them but spent on them, with kind words alongside the spending.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina. Early scholars describe an older custom in which the bridal payment went to a woman's father or guardian rather than to her, and they read the word chosen here as undoing that custom. The second verse is read alongside the passage on orphans around it, though its wording is wider and covers anyone unable to manage property. Both belong to the way this surah opens by reordering household wealth.

keyTerms.note: From the root for truthfulness and sincerity. The payment is named after truth, which marks it as evidence of how serious the commitment is rather than as a price paid for a person.
A word for something given without expecting anything back. It takes any sense of exchange out of the transaction, and it makes what she receives completely her own.
Not an insult about intelligence but a description of capacity. The word covers anyone unable to manage property well, and the verse pairs it at once with an instruction about how to speak.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marriage talks in that world ran between families, and the payment was part of what settled how two households stood with each other. Sending it to the bride gave her something of her own inside the marriage. She could carry it, and it stayed hers if the marriage ended. Otherwise household wealth moved as one mass under whoever was head. So property held separately really did change a woman's position.
studies.didYouKnow: The second verse calls the property your money, while it seems to speak of wealth held for somebody else. Early scholars differ over that possessive. Some read it as the guardian's own funds. Others read it as the ward's, described as the whole community's charge. The grammar carries both, and the tradition keeps the double sense rather than settling it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Both verses correct one instinct: treating a dependant's property as an extension of your own. One does it by calling the dowry a gift, so ownership passes cleanly. The other lets control stay where it is while taking away the benefit. Between them they set out that power over somebody's money and a right to it are two different things. The right does not follow from the power.

crossReferences.why: Addresses reclaiming a dowry when a marriage ends, and refuses it even where large sums are involved.
Gives the point at which property held for a ward is handed over, and how that handover is recorded.
Joins kind speech to the same cluster of duties towards parents, orphans, the needy and the near.

studies.applyIt: If you manage money for someone who cannot manage it, a child, a parent, someone unwell, spend an extra minute today. Explain what you did with it, in words they can follow. These two verses put provision and speech together on purpose. Being provided for without being spoken to is its own kind of poverty, and it is easy to miss.
studies.explainEasier: Give a woman her dowry as a gift that is hers. If she chooses to give some of it back, that is fine. Do not hand money to people who cannot handle it yet. Feed them and clothe them from it, and speak kindly to them.

studies.title: Until They Are Ready
studies.meaning: Guardianship is given both an end point and a method. The ward is tested as marriage age comes near, so the handover depends on judgement actually shown rather than on age alone. Two temptations are named: spending the estate lavishly, and hurrying to spend it before the child is old enough to claim it. A guardian with means is asked to take nothing, while one in need may take modestly. The handover is then witnessed, and the sentence closes by naming a witness beyond the human ones.
studies.historicalContext: This carries on the run about orphans that opens the surah in Medina. Early scholars place these instructions in a community where guardianship was normal and hardly watched. Deaths in the early fighting had multiplied the number of estates held for children. No single occasion is reported. What arrives here is a working frame built onto the warning before it.

keyTerms.note: The verb used across the Quran for trials God sets. Applied here to a guardian judging a ward, it makes that judging serious and continuing rather than one formal question asked once.

Not physical growth but the capacity to manage. Early scholars discuss whether it means competence with money, uprightness of character, or both together, and they record the range without settling it.
From a root for counting and calculating. It closes the verse on the picture of an audit, which is exactly what the witnessed handover has just been arranged to make possible.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A handover meant moving things and naming them: which palms in the grove, which she-camels, how much silver. With no documents, ownership lived in the memory of whoever watched. Calling witnesses was the only lasting record a family had. That is why the verse asks for them at the moment of transfer. A guardian who was poor lived beside the property he managed every day.
studies.didYouKnow: This is among the longest single verses in the surah. It moves through five separate concerns with no story to link them: testing, transfer, restraint, what the guardian may take, and witnessing. Surah 4 comes back to orphans in seven different verses, more than any other surah. And yet it is named for women rather than for them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse builds a chain of answering for what you do, then carries it past the point where people can see. Witnesses cover the moment of transfer. God as the Reckoner covers the years before it, when nobody was watching. It also will not make poverty an excuse or wealth a licence. What is asked of a guardian fits what he can afford, and the trust underneath never loosens.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same instinct for witnessing to debts, since memory and goodwill are not enough.
Joins care of an orphan's property to full measure and honest weight, as one continuous ethic.
Repeats the boundary around an orphan's wealth and adds that every commitment will be asked about.

studies.applyIt: When you next hand back something that was in your keeping, a borrowed tool, a key, money held for someone, do it in front of a third person. Or send a short message confirming it. Between people who trust each other this feels like too much. That is exactly the moment being described. A record protects the honest party as much as anyone.
studies.explainEasier: Look after an orphan's property and test the child as he grows up. When you see he can handle it, hand it over. Do not waste it or rush to spend it first. Get witnesses when you give it back.

studies.title: A Share For Each
studies.meaning: One clause is said twice here, once for men and once for women, with nothing changed except who is named. Whatever the estate is worth, little or much, both stand inside it. The words at the end make the portion a due already marked out, not a gift the family chooses to make. Exact fractions arrive only in the verses that follow. This one establishes that there is something to be divided at all.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina. Early scholars report that inheritance among the Arabs of the time usually followed who could ride and fight, so women and young children of a dead man often got nothing. A widely reported early account describes a widow bringing the case of her daughters forward after her husband was killed. This passage and the ones after it are read as the answer to her.

keyTerms.note: A word for an allotted portion, used elsewhere of a share of good or of punishment. It names something already assigned rather than something granted by a family's goodwill.
From a root meaning to cut or mark out precisely. It turns the share from a moral expectation into a defined quantity, which is what the verses after it go on to supply.
A form from the root for nearness, meaning those closest. It widens the estate beyond parents to the surrounding kin, which is how households actually held property at the time.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Property in that society was usually held by a household, not by a person, and it stayed with the men who could defend it. A widow could end up living in a house that had passed to her husband's brother. Daughters were counted as future members of another family. They were often treated as out of the estate altogether. The repeat in this verse lands differently against that.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about what parents and relatives leave is written out twice in full, where Arabic would happily have shortened the second one to a pronoun. Early scholars read that repeat as the substance of the verse, not its style. It is balance made audible, so that one half cannot be heard as an add-on to the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A question of family custom is moved into the language of a share set by God. Once a portion is described as marked out, holding it back becomes a matter between the one who holds it and God. It stops being a family decision open to haggling. The verse also frees nobody because an estate is small. The words covering little and much remove the handiest excuse before anyone can offer it.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the fractions this verse promises, opening with a direct instruction concerning children.
Attacks the older custom from another direction, refusing to let women be inherited as property.
Shows the same concern that an estate be settled deliberately rather than left to whoever is nearest.

studies.applyIt: Look at something you handle for other people: a family fund, a shared bill, a rota, an estate still undivided. Write down plainly who is owed what, and show it to them. Much unfairness inside families is never decided. It builds up because nobody wrote anything down while everyone was still on good terms.
studies.explainEasier: When parents and close relatives die and leave things behind, men get a share of it. Women get a share of it too. It does not matter whether the amount is small or large. The share is set, not a favour.

studies.title: Those Standing At The Division
studies.meaning: A moment is described here rather than a rule laid down. When an estate is divided, people with no claim are often standing there: a cousin outside the line of inheritance, a neighbour's orphan, someone poor. The passage asks that they be given something from it and spoken to well. Early scholars differ over whether this describes a settled practice of the early community or a strong recommendation, and both readings are kept. The words are not a stand-in for the giving. Both are asked for.
studies.historicalContext: This sits in Medina, right after the verse saying that men and women alike hold shares, and right before the fractions are given. Where it falls carries weight. It comes between the principle and the arithmetic, so that exact accounting is framed by a gesture no accounting calls for. Early scholars report the practice in the early community. They also record that later generations differed over whether it continued.

keyTerms.note: A noun for the act of dividing, from the same root as the words for equity and for portion. It names the occasion rather than the property, which is what makes this verse about a moment.
The verb comes from the root for provision, normally used of God providing. Applying it to the heirs casts their giving as a channel for something they did not make in the first place.
Literally what is known and recognised. The standard is whatever any decent person present would recognise as decent, which leaves the form open while keeping the substance clear.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A division happened in the open, in a courtyard or beside the palms, and it drew a crowd. Relatives who would get nothing came anyway, since the fortunes of a household were everyone's business. Watching a share of dates counted out to someone else while your own family had none was an ordinary thing. This verse is written for the awkwardness of that crowd, and everyone there would have felt it.
studies.didYouKnow: A phrase asking for good words appears three times in the first nine verses of this surah. Twice the wording is the same, and once the adjective differs. Each time it is attached to a different party who cannot push back: those managing another's wealth, the immature, and the onlookers at a division. Speech is made part of handling money, not a courtesy beside it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This works against a particular hazard of fair systems. Once shares are exact, anything outside them can start to look like nothing owed. By putting an unmeasured gesture between the principle and the fractions, the passage keeps generosity from being crowded out by correctness. It also treats the poor as people standing there, not as a category. That changes what the moment of division is.

crossReferences.why: Extends the same attention outward to neighbours near and far, and to travellers passing through.
Places giving to relatives, orphans and the needy at the centre of what righteousness consists of.
Explains distribution as keeping wealth from circulating only among those who are already rich.

studies.applyIt: The next time something good arrives that others watched arrive, a bonus, a gift, an inheritance, give a small part of it away that same week. Give it to somebody who was nearby and received nothing. Not as payment, and not as an apology. This verse is describing the difference between a room where that happens and one where it does not.
studies.explainEasier: When a family shares out what a dead person left, other people are often standing there: relatives with no share, orphans, poor neighbours. Give them something out of it too. And speak to them kindly.

studies.title: Fire In The Belly
studies.meaning: The first of these verses works by moving a feeling across. It asks people advising a dying man about his estate to picture their own children left behind weak, and then to let that fear shape what they say. The second turns to those who take an orphan's property. It describes the act as already being what it will become: swallowing fire. Early scholars note that only the burning is put in the future. So the punishment is shown as the same act, seen truly.
studies.historicalContext: This sits in Medina, between the verse about onlookers at a division and the detailed shares. Early scholars connect the first of the two to counsel given at a deathbed. A visitor might urge a dying man to give away more than his household could spare, or to pass over the heirs nearest him. Pairing that with the warning that follows suggests one situation seen from both ends: advice given, and property taken.

keyTerms.note: A plural of the adjective for weakness, covering the physically small and the powerless together. It describes children exactly as they look to a father imagining his own absence from the house.
From a root for closing a gap or hitting a target. It asks for speech that is true and well aimed rather than merely inoffensive, which is a higher standard than kindness alone.
The verse places it inside the body rather than around it, which is unusual. The picture collapses the distance between an act and what comes of it, instead of describing a penalty applied later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dying man in Medina was surrounded, not left alone. Relatives, creditors and interested neighbours gathered in the room. Words spoken over him in his last hours could send a whole estate elsewhere. The pressure was real, and the advice was rarely free of interest. Everyone in that room had also pictured lying in that bed, with their own small children standing where these ones stood.
studies.didYouKnow: The second verse uses the ordinary verb for eating, the same one used of meals, and attaches it to fire in the stomach. Early scholars noticed that the picture is never announced as a comparison. The sentence simply reports the eating and then the burning, and leaves the reader to join the two.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Imagination is treated here as part of religion. The first verse does not argue that taking from orphans is wrong. It asks you to stand somewhere else and see what you already know. The second shows that results are not added to acts by a judge. They lie inside the act itself. That is a claim about how the moral world is built, not about penalties.

crossReferences.why: Draws a parallel picture, a man with weak children watching his garden burn, to produce the same feeling.
Names devouring inheritance greedily among the failings of a society that neglects its orphans.
Opens this surah's treatment of an orphan's property with the offence this passage reports the end of.

studies.applyIt: Before you next give someone advice about their money, their will, or their family, ask what you would want said if the person receiving it were your own child. Then say that, even if it is harder. Most bad counsel is not malicious at all. It is simply given by somebody who never troubled to put themselves inside the room.
studies.explainEasier: Think how you would feel about your own small children if you died and left them behind. Then be careful of God and say the right thing. People who eat up an orphan's money are swallowing fire.

studies.title: Shares You Did Not Choose
studies.meaning: Fixed portions are set out for children and parents, case by case: daughters alone, a single daughter, parents with and without grandchildren, and what surviving brothers and sisters change. Debts and bequests are settled before anything is counted. What early scholars dwell on is a sentence near the end that cuts across all the arithmetic. You do not know which of your parents or children will prove nearer to you in benefit. That is why the sharing is closed to sentiment.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina, among the verses that replace an inheritance practice based on who could fight with one based on set relationships. Early scholars report a case brought soon after a battle. The daughters of a man killed got nothing, while a male relative took the whole estate. They read these verses as the answer to it. The detailed shares arrive here, once the principle has already been stated.

keyTerms.note: From the root for making a bequest. God uses the language of a testator about His own instruction, which puts the whole passage in the register of a will rather than of a decree.
A word for an allotted share carrying an older sense of fortune. Its use keeps attention on the portion assigned rather than on any judgement about the worth of the person receiving it.
From a root meaning to cut precisely, the same one used a few verses earlier. It marks the fractions as settled rather than proposed, which is why the passage never argues for them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Estates were physical and awkward to divide: a grove, a well, a herd, a house. Splitting them meant real decisions about who took which trees and who watered when. Families that could not agree brought the matter into the open before witnesses, since there was no registry to appeal to. Precise fractions were not paperwork in that world. They were what stood between a household and a feud.
studies.didYouKnow: The two long inheritance verses of this surah are followed at once by two short ones about obeying and disobeying God. The order is striking: careful arithmetic, then a sudden turn to the Gardens and the Fire. Early scholars read the pairing as deliberate. It marks the fractions as something other than paperwork.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The words about not knowing who will benefit you rest the passage on human ignorance rather than on family structure. People share things out by affection, by expectation, or by a sense of who will repay attention. All three rest on guesses about the future. The passage takes the guess out of the sum. Debts and bequests, early scholars note, are cleared first.

crossReferences.why: States the principle these fractions carry out, that both men and women hold a fixed portion.
Argues the same way: your view is limited, so the instruction stands above your reading of it.
Closes the surah with the remaining case, an estate left by someone with neither parents nor children.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your own planning quietly assumes you know who will need what, and who will be there for you later. Take one such assumption and hold it loosely for a week. The passage is not asking you to distrust your family. It asks you to notice that you are forecasting, and that a forecast is not knowledge.
studies.explainEasier: God sets out how much each person gets from what someone leaves behind. Sons, daughters, mothers and fathers all have a set share. Debts and any gift promised are paid first. You do not know which of them will end up meaning most to you.

studies.title: Without Any Prejudice
studies.meaning: The picture is finished here. A husband's share from his wife's estate is set out, and a wife's from her husband's, each changing with whether there are children. Then comes the case of a person who leaves neither parent nor child. Debts and bequests come first, and the words saying so are repeated three times inside one verse. A phrase about causing no injury attaches to the bequest, and early scholars read it as blocking a will written to wound rather than to help anyone.
studies.historicalContext: This follows straight on from the shares for children and parents and completes them, in Medina. Together the two verses form the most detailed passage of law in the Quran. Early scholars place them in the years after the community had settled, as older inheritance customs were reordered. They note that the case of a person with no direct heirs is left partly open here. It is taken up again at the very end of the surah.

keyTerms.note: A rare term whose exact scope early scholars discuss at length, reading it either as an estate with neither parent nor child, or as the relatives themselves. They record the difficulty rather than settling it.
An active participle from the root for harm. Attached to the bequest, it names a will written to wound somebody as a wrong distinct from a will that is merely unfair.
A divine name for patient restraint rather than mildness. Closing a verse of exact fractions with it suggests room is being left for the many people who will get this wrong.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A wife in that society usually brought her dowry into the marriage and kept it. She was not absorbed into her husband's property. When he died she needed a claim of her own, or she went back to her father's people with whatever she could carry. The repeated clause about debts mattered because debt was constant in a world with little coin. It was held in memory, and easy to deny once the debtor was gone.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about settling bequests and debts occurs three times in this one verse, and once in the verse before it. That is four times across two verses in a row. Early scholars read the repeat as insistence, not as style. No share is worked out from an estate until whatever the dead person owed has left it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two divine names close these verses: Knowing and Judicious in one, Knowing and Forbearing in the other. That pairing does something specific. Knowledge grounds the fractions, and forbearance meets the people who have to live with them. A passage of pure arithmetic ends on an attribute about how God treats those who fall short, which keeps the shares from reading as a machine.

crossReferences.why: Carries the shares for children and parents that this verse completes with those for spouses and siblings.
Returns at the close of the surah to the estate with no parent or child, left partial here.
Shows the bequest as an established practice, which is why it is cleared before any share is counted.

studies.applyIt: Take an hour this month to write down what you owe and what is owed to you, and tell one person you trust where the list is kept. This passage assumes debts outlive people and that memory makes a poor record. Doing it is not morbid. It is a small kindness to whoever will one day have to sort everything out.
studies.explainEasier: If your wife dies and leaves no children, you get half of what she left. If she has children, you get a quarter. Wives get a quarter, or an eighth if there are children. Debts are paid first.

studies.title: The Bounds And The Gardens
studies.meaning: One word gathers up everything before it, the shares, the settling of debts, the care of orphans, and calls the whole of it a boundary. Then an outcome is attached, not to the arithmetic but to the attitude behind it. Early scholars note the choice of a word for limits rather than for laws. What has been described is an edge. The moral question is whether a person stays inside it, or keeps pressing against it.
studies.historicalContext: This closes the inheritance verses in Medina. The community was getting detailed instruction for the first time on matters that had run on custom, and this verse supplies the reason to take it. Early scholars note that the surah keeps following practical instruction with an appeal to the hereafter. The detail is never left standing on its own.

keyTerms.note: The word for the edge of a piece of land or the border of a territory. It pictures the instructions as a marked perimeter, with a wide space inside it rather than a narrow path.
From a root carrying willingness rather than submission under force. The verb suggests someone who goes along with something readily, which is part of why a reward can be attached to it.
A word for winning through and coming out safe, used of escaping danger as much as of gaining a prize. It frames the Gardens as a successful arrival rather than as a payment received.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Boundaries were the most fought-over thing in that landscape. The edge of a grove, the radius of a well, grazing rights along a dry riverbed: all of it held by stones, memory and agreement. Moving a marker at night was a known form of theft. And rivers running beneath gardens described the one thing the region did not have: lasting water arriving without anyone's work.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of gardens with rivers running beneath them occurs more than thirty times in the Quran. Here it follows straight on from a passage of fractions and debts, with no bridge at all. That abruptness is typical of this surah. It keeps setting the smallest household detail against the largest horizon there is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse makes a link that is easy to miss. Honouring a widow's eighth is put on the same footing as the great matters people attach to the word obedience. Nothing is turned into a metaphor. What is asked is that a person accept a limit on their own gain at a moment when nobody could have stopped them from crossing it. The reward attaches to that acceptance.

crossReferences.why: States the reverse case at once, so the boundary is given two sides in the same wording.
Uses the same word for the limits of God in another household passage, warning against overstepping them.
Closes another set of family instructions by naming them limits and warning against crossing them.

studies.applyIt: Find one place today where a rule stands between you and something you could take with no consequence: a queue, an expense claim, a colleague's credit, a family arrangement tilted your way. Stay inside it on purpose. Notice that nobody saw you do it. That unseen moment is what this verse attaches a garden to.
studies.explainEasier: These shares are the lines God has drawn. Stay inside them, and do what God and the Messenger say. Then He will bring you into gardens with rivers running under them, to stay there for ever. That is the great win.

studies.title: Overstepping The Line
studies.meaning: Everything the verse before promised is turned over here, term by term. But one thing is added that breaks the match. Beside disobeying, the sentence names overstepping the limits, so the offence is described twice: once as refusal, once as trespass. The punishment at the close is not only harsh but shaming. Early scholars read that as an answer to an offence done to gain an edge over other people.
studies.historicalContext: This is the other half of a pair that closes the inheritance verses in Medina. The community was young and the instructions were new, and they replaced arrangements that had favoured whoever held power inside a family. Early scholars note that the warnings in this surah are usually aimed at people inside the community rather than at outright deniers. That shapes the reading. It speaks to somebody who accepts a line and crosses it anyway.

keyTerms.note: From a root connected with a staff, carrying the sense of breaking away rather than merely failing. It describes a refusal with will behind it, not a lapse of attention or of memory.
From the root for going beyond, and for enmity. Adding it to disobedience names a second thing: not only declining a limit but pushing past it into what belongs to somebody else.
An active participle from the root for lowliness. It specifies the quality of the punishment rather than its intensity, answering an act that raised one person by lowering another.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Honour was the working currency of that society. It was worth more than property and far harder to win back once lost. A man who took a niece's share might gain a grove and lose nothing in public, since family matters stayed inside families and the wronged party had nowhere to go. A punishment described as shaming speaks straight to that sum. It names the one cost he thought he had dodged.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verses form a matched pair in Arabic, almost the same in build, and yet this one runs noticeably shorter. Scholars across the tradition have noticed the same thing in the pairs of reward and punishment throughout the Quran. Descriptions of mercy are usually given more room than descriptions of the Fire.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting this straight after the Gardens shows one act described from two directions, and the reader already stands somewhere along that line. The word for shame matters. It suggests that the hereafter answers not only what was done but what was wanted by doing it. Someone who crossed a line to gain standing is met with the loss of standing.

crossReferences.why: Gives the matching promise in the same wording, so the two verses work as a single statement.
Warns in almost identical terms against overstepping the limits of God, in another family passage.
Attaches a humiliating punishment to those who set themselves against God and His Messenger.

studies.applyIt: Think of a boundary you crossed quietly in the past year and got away with. Do not dwell on the guilt, since this verse is not asking for that. Instead name what you hoped to gain by crossing it, and ask whether you actually got it. That one question is often enough to make the next boundary easier to keep.
studies.explainEasier: If someone goes against God and His Messenger and pushes past the lines He drew, he goes into a Fire and stays there. His punishment is a shameful one. Staying inside those lines leads the other way.

studies.title: Or God Makes A Way
studies.meaning: A procedure is described here, and the bar for proof is unusually high. Four witnesses are needed, drawn from among your own people, and nothing goes ahead without their testimony. What follows is being kept at home. Then the sentence points past itself, holding open the chance of something more. Early scholars read this as an early measure for the time being. It was given as the young community was first being given law, and set aside once more came.
studies.historicalContext: This comes early in the surah's treatment of household matters, in Medina. Early scholars place these instructions at the start of the community's legislation on such cases, when much was still being given in stages. They read the closing words as a plain signal that the arrangement was for the time being. They report that a later passage supplied what it pointed to. The reports agree on that order, while differing over details.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb for witnessing that means to seek witnesses out. The burden falls entirely on the accuser to produce them, which in practice makes such an accusation extremely hard to sustain.

The number stands far above what any other claim requires, and the Quran uses it only for accusations of this kind. Early scholars read the figure as protective, made to put casual accusation out of reach.
The ordinary word for a road. Left indefinite at the end of the sentence, it marks the passage as open towards something not yet given, which is how the tradition has always read it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in a small town was a household's main asset. Rumour moved through it faster than any correction could follow. A woman accused without proof had nowhere to appeal and no record to turn to, so her name could not be cleared. Asking for four eyewitnesses to the act itself set a bar that ordinary gossip could never reach, however loud it got.
studies.didYouKnow: Four witnesses are unique in the Quran to accusations of this kind. Other matters, debts and bequests among them, are settled with two. A later surah sets a penalty for accusers who cannot bring the four. That turns the rule into a shield for the accused rather than a way of pursuing them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows revelation coming in stages, and says so openly. A clause left unfinished on purpose inside the text is unusual. The tradition has treated it as a sign that guidance was given step by step, matched to what the community could carry. The bar for proof also shows what the moral order runs on. It runs on certainty, not on suspicion.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the parallel case in the next verse and closes on repentance and on God turning in mercy.
Sets a penalty for accusers unable to produce four witnesses, completing the protective logic here.
Records an episode of unfounded accusation and rebukes a community for repeating what it could not verify.

studies.applyIt: When you next hear something damaging about someone, ask what you would actually accept as proof. Then notice that you have not got it. Do not pass it on while that answer stands. The bar set here is impossibly high on purpose, and the reason is simple: reputations do not recover.
studies.explainEasier: If a woman is accused of a shameful act, four people from among you have to say they saw it. Without that, nothing goes ahead. If they do say so, she is kept at home until God opens a way.

studies.title: Then Leave Them Alone
studies.meaning: An instruction in two parts, with the weight falling on what comes second. Some form of censure is indicated and left deliberately unspecified, and early scholars remark on how little detail is given. Then the sentence turns: if the two repent and set things right, the matter is dropped and attention is withdrawn. Two divine names close it, one built on turning and one on mercy. The whole movement runs towards closure rather than towards pursuit.
studies.historicalContext: This is paired with the verse before it, from the same early stage of the community's legislation in Medina. Early scholars read both as temporary, given while much was still being set up. They record that later revelation changed the arrangement. What stays is the shape of the passage: a response, then a way out through repentance, then a deliberate turning away of attention.

keyTerms.note: The verb means literally to return, and it is used both of the two people here and of God in the same verse. One word covers the human turning and the divine acceptance of it.
From the root for repair and reconciliation. Repentance is paired with an action, so that turning inwardly is joined to mending whatever was actually damaged.
A verb for averting the face. Used elsewhere of ignoring the ignorant, it instructs a community here to stop looking, which is a deliberate act rather than the absence of one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was small enough that everyone's business was partly public. A household's standing rested on what neighbours were willing to remember and repeat. There was no way to move elsewhere and start again. So telling a whole community to stop looking at somebody was a real step, not a formality. It meant a person could still be spoken to in next season's market.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for turning back in repentance and the divine name that closes this verse come from one root. The human move and the answer from God are named by a single word in two forms. That doubling comes up across the Quran. It is part of why the tradition calls repentance a return rather than a plea.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse builds a way out, then names God by the quality that guarantees it. Communities are far better at blaming than at stopping. The instruction to look away is aimed at that weakness, not at the two who did wrong. It also ties repentance to repair, which keeps an inward turn from standing in for fixing anything.

crossReferences.why: Takes up repentance directly in the next verse and describes whose turning is accepted.
Asks a community to pardon and to overlook, since they want forgiveness from God themselves.
Places pardon above an equal response, while conceding a proportionate response is not itself wrong.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone in your circle who did something wrong, apologised, changed, and is still talked about. Next time it comes up, be the one who moves the conversation on. What is asked here is not private forgiveness in your heart. It is the stopping of a community's attention, and that only ever stops one person at a time.
studies.explainEasier: If two men among you do this, both are to be told off for it. But if they turn back and put things right, leave them alone. God takes people back, and He is full of mercy.

studies.title: Turning Back Soon After
studies.meaning: Two conditions are attached here, and early scholars read both widely. One is that the wrong was done in ignorance, which they take to cover anyone acting under the pull of appetite rather than in cold defiance, since a person choosing badly is not fully seeing. The other is that the turn comes soon after. What soon means is discussed at length. The common reading is at any point before death has come into view.
studies.historicalContext: This comes in Medina, after a run of hard household instructions and before a longer passage on marriage. Early scholars note where it falls. Instructions people will fail to keep are followed at once by the terms on which failure is answered. No particular occasion is reported. What arrives is a general statement, set exactly where the community would need it.

keyTerms.note: A noun from the verb for returning to a place you have left. It carries no sense of grovelling; the picture is a traveller reversing direction on a road he has just recognised.
Early scholars read this widely, taking it to include anyone acting rashly or under appetite and not only the genuinely uninformed. On that reading almost every wrong counts as a kind of not-seeing.
A strong preposition, naming something as though it were an obligation. Early scholars stress that God bound Himself to it, since nothing outside Him could impose an obligation on Him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in that economy was often settled by a return: a borrowed animal brought back, a share given back to whoever was owed it. The language of turning back had a plain daily use long before it carried a religious one. Roads out of Medina were long and hard. Turning round early cost far less than finding at the last watering place that you had gone wrong.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse and the next state one principle from opposite sides, and both open with the same noun for repentance. Arabic could have joined them with a simple negation inside one sentence. Setting them apart gives each its own weight. The promise is not heard as a clause qualified by the warning attached to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Acceptance is something God has taken on Himself. That turns repentance from a gamble into something you can count on, without making it automatic. The two conditions do the limiting. And by reading ignorance widely, the tradition keeps the door open. A person who knew the rule and broke it anyway is not shut out, because acting against what you know counts as its own kind of blindness.

crossReferences.why: Addresses those who have wronged themselves greatly, and tells them not to despair of mercy.
States the reverse case, marking where a turning at the point of death stops counting.
Names God as the one who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons their misdeeds.

studies.applyIt: Notice how long you usually leave it between doing something you regret and doing anything about it. The condition set here is not severity but speed. Take the thing still sitting unaddressed and close it today. Send the message, give the thing back, say sorry, while it is still small enough to close in one move.
studies.explainEasier: God takes people back when they do something wrong without really seeing what they are doing, and then turn back to Him soon after. He accepts them. He knows everything, and He is wise.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Now I Repent
studies.meaning: Two cases are shut out here, and they are not the same. One is a man who kept doing wrong until death was already in the room, and only then said the words. Early scholars place the failure in the timing rather than in how he felt, because by then nothing is being chosen. The other is those who die still refusing. And the quoted speech is striking: the verse puts three words in a dying man's mouth and lets them stand.
studies.historicalContext: This follows straight after the verse on the repentance God accepts, in Medina, and the two work as one argument. Early scholars ask where the line between them falls: how long soon lasts, and when a turning stops counting. They report wide agreement that the shut-out moment is the one where a dying person sees what is coming. They differ on how much earlier the door starts to close.

keyTerms.note: The verb for something that comes into the room. Death is called present, not drawing near, and that fixes the shut-out moment exactly: the point where death is no longer news.
One plain word of everyday speech, quoted as spoken. It turns a general statement into a scene, and early scholars note how much of the verse's force comes from that one word.
A verb for getting something ready ahead of time. The past tense puts the outcome before the death rather than after it, which matches the whole concern of the passage with timing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Death in that world was watched, not hidden away. Families sat with the dying, and the last words a man spoke were kept and repeated for years. A deathbed statement could turn an estate, settle a quarrel, or end a feud. So the room held real weight. Everyone who heard this verse had sat in such a room and watched someone try to settle it all at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran puts almost these same words in the mouth of a drowning ruler, at the instant the sea closes over him, and the answer given there is that it comes too late. The two passages share a shape: a statement at the last moment, and a refusal. Early scholars read them together as one rule.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Turning back to God is an act of freedom, and freedom needs a future you could still have gone on wasting. Once the end is in plain sight, the turning costs nothing and settles nothing. This is not God being unwilling. It is a claim about what turning actually is. The verse also keeps the late repenter apart from the flat denier, while still putting them on one side of the line.

crossReferences.why: Holds the same last-moment words from a drowning ruler, and the refusal that answers them.
Gives the case God accepts, which this verse marks out by what it shuts out.
Shows a man asking at death for a short delay to give charity, and getting none.

studies.applyIt: Take something you have been telling yourself you will deal with eventually: a rift, a debt, a habit, a conversation you owe someone. Put a date on it this week, in writing. This verse is not describing a cruel cut-off. It is describing what becomes of intentions that are never given a time.
studies.explainEasier: God says sorry comes too late when death is already there. A person who does wrong all his life, then says sorry as he is dying, has waited too long. The same is true for those who die still saying no.

studies.title: Live With Them In Kindness
studies.meaning: Three things are set aside in turn: treating a widow as part of an estate, pressing a wife to get back what was given her, and treating a marriage as merely something put up with. Then the standard is stated in the positive, with a word for whatever is known to be good. The closing words do something else again. They do not promise the dislike will pass. They say your reading of it may be wrong, and they say so with a word of mere maybe.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina. Early scholars report a practice in which a dead man's heirs could claim his widow, either marrying her themselves or keeping her from marrying elsewhere so that her dowry stayed in the family. This verse speaks to that practice directly. It sits inside the larger work this surah is doing on what happens to a household when the man at its head dies.

keyTerms.note: From the root for aversion, describing the woman's state rather than the heir's intention. It names consent as the missing element, which is what makes the older practice a wrong.
A verb used of an obstruction that will not move, and elsewhere of blocking a woman from remarrying. It describes pressure applied by the simple refusal to release someone.
From the root for close association and for a group living together. It asks for the texture of shared daily life, not merely for the absence of harm between two people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: When a man died, his widow's future was settled by whoever inherited his house. She might be kept unmarried so her dowry stayed put, or married to a son by another wife. She held no property beyond that dowry and had nowhere independent to live. The instruction to keep good company was addressed to men who held every one of those decisions in their hands.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing words here are quoted widely in Arabic outside religious settings, and so is a similar line earlier in the Quran about disliking what is good for you. Both are built on the same word of mere maybe. That is exactly why neither can be read as a claim that every dislike hides a hidden good.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse moves from a ban to something far harder to set in law: the quality of ordinary company. It does not lower the demand in that move. Then it turns to the feeling itself. It does not ask a husband to feel differently. It asks him to hold his judgement of the marriage open for now. That is a claim about the limits of what anyone can see from the middle of their own life.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle in another area: you may dislike what is good and love what harms.
Concedes that perfect evenness between wives lies beyond reach, and asks that no one be left suspended.
Names affection and mercy between spouses as a sign placed there by God, not an achievement.

studies.applyIt: Pick the relationship you find hardest this month and give it one hour of plain good company. No agenda, and nothing to sort out. Not a talk about the relationship, just time spent well. This verse asks for the texture of daily life before it asks anything about feeling, and the feeling often follows.
studies.explainEasier: God tells men not to treat women as property to be passed on when a husband dies. They should not squeeze a wife to take back gifts. They should live with her kindly. What you dislike may hold much good.

studies.title: Take Nothing Back From It
studies.meaning: One move is named here and shut off. A man ends one marriage to start another, then takes back the first wife's dowry to pay for it. The sum named is huge on purpose, a word for a great heap of gold, which removes the plea that the amount was simply too big to walk away from. Then the passage stops arguing and asks a question. It names the act with two separate words, one for deceit and one for wrongdoing.
studies.historicalContext: This carries straight on from the instruction about living well with a wife, in Medina. The surah has been reordering property that moves between households at moments of change: death, division, marriage, and now parting. Early scholars report no single occasion for this verse. They read it as speaking to a known practice, not to one incident brought to the Prophet.

keyTerms.note: The verb for swapping one thing for another. The same root is used earlier in this surah for putting bad goods in place of good ones in an orphan's estate. The reuse is pointed.
A word for a huge quantity of gold, used elsewhere of wealth piled up. Naming the largest dowry anyone could picture removes the size of the sum as a reason for taking any of it back.
From a root meaning to leave someone stunned. It names the kind of lie that startles by its boldness, placing the act with slander rather than with ordinary theft.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dowry was often the only property a woman held outright, and it was visible: jewellery, cloth, sometimes camels. Taking it back at the moment of parting was easy to arrange. Household goods were mixed together, and she was the one leaving. The word for a heap of gold would have sounded almost comic to the first listeners, since most of them had never seen a dowry come near it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verse ends on a question rather than on a statement, which is rare in passages of this kind. Early scholars note that the question is not seeking information. It puts the act to the person about to commit it, and lets the naming do work that a further instruction would otherwise have had to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A wrong arranged inside the rules is treated as a lie, not as a quarrel about debt. That is the sharper claim. A man taking back a dowry could tell himself a story about what he was owed. The passage answers the story rather than the deal, and names it as something said falsely. It also refuses to scale the wrong to the size of the sum.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same question in the next verse, grounding it in the covenant the marriage created.
Establishes the dowry as a free gift, which is what makes any reclaiming of it a contradiction.
Addresses the same moment of separation and warns against taking back what was already given.

studies.applyIt: When something ends badly, notice the moment you start building the case for what you are owed. Everyone does it, and the story is usually plausible. Write it down and read it once as though a stranger had written it. Usually the sentence that will not survive that reading is the one you were about to act on.
studies.explainEasier: If a man wants to leave one wife and marry another, he does not get to take back what he gave her. The gift stays hers. That holds even when the gift was very large.

studies.title: A Solid Covenant
studies.meaning: The question from the verse before is asked again, then answered from two sides. The first is intimacy. The verb describes a coming together that leaves nothing at all in between, which makes taking a gift back afterwards look out of place. The second is a covenant, named with a word for something thick and heavy. Then the next verse shuts off marriage to a father's former wife. It names that practice with three separate words of rejection rather than one.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina. Early scholars report that marrying a father's widow was a known practice in Arabia before Islam. It was sometimes used to keep property and standing inside one family line. The words excepting what is already past spoke to unions made before the community received this. The passage belongs to the steady revision this surah makes of how households and inheritance had worked.

keyTerms.note: A verb for arriving somewhere with nothing left in between. Used of intimacy it describes the removal of every barrier, which is why reclaiming a gift afterwards is treated as out of place.
From the root for tying firmly. The same word is used of covenants God takes from the prophets, which places a marriage agreement in unexpectedly weighty company.
An adjective for physical density, used of coarse cloth and of heavy things. Applied to an agreement it suggests substance, something not easily torn or quietly set aside later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Family line ordered everything in Arabian society, and the shape of a household told everyone where it stood. A son who took his father's widow drew a family's wealth and its dependants together in one move. That is why the practice held on, though many disliked it. The word for a heavy covenant would have called to mind formal pledges between tribes, sworn in public and held to in war.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a solid covenant appears only a handful of times in the whole Quran. It is used of the pledge God took from the prophets, of the covenant made with the children of Israel, and here, of a marriage. The tradition has long noted that a household agreement is placed in exactly that company.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A duty about money is rooted here in something that is not about money at all. Rather than argue over who owns what, the passage points at what has already passed between two people, and treats that as settling the matter. Calling the marriage a heavy covenant shows that deals between people carry weight in themselves. They are not just plans to be redrawn when things change.

crossReferences.why: Poses the question this passage answers, about recovering a dowry when a marriage is ending.
Uses the same phrase for a solid covenant, there of the pledge taken from the prophets.
Describes spouses as garments for one another, another image of closeness with nothing between.

studies.applyIt: Think of a commitment you made to someone years ago that no longer suits you and that nobody would enforce. Do not cancel it this week. Instead say out loud what you actually agreed to, in the plainest words you can manage. Agreements survive far more often on being remembered accurately than on being enforced.
studies.explainEasier: A man cannot take back the gift he gave his wife. They have been close, and she holds a strong promise from him. Also, a man may not marry a woman his own father was married to.

studies.title: Where Kinship Draws A Line
studies.meaning: Most of us know without thinking who counts as family. This verse draws that line out loud, naming the women a man may not marry. Three kinds of bond appear: blood, marriage, and nursing. The third is the one that catches people. A woman who nursed a baby, along with the other children she fed, stands beside his blood relatives for life. Even the part about stepdaughters sorts the cases gently, turning on whether the marriage was consummated. Then the whole list closes on forgiveness, spoken to households already standing when it arrived.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina, right after the verse that shut off marriage to a father's former wife. The same reordering now spreads across the whole family. Early scholars note that much of the list matched what Arabian custom already kept, so most families heard nothing new. What was new was the bond through nursing and the pairing of two sisters. The closing words about what is past are read as covering marriages already made when this arrived.

keyTerms.note: The word for breastfeeding. By making it a source of kinship, the verse gives the woman who fed an infant a permanent place in his life, named beside his blood relatives.
From a root meaning to rear or bring up. The word names the girl by the upbringing she received rather than by descent, which is why the phrase about being in your care follows it.
The plural of a word for the lap, the space under someone's protection. It pictures guardianship as something physical, a child sitting close, rather than as a legal category.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Babies were often nursed by women other than their mothers, sometimes for years. In Mecca, children were sent out to desert households for their health and for their Arabic. The wet nurse's family became a second family in fact, not just in feeling. Children grew up beside another set of brothers and sisters and never stopped counting them. This verse named what those children had already lived, and gave it a word.
studies.didYouKnow: Two adults can be brother and sister through a woman neither of them remembers. Kinship through nursing has no close match in most legal traditions anywhere, and no paper records it. The classical scholars discuss at length how much nursing is enough to make the bond. They keep a real range of views rather than settling on one answer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God treats family as something made by care, not only by birth. The woman who fed you as a baby made a bond that this list sets beside blood. That says a great deal about how kinship is counted. Notice too where the verse ends. Words of forgiveness and mercy close a list of limits, spoken to people whose own households this unsettled. Limits arrive here with a door left open, and the mercy is not an afterthought.

crossReferences.why: Sets out nursing arrangements at length, including women who nurse a child other than their own.
Begins the same reordering by naming one practice, which this verse then extends into a full list.
Turns to another way of forming family, and insists that relationships be named accurately.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who raised you or fed you and is not related to you by blood. A neighbour, an aunt by kindness, a teacher, a family friend. Contact them this week. Most of us carry bonds like that for decades without ever saying so out loud, and this verse takes them seriously enough to set them beside descent.
studies.explainEasier: This lists the women a man may not marry. Some are close blood family, like a mother or a sister. Some come by marriage. And some come through nursing: the woman who fed him as a baby counts as family too.

studies.title: Marriage And What Is Given
studies.meaning: Here the list of who is off limits ends, and the verse turns to everything that lies outside it. Marriage is opened wide, with two conditions attached. Property has to change hands, and the aim has to be a settled union rather than a passing arrangement. The dowry is called a fixed due, the same word this surah uses for inheritance shares. That is a deliberate choice: a due is claimed, not requested. The verse ends by leaving the two of them free to change the amount later, if they both agree.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, this verse sat inside a long run of passages reordering marriage and property. It opens by speaking to captivity, a state found across the whole ancient world. It speaks to that world in the terms of its own day. Early scholars went through these phrases in close detail, weighing each one. What follows would have sounded familiar to anyone there. It describes the marriage the community already knew, with the dowry at its heart.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning a fortress. The word describes a woman as fortified, whether by marriage or by chastity, and early scholars read it in different senses in different places for exactly that reason.
The ordinary word for a wage, used here of the dowry. The choice keeps the payment in the language of what is owed rather than of what is kindly offered.
From a root meaning to spill water wastefully. The image is of something precious poured onto the ground, which is how the verse pictures a union entered without commitment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marriage in that world was a public deal between families, witnessed and remembered by neighbours. The dowry was the part everyone could see and name. Looser unions ran beside it, and left a woman with no claim on anything after. So property changing hands did real work: it made the marriage plain to everyone. Where a woman's standing rested on what others could confirm, being seen was protection.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this verse uses for the dowry is the same one the Quran uses for a workman's wage. It turns up again in the next verse. The tradition noticed the choice and remarked on it: this is a term drawn from the language of what is owed. Earlier in the same surah, a different word was used for the same payment, one meaning a free gift.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God anchors a marriage in two things: something given and something meant. Neither is left to be assumed. Calling the dowry a fixed due lifts it out of the realm of kindness, where a payment can be quietly trimmed and nobody complains. It becomes something a woman can claim. Then the permission to change it by agreement hands the choice back to the two people themselves. God sets the floor and leaves the rest to them.

crossReferences.why: Names the dowry a free gift, a different emphasis on the same payment earlier in this surah.
Carries on into the case of those without means, and closes by calling restraint better.
Concerns the seriousness of forming a marriage and warns against hiding your intentions along the way.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often the things you value most are the ones you never had to put anything into. This verse puts a real cost at the start of a marriage, on purpose. Take one promise you have been keeping cheaply. Put something solid into it this week: time you cannot spare, money, or a word given where others can hear it.
studies.explainEasier: This says which women a man may not marry, and then how a proper marriage works. He gives the woman a gift of his own money. He means it to last, not to be a short thing. The two of them can agree to change the amount later.

studies.title: You Are From One Another
studies.meaning: This speaks to a man who cannot afford the marriage he expected to make. In the middle of it sits a short line that cuts under the whole social ranking in play. God knows your faith best, and you are from one another. Around that line come practical things, the guardian's permission and a dowry paid fairly. Then the ending surprises you after all that detail. It says patience is better. So everything described here is offered as a way through a hard spot, never as the ideal.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in a community where servitude was a settled part of life across the whole region. The verse works inside that reality while steadily narrowing it. Early scholars read the line about shared origin as levelling the very distinction the sentence had just named. This closes the surah's long run on marriage, and the next verses turn to what God intends in giving any of it.

keyTerms.note: From the root for length and reach. The word pictures wealth as being able to stretch far enough to reach something, which frames this man's situation as a limit rather than a judgement on his worth.
Three words with no verb between them. The clause states a shared origin flatly, right in the middle of a passage about social distinction, and it offers no argument for itself.
From a root for breaking a bone that had already been set. It names a strain a person cannot carry, and that is what the allowance described here is measured against.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Servitude was ordinary across the whole region, in Byzantine and Persian lands as much as in Arabia. It was lived out in the household, day by day, among people who saw each other constantly. Marriage across that line touched a family's standing directly, and everyone knew it. Poorer men in Medina often could not raise a dowry at all. That is why the short line about shared origin lands as pointed rather than merely pious.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause saying you are from one another turns up twice in the Quran, in slightly different forms. The other time is in a passage about men and women being equal in what they strive for. Both times it breaks into an argument about social difference. Both times it is simply stated, with no support offered, as something the hearer already knows.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things happen here at once, and they are easy to miss when you read them apart. God gives a workable way through to someone in a hard spot. In the same breath, He removes the ground on which that spot was thought lower. Then restraint is called better, which places the whole allowance under something else. What you are shown is a door opened without being pushed through, and it never becomes the standard.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same clause about being from one another, there of men and women in their striving.
Meets the same difficulty of poverty in marriage, and answers it with a promise of provision.
Sets out the dowry and the seriousness of the union that this verse adapts to hard circumstances.

studies.applyIt: Find the social distinction you most quietly rely on: an accent, an income, a neighbourhood, a job title. Spend real time this week with someone on the other side of it, in their setting rather than yours. The line at the centre of this verse is not an argument but a statement. Statements like that mostly become convincing through nearness.
studies.explainEasier: If a man cannot afford to marry, he has another way open to him. God says he should not look down on the woman he marries. You all come from one another. And waiting patiently is still better.

studies.title: The Ways Of Those Before
studies.meaning: After a long stretch of detailed instruction, God says plainly what He is after. He wants to make things clear to you. He wants to guide you along the paths of those who came before. And He wants to turn toward you and take you back. The second of those is the surprise: guidance here means walking a road other people have already walked, not receiving something brand new. Early scholars read that word for ways as the practices of earlier prophets and their communities.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at the end of a long run of rules about marriage and family. Imagine hearing all that in one stretch, item after item, and feeling the weight of it. Early scholars noticed the shape of what comes next: detailed instruction, then a statement of purpose. They read the placing as an answer to that weight. What God intends is set here against what people who follow their appetites intend.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning separation, the space between two things. In Arabic, clarity is pictured as things being set apart from one another rather than as light being shone on them.
The plural of a word for a worn track or a customary practice. It suggests a road made by repeated walking, which is why guidance here means joining something rather than starting it.
The verb of returning, used here of God turning toward people. Set beside clarity and guidance, it makes forgiveness part of the same act as instruction rather than a separate mercy alongside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A desert path was never built. It was worn, made by caravans crossing the same ground for generations. To follow one was to trust people you would never meet, and losing the track was the real danger of any journey. Guides were hired for their memory of what earlier travellers had done. The word this verse uses for a way carries exactly that sense: a route proved by use.
studies.didYouKnow: Three verses in a row here begin by saying that God intends something. Each names a different aim: to make clear, to turn toward you, and to lighten your load.
