Nothing else in this surah repeats an opening three times running. Early scholars read the run as a chosen answer to the sheer length of the instructions before it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance here is carrying on, not starting fresh. That places you inside a long history rather than at the head of it. God also has aims toward people, and He names them out loud. Instruction is not simply handed down; it is pointed at something. And that something includes being turned toward and taken back. Clarity, direction and pardon arrive together, as one movement rather than three favours.

crossReferences.why: Carries the sequence on with two more intentions, including the lightening of the burden people carry.
Describes distinct paths given to different communities, all measured against one and the same truth.
Names the religion given to earlier prophets as the same one enjoined here, stressing continuity.

studies.applyIt: When something you have been asked to do feels arbitrary, look for who has done it before you. Ask an older person in your family or community how they handled the thing you are struggling with now. This verse describes guidance as a track worn by other feet. Most of what you meet has been met already, usually by someone still nearby.
studies.explainEasier: God wants to make things clear to you. He wants to show you the paths that good people walked before you. And He wants to turn to you and take you back. He knows what He is doing.

studies.title: Created Weak
studies.meaning: God wants two things for you here, and someone else wants the opposite. He intends to accept you and to lighten what you carry. Those who follow their appetites want you to swerve, and the word means a whole person tilting off line, not one misstep. Then comes the reason for the lightening, and it is not about your circumstances. Human beings were made weak. Early scholars read that as a plain description of how people are put together, not as an excuse being offered for them.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at the close of a long run on marriage and the household, where a statement of purpose now lands. Early scholars tie the mention of those who follow their appetites to real opposition the community was meeting. Some people wanted the new arrangements dropped. So the passage sets out two directions, and the community was being pulled both ways at once. Scholars do not read it as a report of one incident.

keyTerms.note: The verb for tilting off a straight line, used of a wall out of true. It describes a slow drift rather than a decision, which is why it fits people being pulled by appetite.
A causative form from the root for lightness. It implies a weight that is real and stays real, made lighter rather than taken away, which shapes how the words after it are read.
A plain adjective, said of the human being with nothing attached to soften it. Early scholars note that it comes as a fact of creation rather than as a fault, which changes what follows.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Loads were measured against the animal carrying them. A good handler knew what a camel could bear, and over what distance, before it gave out. Too much weight was a real danger on a long stage of the road. Drivers lightened the packs at the last well before crossing open country. So hearing that God intends to lighten came out of that daily world, where the load was admitted rather than denied.
studies.didYouKnow: The words saying the human being was created weak are three words in Arabic. That is among the shortest full claims about human nature anywhere in the Quran. It sits at the end of a long passage of detailed instruction. So demanding material closes by granting how hard people find such things.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Your weakness is stated as a fact of how you were made. That lifts it out of the language of blame, and the result matters. If the instruction is given to a creature made weak, the instruction is cut to fit that creature. You are not being measured against some standard set apart from you. The passage also gives desire aims of its own, pulling in a direction, rather than treating it as a simple lack of discipline.

crossReferences.why: Says God does not burden a soul beyond what it can bear, the same idea from another angle.
Says no hardship has been placed on this community in religion, closing another passage of instruction.
Opens this sequence with the first stated intention, to make things clear and to guide.

studies.applyIt: Take the demand you place on yourself that you have failed most often, and cut it down to something you know you can hold. Not as a defeat. God's own stated intention here is to lighten, and the creature being addressed was made weak. Being steady at a smaller size is nearer the point than collapsing at a larger one.
studies.explainEasier: God wants to accept you and to make things easier for you. People who chase what they want would rather see you go badly wrong. God knows that people were made weak, so He makes the load lighter.

studies.title: Do Not Consume One Another
studies.meaning: Two very different harms sit side by side here with nothing joining them: taking each other's property wrongly, and killing. Early scholars read that pairing as chosen rather than accidental. What is allowed instead is trade both sides are happy with. So contentment becomes the dividing line, not the shape a deal happens to take. The words about killing are read two ways in the tradition. One is killing one another, since a community is one body. The other is destroying yourself, and both readings are kept.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, a settled trading town, and the long run on marriage has just ended. A short passage on property and life opens here instead. New arrangements were being worked out and older practices questioned, all at once. Early scholars report no single occasion for this verse. It speaks to believers as a group, and its subject is what members of one community do to each other rather than to outsiders.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be void or to come to nothing. It names a deal with no real basis under it, which covers deception and pressure alike without having to list them.
A shared form from the root for contentment. Both sides have to be pleased and not merely agreeing, which sets a standard well above consent won under pressure.
The word means a person's own self and also one's own people. That double sense is what allows the classical reading covering both self-destruction and killing within the community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina's economy ran on face-to-face bargaining. Prices were settled by haggling, with no fixed rates anywhere in the market. A hard bargain and a fraud could look much the same from outside. Disputes over sales were common enough that the market kept its own customs for settling them. Blood feuds worked at the level of the group, so one killing pulled in whole families for years.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse moves from trade to killing inside a single sentence, with no bridge at all. Early scholars notice the join and leave it standing rather than smoothing it over. Property taken wrongly and blood spilled are treated as one kind of harm inside a community. That is why the closing words name God's mercy toward the group, not toward the single person.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Making mutual contentment the test puts the weight on how both parties actually feel. It does not put it on the outward form of an agreement. So a contract drawn up correctly, but signed under pressure, fails. Then the pairing with killing sets a scale you can feel. A community's wealth and its lives belong to one order, and cheating a member is placed beside taking a life.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly the same wording about consuming property wrongfully, and adds bribing officials to get it.
Treats the killing of one person as the killing of all, widening the logic of this pairing.
States the consequence for doing this out of hostility, right after the instruction itself.

studies.applyIt: Look at one arrangement you are in where the other side agreed but was not really pleased: a price you pushed, a favour they could not refuse, a deal struck when they had no options. Reopen it this week and offer something back. The standard here is not that they consented. It is that both of you are content.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people not to take each other's money in a false way. Buying and selling is fine when both sides are happy with the deal. And do not kill each other, or yourselves. God cares about you.

studies.title: The Gate Of Honour
studies.meaning: These two verses sort outcomes by motive first and by scale second. The Fire is tied not simply to the act just named, but to doing it out of hostility and wrongdoing. So what a person meant is what the sentence turns on. Then comes a wide pardon. Avoid the gravest of what has been shut off, and the rest is covered. Early scholars have long argued about which wrongs count as grave, and they hand down differing lists rather than one agreed set.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, right after the instruction about property and life inside the community. Early scholars note the rhythm the surah keeps here: a serious instruction, then a result, then an opening. No occasion is reported for either verse. Both speak to people taking in a large body of new material all at once. They needed to know what happens when they fall short of parts of it.

keyTerms.note: From the root for crossing a boundary against somebody. It names the attitude behind an act rather than the act itself, which is why the verse can tell two people apart who did the same thing.
A comparative form meaning the greater. The category is named without being listed, and classical scholars discuss its contents at length while agreeing that a real boundary exists.
A noun of place from the verb to enter. The reward is described as a doorway rather than a destination, which leaves whatever lies beyond it entirely unstated here.
An adjective carrying nobility and open-handedness together. Applied to an entrance it suggests the manner of the welcome rather than the size of the gate or what waits behind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A city gate was where a person's standing showed. Who met you, whether you were kept waiting, which entrance you used: all of it was public, and all of it was remembered. Groups arriving in Medina were received at known points. The honour of an arrival lay in the welcome, not in the place you had reached. Anyone who had walked into a strange town as a stranger understood the picture at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names grave sins as a separate class several times and never once gives a closed list of them. The classical scholars drew up lists that differ a great deal in length. Some run to a handful; some run to dozens. Most of them treated that open edge as intended rather than as something missing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Read together, these two verses say the moral life is not checked off item by item. A line exists, and staying on the right side of it draws everything smaller along with it. That is a claim about proportion, and it cuts against two errors at once. One is treating every slip as a disaster. The other is treating none of them as serious. Motive decides the first verse; scale decides the second.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who avoid grave sins and indecencies apart from small lapses, and God's wide forgiveness.
Names avoiding grave sins and indecencies as a mark of those who trust their Lord.
Gives the instruction about wealth and life whose breach in hostility this passage answers.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list of the things you would count as serious if someone else did them to you. Keep it to five. Then notice that most of your worry sits elsewhere, on smaller things you can name easily. This passage sorts by weight for a reason, and attention paid to the top of that list is worth more than anxiety spread evenly across it.
studies.explainEasier: If someone breaks these rules out of spite, God says there is a fire waiting. But if you stay away from the worst wrongs, God will wipe out the smaller ones. He will bring you in through a gate of honour.

studies.title: Do Not Covet Another's Share
studies.meaning: Everyone knows the sting of seeing what someone else was given. This verse names that sting and puts a limit around it. The limit falls on wishing for the particular thing another person has, not on wanting a good life. Early scholars keep that distinction carefully. Wanting the like of what your neighbour has is not what is named here. Wanting it taken from him is. Then two matching lines give men and women each what they have earned. The verse sends the whole urge outward: ask God for His bounty instead of measuring it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina, and this line sits in a long passage on property, inheritance and household rights. Early scholars report an occasion behind it. Women asked about the difference in inheritance shares, and about the reward for going out to fight. The reports vary in their detail. What came back does not settle the comparison at all. It changes what the questioner is invited to do with the feeling.

keyTerms.note: A verb for wishing something into being, formed from the root for a wish. It describes an inward act rather than a demand, which is why the verse speaks to the imagination before any behaviour.
A portion cut off and set aside, used of a share in an inheritance or of the part of an animal that falls to you. The word assumes a division that has already been made.
A form of the verb for earning that implies deliberate effort on your own account. Using it of women and of men in identical lines gives each the same relation to what they gain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was visible in a way it rarely is now. It showed in the number of date palms a family held, the camels in the yard, who ate meat and how often. Neighbours knew each other's holdings down to the tree. In a small oasis town, comparison was not an occasional temptation. It was the standing condition of daily life, and a family's fortune could turn in a single season.
studies.didYouKnow: Men and women get matching lines here, built from the very same verb. The Quran does this in several places, stating something twice with only the gender changed. Surah 33 does it at greater length in its thirty-fifth verse, running ten such pairs in one sentence. The repetition is deliberate: Arabic could have used a single plural covering both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God treats your wanting as something with a direction, not as a quantity to be reduced. You are not asked to want less. You are asked to turn and speak to the One who gave, which quietly turns a comparison into a request. And the closing words, that God knows everything, are not a threat here. They are a reason. The share-out was made by someone with the full picture, which is exactly what you lack when you compare.

crossReferences.why: Tells the Prophet not to strain his eyes toward what others have been given to enjoy.
Says God apportions livelihood and raises some above others so they may serve one another.
Describes the same unequal sharing out of provision and turns it toward giving rather than envy.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you scroll past something that stings. Instead of closing the app, say one specific thing you would want, as a request rather than a comparison. Say it out loud if you can. This verse does not ask you to stop wanting. It asks you to change who you are talking to.
studies.explainEasier: Do not wish you had what someone else was given. Men get what they earn and women get what they earn. If you want more, ask God for it.

studies.title: Give Them Their Share
studies.meaning: Heirs arrive here as assigned, not chosen. The word behind them means those closely bound to a person, the ones already tied to your life. Then comes the harder part of the verse, about people joined by a sworn agreement rather than by blood. Early scholars differ over what it points to. Some read a pact of mutual inheritance from before the community began. Some read the bond tied between the emigrants and the hosts who took them in. Some read a general duty to keep whatever you swore.
studies.historicalContext: When the emigrants first reached Medina, each newcomer was paired with a local host. Early scholars report that for a time the two inherited from one another, like brothers. Then the shares set out earlier in this surah took priority. This verse is read against that arrangement. The reports differ over whether it confirmed the old practice or kept a narrower duty alive inside it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for nearness and mutual support. The word covers a patron, a client, an ally and a relative at once, which is why early scholars read this clause in several different ways.
The verb for tying a knot, used of agreements. It pictures a commitment as something physically fastened, which is why a broken agreement is elsewhere described as an untying.
From the root for being present. God is named as present to everything rather than as informed about it, which places the closing words about agreements under constant watch.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society ran on pacts as much as on blood. Two men could swear mutual support and inheritance before witnesses, and that tied their households together for life. The emigrants who reached Medina came with nothing at all. They were paired with hosts who fed and housed them. Those pairings were not warm gestures only; they carried real claims on property, and this verse speaks straight into that arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: An inheritance claim and a knotted rope are named by one family of words in Arabic. The word for those tied by agreement comes from a root about knots. The same three letters give the language its word for a contract and its word for a cord. The physical picture stays inside the term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God sets chosen bonds beside given ones and does not treat the chosen as lesser. Blood assigns your heirs. An oath makes duties that are just as much to be kept. The pointed part is that God is named here as witness rather than as judge. Agreements between people are held mostly by memory and by shame. This verse adds a party to every one of them who does not forget.

crossReferences.why: Describes the bond between emigrants and their hosts, and the mutual protection it created.
Opens by calling believers to fulfil their contracts, the same instinct stated as a general rule.
Sets out the assigned shares this verse points back to, of what parents and relatives leave.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise you made informally, without paperwork, to someone who could not hold you to it: help with a move, a loan, an introduction, time you said you would give. Do it this week. The closing words here are not a threat. They note that someone was present when you said it, and that He remembers exactly what you said.
studies.explainEasier: God has set who gets a share of what parents and relatives leave behind. If you made a promise to someone else about this, keep it and give them their share. God was there and saw it all.

studies.title: Seek No Way Against Them
studies.meaning: A household has to be kept, and this verse opens by placing that duty on men. It gives two grounds for that: what God has given out differently, and what is spent from a man's wealth. Upright women are described next. Then the verse turns to a marriage in serious breakdown, and sets out a graded sequence of responses. Every stage of it is fenced in by the words that close the passage, which cut off any further step the moment the breach ends. Early scholars go through each term at length and differ over how far it reaches.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, a complaint was brought to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). A woman had been struck. Early scholars record his answer as one of strong disapproval, and they also pass on that he never struck a woman in his life. The verse sits inside a long run of passages reordering household relations. The verse straight after it moves the same situation out of the home and into arbitration between two families.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the verb to stand. It carries responsibility and upkeep rather than rank, and the verse grounds it in what is spent rather than in any claim about worth.
From a root meaning raised ground. It names a rupture in the marriage rather than ordinary disagreement, and the very same word is applied to a husband later in this surah.

The verb has an unusually wide range in Arabic, from travelling to setting forth an example. Early scholars discuss its scope here at length, and the tradition constrains it heavily by prophetic practice.

keyTerms.gloss: seek no way, do not press
keyTerms.note: A verb for seeking or pursuing, carrying a sense of overreach. It shuts off every earlier stage the instant the breach ends, leaving no grievance to be carried forward afterwards.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A marriage in seventh-century Arabia was a deal between two families as much as between two people. A household in trouble was everybody's business. A wife had her own kin living nearby, and they would hear of any ill treatment fast. Their own standing was caught up in how she was treated. The verse that follows brings both families straight into the room, which is how such matters were actually settled.
studies.didYouKnow: The same word for a breach in a marriage is used of a husband later in this surah. There a wife who fears it from her husband is told that a settlement between them is better. The tradition reads the two passages together, precisely because one term covers both parties rather than two different terms.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage ends on two names of God, the Exalted and the Great. Early scholars read them as spoken to the husband. Whatever authority the sentence describes, someone stands above him. That move comes back again and again in this surah: instructions about power over dependants end by naming a power over the one being instructed. And the last words make the aim plain. It is putting things right, not being obeyed.

crossReferences.why: Moves the same breakdown out of the household and into arbitration by one relative from each family.
Uses the same term for a breach when the fear is a wife's, and calls settlement better.
Names tranquillity, affection and mercy as the purpose for which spouses were created at all.

studies.applyIt: In your closest relationship, notice what you do at the moment a disagreement ends. Most damage in a household is done afterwards, in the carrying forward of grievance. The last instruction here is to stop completely once the breach has closed. Try that once this week, deliberately and visibly, and watch what it changes.
studies.explainEasier: Men are told to look after women and to pay for the home. Good wives keep what God wants kept. If a marriage breaks down badly, the verse gives steps to take. The moment things are put right, all of it stops.

studies.title: One From Each Family
studies.meaning: When a marriage is in serious trouble, this verse gives a method, and the shape of it is deliberate. Two arbiters, one from each side, so that neither husband nor wife faces a panel. The word used names people who judge, not people who merely mediate, and early scholars discuss how far their decision binds. The condition that follows is put in the dual. Scholars differ over whether it points to the arbiters or to the couple themselves. Either way, what the outcome hangs on is intention.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, and this comes right after the passage on marriage breakdown. Early scholars read the placing as telling: a private trouble is moved on purpose into the hands of both families. Households there sat inside kin networks that already settled disputes among themselves. This verse gives that standing capacity a set shape. No particular occasion is reported for it in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: From the root for splitting something in two, which also gives the word for a half. It pictures a marriage as one thing coming apart rather than as two people in disagreement.
From the root that gives wisdom and judgement. The word is stronger than mediator; it names someone whose decision carries weight, which is why the appointment is treated so seriously.
From a root for two things fitting together. The verb is used of God here, so a human arrangement is described as making room for something only God is said to accomplish.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in Arabian society were settled by respected figures from the families involved. Their judgements held because both sides had agreed to them beforehand. There were no courts in the modern sense. Taking one arbiter from each household meant neither family could claim the process had been captured, and it bound them both to the outcome once it was reached.
studies.didYouKnow: One clause here mirrors the other word for word: an arbiter from his family, an arbiter from her family. That balance runs through this surah's handling of marriage. It builds sentences in matched halves again and again, so a listener hears both parties named inside one shape.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A marriage belongs partly to the people around it, and this verse says so. Privacy is not the highest value when a household is failing. The deciding factor is put in intention rather than in procedure. Arbiters can be named and the meeting held, and none of it works unless somebody actually wants it to. Then the outcome is handed to God rather than to the process.

crossReferences.why: Describes the situation this verse answers, and is closed off by the arbitration set out here.
Offers settlement as the better outcome when a wife fears a breach from her husband.
Applies the same instinct to conflict between groups of believers, calling for reconciliation between them.

studies.applyIt: When two people you know are in conflict, resist becoming the third voice on one side. If you are asked in, ask whether someone from the other side is being asked in too. The design here is not neutrality but symmetry. Most attempts at helping fail because only one party is ever represented.
studies.explainEasier: If a husband and wife are falling apart, pick one fair person from his family and one from hers. Let them sit down and try to fix it. If the two of them truly want peace, God will bring them back together.

studies.title: The Widening Circle Of Kindness
studies.meaning: One command about God comes first, and then a list that widens in rings around you. Parents, relatives, orphans, the poor. Then the near neighbour, the far neighbour, the companion at your side, the traveller, and those your right hands possess. Early scholars differ over what near and far mean for a neighbour, reading the pair as kinship, as distance, or as shared faith. The list ends not with another group but with a character: the strutting boaster whom God does not love.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, this verse sits in a section about how a household treats everyone with a claim on it. Passages about the property of orphans come just before it, and warnings about holding wealth back come just after. So it stands inside an argument about money as much as about manners. Classical commentaries record no single occasion for it. They read it as a summary, one of several places where this surah gathers scattered duties into one sentence.

keyTerms.note: More than fairness. The root means to do something well and to do it beautifully, so the word asks for a quality of treatment that nobody could demand as a right.
The same root gives the word for a protected person under someone's guarantee. A neighbour in that world was not merely someone nearby; the word carried an implied claim to shelter.

From a root connected with imagination and with horses, describing a person who moves as though watched. It names a bearing rather than a belief, which is why it closes a list about the treatment of others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Houses in Medina were built wall to wall around shared courtyards. A family's cooking smoke, its quarrels and its illnesses were public property. Water came from shared wells, so a household in difficulty could not hide it for long. The neighbour in this list was a person whose food supply you could see. The companion at your side has been read as anyone you travel or sit beside for a while.
studies.didYouKnow: The person you happen to be sitting next to appears in the same sentence as your mother and father. The list runs to nine groups, and it moves outward by closeness rather than by importance: blood, then need, then nearness, then chance. One single word governs the whole series.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Worship and how you treat people sit in one sentence under one verb, which refuses any split between piety and conduct. The ordering makes its own claim: what you owe weakens with distance but never stops. The list keeps going past everyone a tribal society would have counted as owed anything. And closing on arrogance names the bearing that makes the whole list impossible to keep.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the same widening obligation, beginning with parents and reaching the traveller.
Gives an earlier version of the list as a covenant taken from the Children of Israel.
Uses the same word for strutting, warning against turning your cheek away from people.

studies.applyIt: Find out one thing this week about a neighbour you would not recognise in a shop. A name, a job, whether they live alone. You are not starting a friendship. This verse places the person on the other side of your wall in a list with your parents, and learning their name is the smallest way of taking that seriously.
studies.explainEasier: Worship God alone. Then be good to your parents, your family, orphans and poor people. Be good to the neighbour next door and the one further away, to the friend beside you, and to anyone travelling.

studies.title: Teaching Others To Withhold
studies.meaning: Three habits are named here as one pattern. You hold back what you have, you urge other people to hold back too, and you hide what God gave you so that nobody can make a claim on it. The middle habit is the surprise, because meanness is usually thought of as a private thing. Here it recruits. Early scholars note that a person holding back wants company in it, since generosity going on nearby makes his own tight fist visible.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, just after a verse listing everyone to whom good conduct is owed, inside a short run about the proud and the showy. Early scholars link this to opponents of the community who talked others out of helping it. They also link it to people who hid their means to avoid giving. No single incident is reported, so the description is read as general.

keyTerms.note: From a root for tightness and constriction. Arabic pictures the miser as narrowed rather than as merely unwilling, which is why the Quran often sets generosity against expansion instead of against loss.
The verb for suppressing information, used elsewhere of hiding testimony or knowledge. Applied to wealth it makes concealment a form of untruth rather than a matter of simple privacy.
From a root meaning what is left over and abundant. Naming wealth as surplus from God rather than as earnings quietly removes the ground on which withholding would otherwise be justified.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was hard to hide and easy to guess at. Neighbours knew how many palms a family held and how the harvest had gone. So hiding it took social forms instead. A man complained about a poor season, kept goods out of sight, talked down his means at the right moment. Everyone recognised the performance, and this verse names the performance rather than the sum.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact pairing here, holding back and then urging others to hold back, turns up a second time in the Quran. The wording is almost the same, in a later surah about spending. Early scholars treat the repeat as marking a known type rather than a passing description. That is part of why the second habit carries so much weight.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What God names here is a social mechanism, not a private fault. Holding back needs cover, and the surest cover is other people doing the same. So meanness spreads itself in order to stay safe. Then calling wealth a bounty received, rather than property earned, pulls away the ground the whole pattern rests on. Hiding is set beside it as a kind of lie.

crossReferences.why: Warns those who hoard what God gave from His bounty that it will encircle them instead.
Names the opposite failure in the very next verse, spending so as to be seen by people.
Contrasts the one who withholds and thinks himself self-sufficient with the one who gives.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you talk down what you have, in a conversation where someone might be about to ask for something. Everyone does it, usually without deciding to. You do not have to give anything on the spot. Just say the true number, or nothing at all, and see how much of the reflex was really about money.
studies.explainEasier: Some people hold on tight to their money. They also push other people to hold back, and they hide what God has given them. God says there is a shameful punishment waiting for those who refuse to believe.

studies.title: Spending To Be Seen
studies.meaning: A second failure comes right after the first, and it looks like the opposite of it. Here the money is given, not held back. But the audience is people rather than God, and nothing is believed underneath it. The verse gives that giving no partial credit at all. Then it names the companion who walks with such a person, using a word for someone who sits close and travels alongside. It closes on a short cry about that company.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside a short run describing the conduct of the community's opponents. Early scholars link this to people who spent openly on feasts and alliances with nothing believed behind it. They note that the surah has just described the opposite failure. No particular occasion is reported for it. The passage is read as a portrait rather than as a report of one incident.

keyTerms.note: From the verb to see. The word makes the audience part of the act itself, so the spending is not merely observed but shaped by being observed, from the moment it is planned.
From a root meaning to join two things together, used of a yoked pair. It describes closeness that has become permanent, which is why the cry at the end of the verse lands as heavily as it does.
A verb from a root also connected with a tunnel having two openings. It carries the sense of something passing through and out, so wealth is pictured as moving rather than as resting.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Giving was the most publicly rewarded virtue in Arabia, and reputations were built on it. Feasts were counted. Camels killed for guests were remembered in poetry for years. A man's standing rose plainly with what he gave away. In a place keeping such careful accounts of generosity, spending to be seen was nothing odd; it was the ordinary logic of the culture.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for showing off here comes from the same root as the word for sight. It is built on a form that means something done back and forth, and that build carries the point. Giver and audience are performing to each other. Both of them are needed for the deal to work at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The outward shape of an act does not settle its worth. The same coin given makes two different things, depending on what the giver wanted. Value sits in intention rather than in effect. That is a hard claim about you, and the verse softens it in no way at all. It also treats a settled turn of mind as company you keep, something you have rather than something you do.

crossReferences.why: Compares charity given for show to soil on a rock, washed clean away by rain.
Describes those who pray to be seen and withhold small kindnesses, joining the two failures together.
Names the opposite failure in the previous verse, withholding and urging others to withhold.

studies.applyIt: Give something away this week that nobody will find out about, and take some trouble to keep it that way. Not because being seen ruins a gift; much good giving is properly public. Do it once as a test. Notice how much of your usual drive was quietly resting on being known for it.
studies.explainEasier: Some people give money away just so others will see them do it. They do not really believe in God or in the Last Day. The verse says the devil is with them, and he is a very bad friend to have.

studies.title: What Would They Have Lost
studies.meaning: A question is put here, and its force lies in how little it asks. Not what these people would have gained, but what it would have cost them. The verse stands where someone pricing belief and generosity stands, and it answers that the ledger is empty on that side. The closing words are quieter than they look. God knows them well, which early scholars read as covering both the excuses offered aloud and the reasons lying underneath.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at the close of the short run on holding back and on giving for show. Early scholars note that the question is asked about people rather than put to them. So the community overhears an argument made about others, and applies it to itself. The surah has been building a picture of two failures around wealth, and this verse folds both into one question.

keyTerms.note: A construction using the preposition of burden, so the question is literally what would be upon them. It frames belief and spending as a possible cost, and then leaves the answer unstated.
The verb for granting sustenance, used of God supplying what a creature lives on. Its choice makes the spending a redirection of something received rather than a subtraction from something owned.
An intensive form of the word for knowledge. Placed at the end of a question about motives, it suggests the answer is already available and the question is asked for the hearer's sake.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Giving in that economy carried real risk. A bad season could arrive with no warning, and a family that had been generous in a good year had no reserve to fall back on. For a farmer with one grove, the question about cost was not a figure of speech. It was the sum he worked out every year. The verse answers it by naming where the harvest came from.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of a small number of verses in the Quran built entirely as a question, with no answer stated. Early scholars note that the form does work a flat claim could not. A statement invites disagreement, while a question of this kind makes the hearer supply the missing answer. And only one answer is there to supply.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God reframes what belief actually costs you. It looked like a loss. It turns out to be the moving on of something you were given in the first place, so the sum you were doing rested on the wrong starting figure. Then the closing name for God's knowledge adds one more thing. People rarely refuse for the reasons they give out loud, and the real ones are visible anyway.

crossReferences.why: Calls for spending from what was provided, before a day arrives with no bargaining in it.
Shows someone at death asking for delay so he can give, having refused while there was time.
Describes the spending that fails despite being generous, which this question sets against real giving.

studies.applyIt: Take the thing you have been meaning to give and have not: money, an hour, an apology, an introduction. Write down what it would actually cost you, in specific terms. Not what it would gain anyone, just the cost, honestly stated. Usually the written figure turns out far smaller than the resistance you have been feeling about it.
studies.explainEasier: They lose nothing by believing in God and the Last Day. They lose nothing by giving away some of what God gave them. God knows them very well.

studies.title: A Witness From Every Community
studies.meaning: Two claims are joined here, and the first is about scale. Injustice is denied right down to the weight of the smallest speck. Good is not simply repaid but multiplied, with something further added on top of the reckoning. Then the frame changes. A scene opens in which each community's own witness is brought forward. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is addressed straight, in the second person, so this is put to him rather than said about him.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, early scholars report that the second of these two verses was recited in front of the Prophet. He asked the reciter to stop, moved by what he heard. The passage follows one about those who spend for show and those who hold back. So the reckoning described here answers what such spending is actually worth.

keyTerms.note: The smallest quantity the language could name, a mote of dust or the tiniest ant. The denial of injustice is pitched at that scale rather than at the scale of significant wrongs.
A verb for doubling repeatedly rather than once. Set against the denial of injustice, it makes the two sides of the account deliberately uneven rather than evenly balanced.
From the root for presence. A witness testifies to what he was there for, so the word implies the prophets are brought as people who were present, not as advocates and not as judges.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Justice in that world rested on testimony, because there were almost no documents. A case turned on who would stand up and say what they had seen. False witness was among the gravest offences, since everything rested on it. Witnesses were chosen for their standing, and being named as one was an honour and a burden at the same time. That is the picture the second verse draws on.
studies.didYouKnow: A well-known report describes the Prophet asking a companion to recite from this surah. When the man reached the verse about being brought as a witness, he told him to stop. His eyes were filling with tears. The tradition keeps the account as a sign of how heavily the charge of witnessing over a community was felt.
studies.theologicalSignificance: These two verses set exactness against generosity and let both stand. Nothing you did is lost, down to the smallest measure. Yet the return is not matched but multiplied, which makes exact justice the floor rather than the whole account. The witness scene then adds something else. Judgement is not carried out in the abstract. It comes through people who were there, and who stand in some relation to those being judged.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same measure on both sides: an atom's weight of good or of evil will be seen.
Describes a witness raised from every community, with one brought as a witness over them.
Names this community as witnesses over people, with the Messenger as a witness over them.

studies.applyIt: Think of the smallest good thing you did this week that nobody noticed and that you have already half forgotten. Hold it in mind for a moment without deciding it was too small to count. The first of these verses is about scale. Its claim is that nothing at all falls below the line of being counted.
studies.explainEasier: God is never unfair, not even by the weight of a speck. When you do something good, He doubles it and gives more on top. One day every group will have someone stand up and speak about them.

studies.title: Level With The Earth
studies.meaning: What the verse describes is a wish, not a punishment. On that day some people will want the ground closed over them. The verb suggests being smoothed flat into it, wiped out rather than merely hidden. Then comes the reason the wish arrives. Nothing at all can be kept back from God. Early scholars read the two halves as joined: the urge to vanish follows straight from the fact that nothing can be hidden.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, right after the scene in which a witness is brought from every community. The order of the two matters. The wish described here is a reaction to that scene, not to any punishment. The surah has been speaking to people who worked out carefully what they showed and what they held back. This verse shows the moment when all that working out comes to an end.

keyTerms.note: A verb for smoothing a surface until nothing stands out on it. The wish is not to hide beneath the ground but to be made continuous with it, which is a wish for erasure.
The same verb used earlier in this surah of hiding what God had given. Its reappearance links the showy and the miserly to this scene by way of a single repeated word.
The ordinary word for speech or a report. Its indefinite form here means not one utterance, which puts the emphasis on how complete the disclosure is rather than on its content.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burial in that landscape left a raised mound. Graves were marked so the living could find them again. To be levelled with the earth was to leave no trace at all. In a society that kept lineage and name alive through memory, that was the worst end anyone could picture. Poets threatened their enemies with being forgotten. The wish described here turns over everything such a society prized.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran records several different wishes made on the Day of Judgement, and together they form a pattern. To return, to be dust, to be ransomed, to be levelled with the earth. Each one is impossible in a different way. And none of them asks for what had been open earlier, while there was still time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The terror of judgement here is in being seen, not in pain. What cannot be borne is that everything is known and nothing can be kept back. The answer to that is a wish not to exist at all. That says something about what your hiding was doing all along. It was not really keeping facts from other people. It was holding up a version of you, and that version does not survive being seen.

crossReferences.why: Describes the denier wishing he were dust, the same wish for erasure at the same moment.
Portrays those who arrange what others see of them, which this scene brings to an end.
Says God has recorded what they forgot, while they themselves have forgotten it entirely.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing whose telling you currently manage. Not a secret exactly, just something you shape a little whenever it comes up. Say the plain version of it to one person you trust this week. The relief people report from doing that is out of all proportion, and it is the same relief this verse describes arriving too late.
studies.explainEasier: On that day, people who turned away from God and from His Messenger will wish the ground would swallow them up. They will want to be made flat with the earth. They will not be able to hide one word from God.

studies.title: Until You Know What You Say
studies.meaning: Conditions are set on coming to prayer, and the reason given for the first is unusual. So that you know what you are saying. That makes it a concern about the words, not a verdict on the state itself. The rest deals with the difficulty of water. Where none can be found, clean earth stands in its place. Early scholars note that instruction on this subject came in stages, and that a later passage finished the matter.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in a community where drinking was ordinary and social. Early scholars report that the teaching about strong drink came by stages rather than all at once. They place this verse inside that sequence. They also report a journey on which a group was left with no water. That report is linked with the allowance given here. The sources agree on the general setting.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be blocked or stopped up, the same one that gives the word for a dam. Arabic pictures intoxication as an obstruction of the faculties rather than as an addition to them.
A word for the surface of the ground, dust or soil. Its use makes the substitute universally available, since the one thing a traveller in that landscape always had underfoot was earth.
An intensive form from a root meaning to erase or efface a trace. It suggests not merely overlooking a fault but removing the mark of it, which is why it often appears alongside forgiveness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water set the limit of every journey. Wells stood days apart, and their yield was never sure. A caravan that missed one saved what it carried for drinking alone. Washing was a luxury of settled life, not of the road. So a rule using clean earth was no mere symbol out there. It was the difference between a practice that travelled and one that did not.
studies.didYouKnow: Instruction about intoxicants came in three separate stages, across three different surahs, each going further than the one before. This verse is the middle of the three. The tradition treats the sequence as a chosen method, and early scholars point to it when explaining why guidance on hard matters came by degrees.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are being held together here at the same time. A standard is set for the state you stand in before God, and at once a provision is made for anyone who cannot meet its physical conditions. Neither of them cancels the other out. The passage also grounds its first concern in understanding rather than in propriety. What matters is that the words being spoken are understood by the person speaking them.

crossReferences.why: Gives the first stage of the same instruction, weighing benefit against harm without closing the matter.
Restates the provision using clean earth when water cannot be found, in fuller terms.
Concerns the manner of speech in prayer, neither loud nor silent, another concern with how one speaks.

studies.applyIt: Before your next prayer, take ten seconds to recall what the words you are about to say actually mean. Not to perfect your recitation. Just to arrive at them knowing what they are. The stated concern of this verse is understanding, and for most of us that is the first thing to slip away.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people not to come to prayer when their minds are fogged by drink, so they know what they are saying. He tells them to wash first. If they are sick or travelling with no water, clean earth on the face and hands will do.

studies.title: God Is Sufficient As Protector
studies.meaning: A group who received a portion of earlier scripture is described as choosing error, and wanting others to lose the way. The wording is careful in two ways. It says a portion rather than the whole, and it names a group among them rather than all of them. What follows is not a counter-argument. It simply states that God knows who the opponents are. Then comes an assurance, said twice over, that God is enough.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina the community lived beside older faith groups, and relations were sometimes tense. Early scholars describe attempts to unsettle new believers by argument and by mockery. This passage belongs to a longer section on that setting. Its wording always names a group, never a whole people, and early scholars take care to keep that limit.

keyTerms.note: The same word this surah used of inheritance shares. Saying a portion of the Book rather than the Book keeps the description limited, which early scholars treat as deliberate rather than incidental.
The verb for a commercial exchange. Describing error as bought means something was paid for it, so misguidance appears as a transaction entered into rather than a condition merely suffered.
From a root meaning nearness. The word covers a guardian, an ally and a friend at once, so the assurance offered is relational rather than merely a promise of safety.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Arabia was a formal thing. A traveller or a small group survived by being under someone's declared guarantee. Losing a protector could be fatal. Alliances were announced in public, and their withdrawal was public too. To say that God is enough as a protector was to use the exact words of that system. It was addressed to people who had lost their human guarantees by joining the community.
studies.didYouKnow: The assurance in the second of these verses is stated twice in the same shape, with only the final word changed. Arabic could easily have joined the two nouns inside one clause. Repeating the whole phrase gives each half its own weight. The same doubled build turns up elsewhere in the Quran at moments of reassurance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer to hostility here is not argument and not revenge. It is reassurance, and that is a choice. Opponents are answered by being placed inside God's knowledge rather than by being argued with. The two names given, protector and helper, meet the two things a small community under pressure actually lacks. It lacks someone with the standing to shelter it, and someone who will act.

crossReferences.why: Balances this description by naming an upright group among the same communities who stand in prayer.
Repeats the assurance that God suffices as a trustee, in another passage of pressure and opposition.
Describes persistent attempts to turn believers away, and points them back to God's guidance instead.

studies.applyIt: When someone tries to unsettle what you believe, notice your urge to win the argument. This passage answers hostility by naming who is enough, not by proving anybody wrong. Try leaving one such conversation unwon this week. You will find out fast whether your steadiness was resting on your answers or on something else.
studies.explainEasier: Some people who were given part of God's book chose the wrong path. They want you to lose your way too. But God knows who your enemies are. He is all the protector and helper you need.

studies.title: Twisting With Their Tongues
studies.meaning: A particular trick is described here, and it is worth slowing down for. Words are shifted out of their proper places. Phrases are chosen because they sound like respect while carrying an insult underneath. The verse then sets the honest version of each phrase beside the twisted one, so the difference can be heard. It names a group inside a community, not the whole of it, and early scholars are careful to keep that limit.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at a time of open argument between the community and some of its neighbours in the city. Early scholars explain the quoted phrases as puns. Anyone who missed the wordplay heard ordinary address; anyone who caught it heard an insult. An instruction elsewhere asked believers to use a different word entirely, which closed the double sense down.

keyTerms.note: From the root for an edge or a letter. The verb means moving something off its proper position, so the fault described is displacement rather than invention, which is considerably harder to detect.
A noun for the physical bending of something, used of twisting rope or a limb. Applied to the tongue it describes speech deliberately shaped to bend away from its apparent sense.
A comparative from the root for standing straight. The honest phrasing is called straighter, which continues the verse's picture of language as something that can be bent or held upright.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic poetry prized exactly this skill: the line that could be read two ways. Audiences listened out for it. Satire was a known weapon between tribes, and a well-made double sense could damage a reputation while leaving its speaker free to deny it. So the trick described here was not obscure. It was a known art, done in public and admired, which is why the verse takes trouble to spell it out.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere asks believers to swap out one of the words quoted in this verse. They are to use a near synonym meaning wait for us, which removes the double sense. That gives an unusual glimpse of a community changing its own vocabulary. It changed it because of how one word was being used against it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speech is treated as a moral act at the level of single words. What is described is not lying, since each phrase can be defended as innocent, and that is exactly the point. The harm lives in the intention behind a form of words, not in its content. By setting the honest version alongside, the verse shows that the other option was always there and cost nothing.

crossReferences.why: Asks believers to replace one of the ambiguous words quoted here with an unambiguous one.
Describes a group twisting their tongues with the Book so that it will be taken for scripture.
Names the same displacing of words from their places, alongside an instruction to pardon and overlook.

studies.applyIt: Think of a phrase you use that is technically true and lets you avoid saying something plainly. Most people keep several, held back for difficult conversations. Pick one and replace it this week with the direct version. The method of this verse is to put the honest sentence beside the twisted one, and the comparison usually does the work by itself.
studies.explainEasier: Some people took God's words and moved them around. They picked phrases that sounded polite but meant something rude. If they had just said the plain, honest thing, it would have been better for them.

studies.title: Confirming What You Have
studies.meaning: This speaks directly to people who received earlier scripture, and its whole argument turns on one word. What is being sent down confirms what they already hold. So accepting it is put as carrying on, not as trading one thing for another. Then a warning follows in vivid terms. Early scholars read that warning in more than one way, some taking it literally and some as a picture of reversal and lost direction. The closing words say only that what God decides is carried out.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, where communities long settled in the city shared a scriptural history with the newcomers. Early scholars describe a time of open argument, with claims about earlier revelation right at the centre of it. The mention of those who broke the Sabbath points back to an episode the Quran tells elsewhere. It is used here as a precedent the audience would already know well.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from the root for truthfulness. The new revelation is described as attesting the earlier one, so the relation claimed is confirmation rather than replacement or correction of it.
A verb for erasing features until nothing can be distinguished, used elsewhere of stars losing their light. Early scholars read the image variously, some literally and others as a loss of direction.
From the root for the back or the rear. The image of a face turned toward the back describes disorientation: a person walking one way while looking in another entirely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina held old, settled groups with their own scholars, schools and holy texts. Religious argument there ran between people who knew each other's books. A newcomer to the city could hear a claim about earlier scripture argued openly in the market. This was not a meeting of strangers. It was a quarrel among neighbours who shared a great many words.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for confirming what came before is used again and again in the Quran, of its own relation to earlier scripture. It appears in that sense more than a dozen times. That makes it one of the steadiest self-descriptions in the whole book. It frames the claim made here as carrying on rather than as a new beginning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage claims that revelation is one thing, and it stakes its whole appeal on that. If what is sent confirms what was received, then recognising it turns you away from nothing. It is recognising the same source. That is why the warning that follows is about losing your bearings. What is imagined there is not disobedience so much as no longer knowing which way you face.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same appeal, to believe in what confirms the scripture already held by them.
Describes the Quran as confirming and safeguarding the scriptures that came before it.
Narrates the episode of Sabbath-breaking that this verse calls up as a recognised precedent.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you resist something because of who is saying it, not because of what is being said. The appeal in this verse is to something its hearers already accepted. It was offered by people they were arguing with. Take one thing you brushed off recently for that reason, and look at the content alone.
studies.explainEasier: God speaks to people who were given scripture before. He tells them to believe in this book, which agrees with what they already have. He warns them not to wait until it is too late. What God decides always happens.

studies.title: Anything Less Than That
studies.meaning: One boundary is named here, and everything inside it is opened wide. Setting up a partner with God is placed outside forgiveness. Everything else is described as forgiven to whom God wills. Early scholars read the rest of it carefully. They note the wording leaves the matter to God's will rather than promising forgiveness every time. They also stress that the exclusion concerns a person who dies holding to it, not one who leaves it behind.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, this follows a passage of argument with communities holding earlier scripture, and comes just before one about people who claim purity for themselves. Early scholars place it among disputes over who stands where before God. No particular occasion is reported for it. The verse returns almost word for word later in this same surah, inside a passage on the same subject.

keyTerms.note: From the root for partnership and sharing. The word is commercial before it is theological, meaning to make someone a partner in a business. The offence named is a division of what cannot be divided.
A phrase meaning below or nearer than something. It draws a line and places everything else on the near side of it, without ever listing what is included.
From a root meaning to cut out and fashion, as leather is cut. It describes making something up deliberately, which locates the offence in invention rather than in honest error.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Partnership was the basic form of business in Mecca and Medina. Caravans were funded by several investors at once. Shares in a venture were set out with care, because everything rested on knowing who held what. To describe an offence in those words placed it in the most familiar frame there was. Somebody had been given a share who had no claim to one.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse comes back almost word for word later in the same surah. That is one of very few near-repeats inside a single surah of the Quran. The second one sits inside a different argument. Early scholars read the repeat as marking the boundary twice around the long section running between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God draws exactly one line here and leaves everything else open. That is a particular shape for a teaching about forgiveness. It also refuses to promise anything on the near side of that line, leaving the matter to His will. So this is neither a threat nor a promise but a map. The two halves resist being read apart, and the tradition holds them together.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this verse almost word for word later in the surah, closing the section it opens.
Tells those who have wronged themselves greatly not to despair of the mercy of God.
Calls associating partners with God a great wrong, inside a father's advice to his son.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you divide your reliance. Most people trust God in theory and something else in practice: a salary, a name, one person's approval. Name yours honestly this week, without deciding to change it yet. This verse is about a single undivided loyalty, and seeing where yours has split is the first step you can take.
studies.explainEasier: God says He will not forgive someone who puts anything beside Him as a partner. Everything smaller than that He may forgive. He forgives whoever He chooses. Setting up a partner with God is a very great wrong.

studies.title: Those Who Claim Purity
studies.meaning: A short observation comes first, then a sharper one. People declare themselves pure, and the reply moves the verb: God is the one who purifies whom He wills. The point is not that they are impure. It is that the judgement was never theirs to issue. The next verse goes further and names what the claim really amounts to, an invention attributed to God, and says that invention by itself is enough.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside a run of arguments involving groups who claimed a settled standing before God, based on lineage or on being chosen. Early scholars link the passage to such claims without reporting one specific occasion. It follows straight on the verse naming the single thing not forgiven. So self-declared purity is placed right after a description of the gravest offence.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning both growth and purification, which also gives the word for the purifying due on wealth. The verb appears twice in one verse, first of people and then of God.
The thin filament lying in the groove of a date stone. Arabic uses several such minute objects to mean the smallest measurable thing, and this passage reaches for two of them.
The plain word for untruth, carrying the definite article. Attaching it to what is said about God turns a claim about oneself into a claim about Him, which is exactly the point here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A date stone has a fine groove along one side with a thread lying in it. It has a small dimple on the back. Both were used in ordinary speech to mean nothing at all. A modern speaker might say a hair or a crumb. Everyone handled date stones daily, so these were the most familiar words for a tiny amount.
studies.didYouKnow: Arabic drew several of its words for the smallest possible amount from one date stone. The thread in its groove, the dimple on its back, the thin skin around it. Two of them appear within a few verses of each other here. It is a small window onto how completely the date palm shaped the language.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being pure and calling yourself pure are pulled apart here, and all the weight falls on who is entitled to speak. That is a claim about the limits of your own moral life. You are not placed to certify your own standing, because that would need a view you do not have. Moving up to invention then exposes what a self-declaration quietly assumes about God's judgement.

crossReferences.why: Says plainly not to claim purity for yourselves, since God knows best who is mindful.
Records a claim that punishment will be brief, and asks what promise from God was taken.
Names the single thing not forgiven, immediately before this passage on self-declared standing.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you compare your standing well with someone else's, even silently. It happens fast and feels like a plain observation. You do not need to correct the judgement. Only notice that you issued one, and that this passage puts the issuing of it in someone else's hands.
studies.explainEasier: Some people say they are pure and good. God says it is not their call. He is the one who makes people pure, and nobody gets cheated by even a thread. Making up things about God is a clear wrong.

studies.title: Better Guided On The Way
studies.meaning: A group holding a portion of earlier scripture is described doing two things at once. They put trust in powers their own tradition rejects. And they tell people who deny revelation that these are better guided than the believers. Early scholars note how strange that is, since the judgement comes from people whose own scripture supplied the standard being set aside. The wording again limits the description to a group rather than a whole community.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at a time of alliance-making against the new community. Early scholars report that some who held earlier scripture sought common cause with Mecca's leaders. They were asked to compare the two parties, and answered in these terms. The reports describe the setting the same way while differing on the details. The passage is read against that background of political alignment.

keyTerms.note: A rare word appearing only here in the Quran. Early scholars give a range of meanings including sorcery, divination and idols, and record that the term was already unusual in the earliest Arabic.
From a root meaning to exceed all bounds, the same one behind the word for a tyrant. It covers any authority grown past its limits, whether an idol, a person or a system.
A comparative from the root for guidance. Putting the judgement in comparative form makes it a considered assessment rather than an insult, which is what makes it so striking here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliances in Arabia were made by weighing which party would win and which could pay. Religious difference rarely stopped a useful pact. Envoys travelled between Medina and Mecca to test the ground. Backing one side in public carried real weight, because it signalled to smaller tribes where the momentum lay. Such backing was sought for exactly that reason.
studies.didYouKnow: One of the two words for false powers in this verse occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Its exact meaning was already uncertain to the earliest scholars. They record several readings side by side rather than settling on one. That is a good example of how the classical tradition handled a truly rare word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What the passage describes is one particular corruption. A standard is kept in theory, while the judgements are made on quite different grounds. What is actually being weighed is power and advantage, and the language of guidance gets borrowed afterwards to dress up the result. Naming that pattern matters more than the incident does. The verse stays careful throughout to describe a group rather than a whole community.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same displacement, people professing belief while seeking judgement somewhere else.
Sets rejecting overreaching authority as the first half of holding to the firmest handhold.
Opens this passage with the same phrase about a portion of the Book, and the same limit.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you use moral language to describe a judgement you actually made on other grounds: convenience, loyalty, or which side appears to be winning. Everyone does this. Say the real reason to yourself once, in plain words. You may still decide the same way, but you will know what you decided on.
studies.explainEasier: Some people who had part of God's book put their trust in false powers instead. They even praised people who rejected God. They said those people were on a better path than the believers.

studies.title: They Would Not Give A Speck
studies.meaning: Two short verses sit here, one closing a judgement and one opening an imagined case. The first says these people have been cut off, and that nothing will come to their aid. The second imagines them holding a share of rule, and answers before you can. They would give nobody the smallest thing. So the argument is about character rather than power, and it uses the granting of power to show what is already there.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, this closes the passage about people who preferred one party over another out of alliance rather than judgement. Early scholars read the second verse as answering an unspoken claim to authority. They note that the surah has been circling one theme through inheritance, orphans, and now rule. The theme is what people do with something they hold on behalf of others.

keyTerms.note: The verb means removal from mercy and from nearness, closer to banishment than to a spoken curse. Arabic uses it of an animal driven away from the herd and left outside it.
From a root meaning to give victory or support. It names not a sympathiser but someone who actually acts, which is precisely what the verse says will not be found.
The small dimple on the back of a date stone, used in Arabic for the least imaginable quantity. It belongs to a family of such words all drawn from the same fruit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A share of kingship in that world was never abstract. It meant control of a water source, the right to levy on a caravan route, or a portion of tribute. Everyone had seen what such control did to men who got it. They had watched generosity shrink as holdings grew. The imagined case here was one its first hearers could test against people they knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a speck here names the little notch on the back of a date stone. A few verses earlier the Quran reached for the thread inside its groove. Both times, what is meant is the least a person could hand over. The choice makes the accusation concrete instead of abstract.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The second verse makes a claim about power and character. Authority does not create meanness or generosity in a person. It shows what is already there. That is why the passage can argue from an imagined case at all. It also ties a failure before God to a practical one: a wrong turn toward God is expected to show in what someone will hand over.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same withholding earlier in this surah, along with the urging of others into it.
Says that if people held the treasuries of mercy they would hold back, fearing to spend.
Carries the argument on in the next verse by naming envy as what lies underneath it.

studies.applyIt: Think about what you did with the last piece of authority you were given, however small: a rota, a budget, a decision about someone else's time. Notice whether more of it flowed outward or inward. The claim here is that power reveals rather than changes. That makes any small authority you hold a fairly reliable mirror.
studies.explainEasier: God has turned away from these people. No one can help them. If they held any share of power, they would not give anyone even the tiniest scrap of it.

studies.title: The Family Of Abraham
studies.meaning: The argument turns to motive and names it: envy of what God has given other people. The answer does not deny the gift at all. It widens the frame, recalling that scripture, wisdom and great rule were given to Abraham's family long before. Then the next verse splits the response to that gift: some believed and some held back. That quietly makes the point, because receiving a line of descent is not the same as taking up what came with it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the middle of a long argument about who stands where before God. Early scholars read the mention of Abraham's family as an answer to a complaint. The complaint was that prophecy had appeared outside the line people expected. The answer points to a shared ancestor whose children include both sides. The surah has been building this case for several verses. It turns here on a legacy of a different kind.

keyTerms.note: A verb for resenting a good that someone else holds, distinguished in Arabic from wishing the same for oneself. The word names a wish that the other should lose it, not merely a desire to have it.
A word for a household and its line, used of ruling houses. It names people by their connection to a founding figure rather than by their own achievements or their standing.
From the root for judgement and restraint, connected with the bridle of a horse. Wisdom in Arabic is pictured as something that holds and directs rather than as knowledge accumulated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descent was the main claim to standing in Arabia. It was recited aloud and learned by heart across many lifetimes. The tribes of Mecca and the older faith groups of Medina both traced themselves back to Abraham, through different sons. That link was common knowledge, not a point for scholars. So calling on his house in an argument about prophets touched something shared and fought over.
studies.didYouKnow: Abraham is named in the Quran more often than any other prophet apart from Moses. He turns up across twenty-five different surahs. He is shown as the shared ancestor of communities that disagreed sharply with each other. That is part of why passages of argument return to his household rather than to a figure only one side claims.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God separates the gift from what people do with it. A family received scripture, wisdom and rule. Inside that same family, some believed and some held back. So the inheritance settles nothing on its own. Applied to the argument at hand, that dissolves the premise on both sides. The gift is real, and it does not pass standing to descendants who never take it up.

crossReferences.why: Says God's covenant does not reach wrongdoers, answering Abraham's question about his descendants.
Names the family of Abraham among those God chose, describing them as a single line.
Later in this surah, names Abraham as one whom God took as a close friend.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you inherited without earning it: a language, a faith, a trade, a name within your family. Name one thing about it you have never actually decided for yourself. You do not need to reach a conclusion this week. The point here is that receiving something and taking it up are two separate events.
studies.explainEasier: These people are jealous of what God gave others. But God gave Abraham's family a book, wisdom, and a great kingdom long ago. Some of them believed in it. Some of them turned away.

studies.title: So They May Taste It
studies.meaning: Punishment is described here in unusually physical terms, with skins renewed so that feeling goes on. Early scholars discuss why that detail is there at all. The reason is stated inside the verse itself: so that the suffering is actually felt. What is described is not destruction but a continuing awareness, and that is what makes the imagery necessary. The sentence closes on two names, one of power and one of wisdom.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, after a long stretch of argument about standing and rejection, and right before the matching description of the Garden. Early scholars note the pairing. This surah gives the two outcomes in next-door verses again and again, so that neither is heard on its own. No particular occasion is reported for the passage in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: A cooking verb, used of meat or fruit reaching the point of being done. Its ordinariness is what makes the sentence carry; the language comes from a kitchen rather than from a courtroom.
A verb for tasting, used across the Quran of experiencing consequences. It names direct sensation rather than knowledge, which is the entire point of the renewal being described here.
From a root meaning to be rare, precious and inaccessible. It describes power that cannot be reached or resisted, and it is almost always paired with another name that qualifies it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cooking over an open fire was the daily work of every household. Everyone knew exactly what heat does to flesh and skin over time.
