Burns were a common injury in homes lit and warmed by fire. The words of this verse come straight out of that ordinary skill. That is why it needed no explaining at all for its first hearers.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of a name of overwhelming power with a name of wisdom turns up dozens of times across the Quran. The first almost never appears without the second. Early scholars read the pairing as a set limit. Power described on its own would suggest acting without reason, so the two names are given together at moments like this.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage insists that consequence is felt rather than merely imposed. That marks off what is described from simply being wiped out. It is uncomfortable, and the tradition has not softened it. Closing on power and wisdom together does particular work. What has been described is not force by itself but force under judgement, and the two names are not allowed to come apart.

crossReferences.why: Gives the matching description of the Garden in the very next verse, in parallel construction.
Describes a recompense fitted precisely to what was done, in another passage of the same kind.
Shows those who followed being shown their deeds as regrets, in a scene of the same moment.

studies.applyIt: Notice how quickly you look away from a passage like this one. That reflex is worth examining rather than obeying. Sit with the verse for a minute without resolving anything, and then read the verse that follows it. The surah puts them together deliberately, and reading only one of the pair distorts both.
studies.explainEasier: People who turn away from God's signs will be put into a fire. Each time their skin burns away, it will be made new, so the pain keeps on. God has all power and knows what He is doing.

studies.title: A Shade Of Shade
studies.meaning: This is the matching description of the other outcome, and its last image is the striking one. The Arabic doubles the word for shade in an intensive build that English can only come near. So the last thing named is not a place or a reward but a quality of shelter. Rivers, permanence and purified companions all come before it. Early scholars note that the passage moves from the vast toward the close, not the other way round.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, paired with the description of the Fire just before it. Early scholars observe that this surah always gives both outcomes in next-door verses, in matched builds. The pairing arrives at the close of a long stretch of argument about standing before God. So the two verses together answer the dispute rather than carrying it further.

keyTerms.note: A noun followed at once by an adjective from the same root, an Arabic intensive. The construction has no clean English equivalent; it means shade that is thoroughly and permanently shade.
A passive participle from the root for purity. The passive form matters: the purity is described as given rather than as achieved, which matches how everything else here is described.
A word for unbounded time, added after a phrase that already says abiding therein. The doubling is deliberate, closing off any reading in which the permanence might turn out to be limited.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shade in Arabia was the most valuable thing a landscape could offer. Travel was arranged around it, and midday halts were made for it. Owning a shaded well or a stand of palms was worth fighting over. To promise deep and unfailing shade was to name the exact relief that every listener's body already knew, with no explaining needed.
studies.didYouKnow: The build that closes this verse puts a noun straight beside an adjective from the same root. It is a feature of high Arabic style, and it appears only a handful of times in the Quran. English translators reach for phrases like a shade of shade. They do that only because the build has no direct match in the language.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is described here almost wholly in the passive. They will be admitted; they will have; they will be brought in. Nothing is achieved by the people described once they arrive. That marks the Garden off from a wage. The final image completes that logic, because shade is the one comfort a person gets by being in a place rather than by doing anything.

crossReferences.why: Gives the matching description of the other outcome immediately before, in parallel construction.
Describes extended shade and unfailing fruit in another passage built from the same imagery.
Names perpetual shade and constant provision as what distinguishes the promised Garden.

studies.applyIt: Find some actual shade this week and sit in it for five minutes without your phone. Not as a spiritual exercise. The closing image of this verse assumes a body that knows what relief feels like. Most descriptions of the Garden land differently once you have recently felt the thing being named.
studies.explainEasier: People who believe and do good will be brought into gardens with rivers running under them. They will stay there forever. They will have pure partners. And they will sit in deep, cool shade.

studies.title: Trusts Returned To Their Owners
studies.meaning: Two instructions land here, both aimed at anyone holding something that is not theirs. The first is the return of trusts, and early scholars read that broadly: deposits, offices, secrets, anything placed in a person's keeping. The second is judging between people with justice, put as a condition, as something that happens when it happens. Between the two sits a short burst of praise for the counsel itself. That is unusual in this surah, and it carries warmth rather than warning.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, a widely reported occasion ties this verse to the key of the Kaaba. After Mecca was taken, the key went back to the family that had always held it, rather than to the new authority. Reports differ over the details. Early scholars note that the wording is general in any case. It sits among passages about authority, dispute, and the handling of what belongs to other people.

keyTerms.note: Plural of a word from the same root as faith and safety. What is deposited with you and what you believe are named by the same consonants, so keeping a trust and being trustworthy are one idea.
From a root for making two things equal in weight. The image is a scale rather than a rulebook, which is why the word covers both fairness between people and the balance of creation.
A compressed exclamation of praise, rare in the Quran. It interrupts the instruction in order to comment on it, so the sentence briefly steps back and admires the counsel it is giving.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca before Islam ran on offices held in trust by families. The key of the sanctuary, the watering of pilgrims, the war banner, the right to call the assembly. Each of those was passed down and guarded closely. Traders also left goods and money with people they would not see for months, on nothing but a good name. Losing that name ended a man's business life.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for trusts shares its root with the word for faith. It shares it too with the response people say after a prayer. The Quran uses the same root at the end of surah 33, for the trust the heavens and the earth declined to carry. So the vocabulary of a deposit left with a neighbour also carries the largest thing said about the human being.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Public and private integrity are given one vocabulary here. The verse moves from a small deposit to judgement between parties without changing verbs. So the qualities needed in a courtroom are the ones you already use over a borrowed tool. Naming God as hearing and seeing at the close is precise rather than decorative. The two failures in view are things said, and things done behind closed doors.

crossReferences.why: Warns against betraying trusts knowingly, using the same word in a Medinan setting.
Uses the same root for the trust offered to the heavens and the earth and carried by humanity.
Repeats the demand for just judgement, adding that hatred must not push you off it.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are holding that belongs to someone else: a borrowed book, a password, a piece of information told to you in confidence. Return one of them this week. Or check that you are still keeping it the way its owner would want. The verse begins with objects and moves to judgement, in that order.
studies.explainEasier: If someone leaves something with you, give it back to them. If you have to settle an argument between people, be fair. God hears and sees everything you do.

studies.title: When You Disagree, Refer It Back
studies.meaning: The verb for obedience is repeated for God and for the Messenger. It is not repeated for those in authority, and early scholars read that gap as deliberate. Obeying human authority is attached to the first two rather than standing on its own. Then comes the harder part. Disputes are to be referred back, and the condition attached is belief in God and the Last Day. So being willing to be corrected is presented as the test of the claim to believe.
studies.historicalContext: Medina had become one town made of clans that used to be rivals. They were newly living under a single arrangement, and the question of who decides was still open. This line sits in a stretch about authority, arbitration and conflict inside the community. Reports connect the verse with a dispute over a commander appointed for an expedition. The details vary, and early scholars do not settle them.

keyTerms.note: Literally the possessors of the matter. Early scholars read it of those entrusted with command and of those with knowledge, and the phrase is left broad rather than tied to any office.
A verb for returning something to where it came from, used of giving back a borrowed item. The dispute is treated as a thing to be handed over rather than a position to be argued.
From a root meaning to return to an origin. It covers both the interpretation of something and how it turns out in the end, so the closing praise concerns consequences as much as meaning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian disputes were settled by arbitration rather than by courts. Two parties agreed on a judge, often a respected outsider. They accepted his ruling because both of them had chosen him. There was no enforcement beyond honour and pressure. So referring a quarrel to an agreed authority was a familiar step. What changed here was the identity of the judge, and the fact that neither side got to pick.
studies.didYouKnow: Classical commentaries treat this as one of the central verses on governance, and part of the reason is grammatical. The verb for obeying is stated twice and then dropped before those in authority. In Arabic that joins them to the Messenger's clause rather than giving them a clause of their own. A great deal was built on that single omission.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Authority is granted and limited in the same sentence. Something is owed to those who carry the load, but the grammar keeps that owing second-hand rather than original. The passage also treats disagreement as expected rather than shameful, and gives a method for it instead of a ban. The last words make that method a practical claim. This way of settling things actually ends better, not only more properly.

crossReferences.why: Sharpens the same point, that accepting the Messenger's judgement without resistance is the mark of faith.
States that whatever people differ in, its judgement rests with God.
Places consultation before decision, which is the other half of how authority is described.

studies.applyIt: In your next disagreement, before you answer, say what the other person's position is until they agree you have it right. It costs a minute. The method here begins with taking a dispute out of your own hands. There is no smaller version of that than letting someone else define what is being argued about.
studies.explainEasier: Obey God, obey His messenger, and follow those in charge of you. If you argue about something, take it back to God and His messenger. That way works out best.

studies.title: Judgement Sought Elsewhere
studies.meaning: A group is described who profess belief in what was revealed. Then they take their disputes to an authority they had been told to reject. The verse does not label them; it lets the contradiction stand on its own. It describes the pull behind it as a deliberate leading astray. Early scholars connect the phrase for false authority to any arbiter chosen because his ruling is expected to suit better.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, early scholars report a case where two parties to a dispute disagreed over where to take it. One wanted the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The other wanted an arbiter expected to rule differently. Scholars describe this passage as speaking to that, and the reports vary in detail while agreeing on the pattern. The surah has been dealing throughout with where authority actually lies.

keyTerms.note: A verb Arabic uses for an assertion the speaker doubts. Its presence marks the profession of belief as reported rather than accepted, without the verse having to say anything about it directly.
A reciprocal form from the root for judgement, meaning to take a dispute before an arbiter. It describes a choice of forum, which is what the verse identifies as the revealing act.
An adjective of distance applied to going astray. It measures the error by how far it carries a person rather than by its gravity, which suits a passage about a series of small choices.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia you chose your arbiter, and choosing him was in effect choosing the outcome. Each tribe had men known for their leanings. A party expecting to lose would press for a different place. Everyone knew this. So the choice of where to go was read as a sign of what a person really wanted, not of what they said.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this verse uses for false authority comes from a root meaning to overflow all limits. The Quran applies it to idols, to tyrants and to arbitrary systems alike. That breadth is chosen. The term names a relationship of too much deference, rather than any one thing the deference is paid to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief gets put to a practical test rather than left as a statement. What you say you accept is measured against where you take a dispute when something real is at stake. The second one is treated as deciding the matter. That makes conviction something you can actually see. It also explains why the passage describes a slow drift outward, not a single act of rejection.

crossReferences.why: States the test directly: belief is not complete until the judgement given is accepted fully.
Names rejecting overreaching authority as the first half of holding to the firmest handhold.
Asks whether they seek the judgement of ignorance, and who judges better for people of certainty.

studies.applyIt: Watch where you take a disagreement when you expect to lose. Everyone has a friend who will agree with them, a forum that leans their way, a version of events that lands well with one particular audience. Notice your choice of venue this week before you make it. Let the noticing be the whole exercise.
studies.explainEasier: Some people say they believe in what God sent down. But when they argue, they take the case to a judge God told them to refuse. The devil wants to lead them far off the path.

studies.title: Turning Aside Completely
studies.meaning: One moment is described here: an invitation is given, and the answer is a turning away. The Arabic strengthens the verb with a noun from the same root, a build that adds force, so the turning is emphatic rather than casual. The invitation itself is worth noticing. It is neither an argument nor a demand but a call to come. What this verse records is the reaction that call draws.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, carrying straight on from the description of those who sought judgement elsewhere. Early scholars read the two verses as one sequence: a preference is shown, then an invitation is refused. The word used for the people described is the term this surah uses for those who professed belief in public while working against the community. It enters the passage here.

keyTerms.note: An imperative from a root meaning height. Arabic invites someone by telling them to come up, so the call carries an upward direction inside the ordinary everyday word for approach.
A verb meaning both turning aside oneself and obstructing others. The double sense matters, since the verse describes people whose refusal is public enough to influence anyone watching it.
A verbal noun from the same root as the verb before it, added purely for emphasis. Arabic intensifies an action by naming it twice, which English usually renders with an adverb like completely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Refusing an invitation in public was a serious act in a society built on honour. To be called to a gathering and decline visibly said something about the standing of whoever made the call. Everyone present read it that way. This verse describes something that happened in the open, in front of people who had not yet made up their own minds.
studies.didYouKnow: A verb followed at once by a noun from its own root is how Arabic adds force. That is what closes this verse, and it happens often in the Quran. It is among the harder features to carry into English, so translators generally add an adverb. A single Arabic word becomes the difference between turning away and turning away completely.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names one particular kind of refusal. It is not argument and not denial. It is simply turning aside. Nothing is claimed and nothing is contested; the call is just not taken up. That is harder to answer than open opposition, because there is no position to address. So the response here is to describe what people did, exactly, and leave it standing.

crossReferences.why: Describes the preference for another forum that this refusal of an invitation follows immediately.
Records a similar scene in which heads turn away when they are called to seek forgiveness.
Shows the same pattern: turning away when summoned, and coming readily when the outcome favours.

studies.applyIt: Notice the invitations you decline without ever refusing. There is the message left unanswered, the gathering you were vague about, the talk you keep not having time for. Pick one this week and simply go. This verse describes avoidance rather than argument, and avoidance is undone by showing up, not by deciding anything.
studies.explainEasier: When these people are told to come to what God sent down and to the Messenger, they turn right away from you. You can see them do it.

studies.title: We Only Intended Good
studies.meaning: A sequence is traced here, and the order of it is everything. Something goes wrong because of what people did, and they arrive swearing that they meant only kindness and peacemaking. The verse never calls that oath false. It places the oath after the disaster and lets the timing do the work. Early scholars note that the intention claimed is exactly the one that would excuse the act, which is what makes the swearing suspect.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, carrying on the passage about those who sought judgement elsewhere and then dodged the invitation to come back. Early scholars read this verse as describing what happens when such a plan fails. The parties return, and they return with an explanation ready. No single occasion is reported. What early scholars treat as the subject is the sequence running across these verses.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to hit a target. The word describes a misfortune as something that arrived accurately rather than at random, which fits the clause about what their hands sent forward.
A recurring Quranic image in which deeds are dispatched forward in time and met again later. It makes consequence a matter of arrival rather than of something being imposed afterwards.
From the root for beauty and excellence. It names not merely good intent but doing a thing finely, which is why claiming it is a large claim rather than a modest one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths were the strongest tool available in a society without documents. Swearing by God settled disputes, secured loans and closed arguments. A man's oath was tied to his standing so tightly that offering one was itself a claim. So using an oath to cover a failed move spent something real. That is part of what this verse describes.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about what hands have sent forward turns up in various forms throughout the Quran. Its picture stays the same: deeds are sent ahead of a person, who then catches up with them. That reverses the usual sense of consequence, in which something comes back to you. It recurs often enough to be a settled idiom.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What interests the passage is the moment after failure, when the explanation gets made. Intention is real, and the Quran treats it as deciding things elsewhere. That is exactly why a claim about intention made after the fact meets such suspicion here. The oath is not refuted. It is placed inside a sequence, and the sequence is left for you to weigh.

crossReferences.why: Describes a claim that nothing but good was intended, in another account of an oath afterwards.
Gives the response to the people described here: knowledge of hearts, and words that reach them.
Portrays those who use their oaths as a shield, and what such swearing eventually costs them.

studies.applyIt: The next time something you set in motion goes wrong, notice how quickly the sentence about what you meant arrives. Delay it by a day. Say what happened first, plainly and with nothing attached. Then see whether your account of your own intentions still looks the same to you.
studies.explainEasier: When trouble hits them because of what they did, they come running to you. They swear by God about it. They say they only wanted to do good and to make peace between people.

studies.title: Words That Reach Them
studies.meaning: Three instructions come in a row, and at first they look like they clash. Turn away from them. Counsel them. And say to them, about themselves, words that land. Early scholars resolve the run by reading the first as declining to punish or expose, not as abandoning. So what follows is address rather than action. The last of the three is the unusual one: it asks not for truth alone but for speech built to arrive.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the passage about those who sought judgement elsewhere and then explained themselves under oath. Early scholars note that the instruction given is wholly verbal, although the community had the standing to answer otherwise. The setting is a city where such people lived beside believers and went on doing so. That shapes what a workable answer could be.

keyTerms.note: A verb for averting the face, used earlier in this surah of a community dropping a matter. Here it means declining to act against them, which is why speech follows it immediately.
From a root for advice that moves the heart rather than instructing the mind. It names speech aimed at motivation, which is why it is distinguished from teaching and from argument.
From the root meaning to arrive at a destination, which also gives Arabic its word for eloquence. Effective speech is defined by arrival: words that reach the person, not words well made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Eloquence was the prestige skill of Arabia. A well-made sentence could shift the standing of a whole tribe. Speech was performed in public, judged by experts and remembered for generations. In that culture the word used here defined success by whether the words landed on the hearer. That was a practical standard among people who competed at speaking and could tell.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for eloquence in this verse comes from the verb meaning to reach or to arrive. The whole classical science of Arabic rhetoric took its name from that root. So a whole field of study rests on a picture of speech as a journey. It either arrives at the hearer or it does not.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The standard for correction here is set by effect, not by duty discharged. Saying the true thing is not enough. The words have to reach. That places responsibility on you for how something is heard, which is demanding. The instruction to turn away first is what makes it possible, since speech aimed at arrival cannot be delivered while you are also punishing.

crossReferences.why: Calls for invitation with wisdom and good counsel, and for arguing in the better way.
Instructs Moses and his brother to speak gently to Pharaoh, so that he might reflect or fear.
Describes the people this instruction concerns, and the oaths they came forward offering.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true you have been meaning to say to someone. Now plan how to say it so that it arrives, which usually means privately, briefly, and at a moment when they are not defending themselves. The standard set here is not whether you said it. It is whether it reached them.
studies.explainEasier: God knows what is inside these people's hearts. So let their words go, give them good advice, and speak to them plainly about themselves. Say it in a way that really gets through to them.

studies.title: Had They Come To You
studies.meaning: Two things sit together here. Messengers are sent to be followed, and that following happens by God's leave rather than by any authority of their own. Then a missed chance is laid out in the past conditional. Had they come, had they sought forgiveness, had the Messenger sought it with them, they would have found God turning toward them. Early scholars note that the verse describes something that did not happen, without closing the door on its happening.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, following the passage about those who took disputes elsewhere and then swore that they meant well. What comes now offers another route than the plan just described: instead of explaining, return. Early scholars place it in the ordinary life of a city where such people went on living among believers. So the chance described stayed open to anyone hearing it.

keyTerms.note: From the root for the ear and for listening. Authority is described as delegated and audible, granted rather than possessed, which qualifies the obedience named in the same clause.
The Quran's most frequent way of describing sin. It locates the injury in the person who committed it, which changes what returning is for: repair rather than the appeasement of anger.
An intensive form of the verb for returning, applied to God. He is described with the same word used of the human movement, so the turning is mutual rather than one-directional.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Going to someone to have a wrong put right was a public act in Medina. It meant walking to a known house, being seen to arrive, and stating your business in front of whoever was there. The cost was not the words but the walk, and everybody understood that. The picture of coming in this verse is drawn from a city small enough that arrivals were noticed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verse is built wholly in the past conditional, describing a chain of events that did not occur. Arabic marks this with one particle at the start and another before the outcome. Early scholars observe that the build lets the passage state what would have followed. It does so without claiming that anybody was refused, since nobody had come.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God makes forgiveness something you approach, not merely something granted. A distance is put in the way: a person has to go somewhere and ask. The messenger's authority is framed as given, which quietly removes the ground for resenting it. What early scholars stress is the tense. A chance described as having been open implies that it still is.

crossReferences.why: Instructs the Prophet to pardon them, seek forgiveness for them, and consult them in affairs.
Describes prayers offered on behalf of others as a source of settling and calm for them.
States that whoever does wrong and then seeks God's forgiveness will find God forgiving.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time you wronged someone and handled it by explaining rather than by going to them. The difference this verse draws is between an account and an arrival. Go this week, or call, and lead with the asking rather than with the reasons. The reasons can follow, and they rarely need to.
studies.explainEasier: Every messenger was sent so that people would follow him, with God's leave. Suppose these people had come to you after doing wrong. Suppose they had asked God to forgive them. They would have found God turning to them with mercy.

studies.title: No Resentment Within Themselves
studies.meaning: An oath opens the verse, which is unusual, and then three conditions are stacked on each other. They bring their disputes for judgement. They find no tightness inside themselves about the decision. And they yield fully. Early scholars dwell on the second of those, because it concerns an inner state after compliance. Outward acceptance is plainly not enough for what is being described here.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the passage about those who preferred another forum. Early scholars report a dispute over water rights between two men, brought to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). They describe one party's unhappiness with the judgement as the occasion. The reports vary in detail while agreeing on the shape of the incident. The surah has been circling the question of where judgement is sought.

keyTerms.note: From the same root as the word for a tree. A dispute is pictured as branches grown into each other, which suggests something that developed gradually rather than a single sudden clash.
A word for a narrow place with no room to move, used of thickets and of cramped ground. The condition set is the absence of that inner constriction, not merely the absence of complaint.
A verbal noun from the root that also gives peace and safety. It closes the verse by repeating the verb before it, an Arabic intensive, so the yielding is described as complete.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water rights were the most common source of serious dispute in a farming settlement. Who watered first, how long a channel stayed open, whose palms drank before whose: these choices settled a harvest. Judgements about them were remembered for years. A party who felt wronged carried it into every later dealing with the other family.
studies.didYouKnow: The verse opens with an oath in which God swears by the Lord of the person addressed. Oaths in the Quran usually call on created things, such as the dawn or the fig. This one is aimed at a person. Early scholars note the force of the build, and read it as marking how much weight the statement carries.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The standard set here is about your inner life rather than your conduct, which is a demanding move. Going along with a judgement is visible, and it can be produced without belief. What is asked for is the absence of a private grievance, which nobody else can check. That makes the standard self-administered. The opening oath grants how high it stands.

crossReferences.why: Describes seeking judgement elsewhere, which this verse answers by naming the actual test.
Says believers have no choice left in a matter once God and His Messenger have decided.
Describes the response of believers when summoned to judgement as hearing and obeying.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision that went against you recently and that you accepted outwardly. Check whether the tightness is still there when you think about it now. You do not have to resolve it today. This verse names that inner residue as the actual thing at stake, and most of us have never looked at ours directly.
studies.explainEasier: People do not really believe until they bring their quarrels to you to settle. Then they feel no anger inside about what you decide. And they accept it completely.

studies.title: Except A Few Of Them
studies.meaning: An imagined case is used here as a measuring tool. Had something extremely hard been asked, most people would not have done it. Early scholars note that the two examples given recall what earlier communities were asked. The point is a comparison: what this community was actually asked is far lighter. Then the verse states what following through would have produced, and it names that as firmness rather than as reward.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, following the verses about those who sought judgement elsewhere and refused the invitation to return. Early scholars read the imagined case as aimed at that group. It tests a claim of belief against a demand that was never made. The two examples recall trials the Quran describes elsewhere, given to earlier communities. The audience would have heard them as references, not as proposals.

keyTerms.note: The verb for writing, used of what is made binding. It pictures an instruction as inscribed rather than spoken, which is why the same root gives Arabic its word for scripture.
From the root for advice that moves the heart. Its use later in the verse is deliberate: what was actually asked is described as counsel, against an imagined demand that was written down.
From a root meaning to stand fast and not shift. The benefit named is stability rather than merit, so the verse presents following through as something that steadies the person doing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving one's home was no imagined thing for this audience. A large part of the Medinan community had already done it. They had walked away from houses, groves and family in Mecca. So the second of the two examples had a living case sitting in the same room. That is part of what gives the comparison its edge.
studies.didYouKnow: The verse names two demands, one impossible to survive and one merely ruinous. It reports that only a few would have complied. The Quran uses this kind of counter-to-fact measuring several times. It imagines a harder instruction, so as to say something about the response to an easier one actually given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: How hard an instruction is and how willing you are turn out to be two different things, and the second is the real variable. Then an unexpected benefit is attached to following through. Not reward, but firmness: an inner steadying. That makes obedience formative rather than a trade. It changes the person doing it instead of simply earning them something.

crossReferences.why: Records a request for fighting that was then declined by most once it had been granted.
Recalls a hard instruction given to an earlier community, of the kind this verse imagines.
Describes the same reversal later in this surah, eagerness beforehand and reluctance afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you tell yourself you would do in a crisis: the courage, the giving, the sacrifice. Then look at something small you were asked for this week and did not do. This verse works by comparison. The honest version of that comparison is usually quiet and unflattering, not dramatic.
studies.explainEasier: Suppose God had asked them to give up their lives or leave their homes. Only a few would have done it. If they had done what they were told, it would have been better for them and would have made them stronger.

studies.title: Excellent Are Those Companions
studies.meaning: A hard section about people who would not accept arbitration ends with an invitation rather than a threat. Four ranks are named: prophets, the utterly truthful, the witnesses, and the upright. What is promised is not a rank of your own. It is company, being with them. Early scholars note that the promise is made to whoever obeys, with no limit on degree, so the lowest of the four is not a ceiling for an ordinary person.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, the verses just before describe people who claimed belief while taking their disputes elsewhere to be judged. They also say what those people would have been given had they done otherwise. Classical sources keep a report of a companion who grieved that death would part him from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). They record it alongside the flow of the surrounding argument.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for truth. It describes someone whose truthfulness is a habit, not an occasional act. The Quran gives the same title to Abraham, to Joseph and to Mary.
The word covers both giving testimony and dying for a cause, and early scholars read it here in both senses. Its root meaning is presence: a witness is one who was there.
A word for the person you travel alongside, from a root for gentleness and ease. In the Arabic it is singular, though the company named is plural, which reads as one shared companionship.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel in Arabia was done in company, because it could not safely be done alone. Choosing a companion for a journey was a serious decision. Proverbs about it survive: pick the companion before the road. A bad one could rob you, leave you at a well, or simply make a month of walking unbearable. The word used here for company is the travelling one.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical scholars identify these four groups with the people asked about in the opening surah. Their path is requested in every unit of prayer. Read the two passages together and this verse becomes the answer to that request. Most Muslims make it more often than any other sentence they say.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reward is described as a relationship, not as property. The four groups are not merged, so differences of rank stay real. Yet the promise crosses them. The ordinary believer is placed with the prophets, not at a respectful distance below them. That shifts the aim of a religious life away from piling things up and toward belonging. The closing word makes this plain by choosing the language of travel.

crossReferences.why: Asks for the path of those favoured, whom this passage then names.
Calls those who believe in God and His messengers the truthful and the witnesses.
Sets out the condition these verses reward: accepting the Messenger's judgement without resistance.

studies.applyIt: Think about who you spend your loose hours with. These are the people whose opinions you repeat without having decided to. Name three of them. The verse makes company the reward, which suggests company is also the method. The honest question is whether your current company is taking you where you say you want to go.
studies.explainEasier: Anyone who listens to God and His messenger ends up in very good company. They will be with the prophets and with the best people God has blessed. Being with them is the gift.

studies.title: In Groups Or Altogether
studies.meaning: A short closing word about grace is followed by an instruction of a quite different kind. Take your precautions, then advance either in separate parties or as one body. Early scholars note that both options are given, with neither preferred, so the choice belongs to circumstance. Notice that the word for precaution comes first, before any movement at all. That makes getting ready part of the instruction, not a step before it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at a time when the community faced organised hostility and had to arrange its own defence. Early scholars place these verses among the practical instructions given then. They follow a passage about the company of the faithful. The verse before closes a description of who is gathered with the prophets. This one turns to the immediate situation on the ground.

keyTerms.note: A noun for wariness, treated here as something to be picked up like equipment. Arabic can speak of caution as an object one holds, which makes preparedness a thing rather than a mood.
A verb for starting up suddenly, used of an animal breaking into movement. It suggests rapid departure from a settled state, which is what mobilising out of a town actually involved.
A plural noun for detachments moving apart from one another. Its pairing with the word for all together leaves the practical decision open rather than prescribing any single formation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A settlement under threat had to decide whether to send out parties or to move as one. Splitting covered more ground and guarded the town, but small groups could be cut off. Moving together was safer and slower, and left home undefended. Everyone in Medina had a view on this. The outcome decided which houses would be left exposed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for taking precaution comes again later in this surah. It appears inside the long verse on how prayer was to be done under threat. Early scholars note that surah 4 is unusual. It holds household instruction, argument about God, and practical arrangements for danger inside one chapter of the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing an instruction about caution right after a statement about God's grace is the interesting move. Nothing in the assurance replaces getting ready. The passage assumes both at once and gives no reason for doing so. Early scholars read that as the ordinary shape of the Quran's approach. Trust is described in one breath and precaution instructed in the next.

crossReferences.why: Instructs the community to prepare what force it can, another pairing of trust with preparation.
Sets out how prayer was arranged under threat, using this same word for taking precaution.
Closes another surah with patience, perseverance and remaining stationed and watchful together.

studies.applyIt: Take one situation where you have been relying on things working out. Then do the small practical thing you have been avoiding: the backup, the appointment, the hard message, the money set aside. This passage puts assurance and precaution in back-to-back sentences. It does not treat them as alternatives, and most of us quietly do.
studies.explainEasier: All this is a gift from God, and He knows everything. So stay on your guard. Go out to meet danger in small groups, or go out all together.

studies.title: The One Who Lags Behind
studies.meaning: A character is drawn here in one sentence. He holds back, and when disaster strikes the people who went, he says that God favoured him by keeping him away. The words are pious, which is exactly the point, since nothing in them could be objected to on its own. Early scholars note that the verse exposes him by reporting his speech at a precise moment. Relief at another's loss is dressed up as gratitude.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, during the conflict with Mecca, early scholars connect this to people who said they believed but kept clear of the community's hard times. They read the verse alongside the one that follows as a single portrait, taken under two conditions. No named incident is reported for it. The picture would have been familiar to a town that had lately counted its losses.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for slowness, carrying two emphatic markers in Arabic. The grammar insists on the behaviour, describing not a hesitation but a settled habit of lagging.
From the verb meaning to hit a target. The word is used across the Quran for misfortune, and it carries the sense of something aimed rather than merely stumbled into.
The verb for granting a blessing. Placing it in this man's mouth is what makes the sentence work, since he uses the vocabulary of gratitude to describe his own absence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News of a defeat reached Medina quickly, carried by riders and then by the returning wounded. Households learned within hours which of their men had not come back. In that atmosphere a man who had stayed behind had to say something to the neighbours, and whatever he chose was noted. This verse records one such sentence exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse and the next form a pair. They show one person speaking after a loss, and then after a success. The Quran uses this method elsewhere, holding a character still and varying only the circumstance. That lets a disposition be shown without any need to describe it directly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names a failure that language hides rather than shows. What is said cannot be faulted on its own. The fault lies wholly in the moment it is said in. So religious words can be used to launder a disposition. The check on that is not doctrine but watching: notice what a person is grateful for.

crossReferences.why: Completes the portrait by showing the same man speaking after good news instead of disaster.
Describes those who stayed behind and were glad of it, in another account of this disposition.
Records those who stayed and said of the fallen that they would have lived had they listened.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you feel relief at news that is bad for someone else, and catch what you say out loud about it. Most of us have a phrase ready for the occasion. You do not need to feel differently on demand. Simply decline to say the pious sentence, and let the relief be what it is.
studies.explainEasier: Some people among you hold back and do not join in. Then, when things go badly for the others, they say God was good to them for keeping them out of it.

studies.title: If Only I Had Been There
studies.meaning: Now comes the other side of the same portrait. When good fortune arrives instead of disaster, the same man speaks again. Then a short clause is slipped in that changes everything: as though no affection had ever been between you and him. He stands outside the bond. The wish he voices is for the outcome, not for the company. Early scholars note that he reaches for the words of great attainment used earlier in this surah.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, paired with the verse before it. Early scholars read the two together as one description, seen under two conditions. They place them in the time when the community's fortunes in conflict swung sharply from one engagement to the next. No specific incident is named. The passage is read as a portrait of a type, not a report on one man.

keyTerms.note: A word for love that inclines toward someone, gentler than passion and steadier than liking. The verse says it is absent, and that absence is the diagnosis rather than an aside.
A particle of wishing for the impossible, used across the Quran for regrets that arrive too late. Its presence marks the speech as unfulfillable longing rather than as any kind of intention.
From the root for winning through and coming out safe. He borrows the vocabulary of the great attainment described earlier in this surah and applies it to a share in a gain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gains from a successful expedition were divided in public, and the whole settlement watched. A man who had not gone stood in the crowd and watched too. His absence showed up in the arithmetic. Everyone could see who received and who did not. That is why the wish recorded here was a sentence people actually heard said aloud.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about there having been no affection is an aside dropped into the middle of his speech, breaking the quotation. The Quran uses such breaks sparingly. Early scholars treat this one as the verse's central judgement. It is delivered inside a lesser clause rather than as a statement of its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The failure here is placed in belonging rather than in courage. What is missing is not bravery but attachment. That is why he can wish himself there for a gain, while feeling relieved at having missed a loss. Once affection is gone, the two responses fit together perfectly. The diagnosis is about relationship before it is about morals.

crossReferences.why: Gives the earlier side of this same portrait, showing the man speaking after a disaster.
Describes the same alternation, distress at good fortune and satisfaction at a setback.
Distinguishes those who submitted outwardly from those in whose hearts belief has entered.

studies.applyIt: Think about a group you say you belong to, and ask when you last shared one of its costs rather than its benefits. Not a dramatic cost. A dull one: setting up, staying late, showing up in bad weather. Affection is mostly built there, and this passage treats its absence as visible rather than hidden.
studies.explainEasier: But when something good comes from God, the same man speaks again. He talks as if he never cared for you at all. He says he wishes he had been there, so he could have won big too.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Selling One Life For Another
studies.meaning: A trade is described here in the words of the market: this present life traded for what comes after. Early scholars note that the verb can mean either buying or selling in Arabic. They read it here as selling. Two possible outcomes are then named, being killed or winning through, and the same recompense is attached to both. That is the real claim, since it cuts the reward loose from the result.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the years when the community faced steady hostility from Mecca. Through the Meccan period they had been told not to fight. Early scholars describe real reluctance among believers, some of it moral and some of it fear. This passage follows the portrait of those who held back. It speaks to disposition rather than laying out any rules of conflict.

keyTerms.note: The verb can mean either buying or selling in Arabic, and early scholars read it here as selling. Its double sense means a single word can describe both sides of one exchange.
The word for a road, in a phrase used across the Quran for anything undertaken for God, including the spending of wealth and migration. It is not restricted to conflict elsewhere.
The ordinary word for what a worker is paid. Its use keeps the whole verse inside commercial language, so the outcome is described as the settlement of an agreed price.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Commerce shaped how people in Mecca and Medina thought about almost everything. Caravans were funded by shares, risk was priced, and a venture might return everything or nothing. To speak of a life as sold, and a recompense as owed, put the matter in the frame everybody already used. It was the frame for weighing a choice when the outcome was unknown. That is why the image carries.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered as the path of God occurs many dozens of times in the Quran. In most of those places it refers to spending wealth, to migration, or to effort of other kinds. Early scholars reading any single instance generally note that range. The phrase is not tied to one activity.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sameness of the two outcomes is where the weight of this falls. Killed or victorious, the recompense named is identical. So the reward attaches to what a person offered, not to what happened to them. That takes results out of the moral accounting altogether. It is the same principle the Quran applies elsewhere to spending and to effort.

crossReferences.why: Describes a person who sells himself seeking God's pleasure, using the same commercial image.
States the exchange as a purchase by God of lives and property, in fuller form.
Concedes the aversion such an instruction provoked, and answers with the limits of human knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you did recently that was right and did not work. Notice how quickly you rated it by its outcome. The claim here is that the two outcomes carry the same recompense, which is a different accounting from the one most of us run. Try applying it once, deliberately, to that thing.
studies.explainEasier: Some people trade this short life for the life to come. God calls on them to fight for His cause. Whether such a person is killed or wins, God will give him a great reward.

studies.title: The Cry Of The Helpless
studies.meaning: A question is asked here, and then answered by a quotation. The question put is why anyone would hold back, when men, women and children who have been made powerless are calling out. Their words are given directly, in the form of a prayer, asking for deliverance and for a protector and a helper. Early scholars note that the argument rests on their voice rather than on an instruction. The reason offered is what you hear them say.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, early scholars identify those described as believers who stayed behind in Mecca, unable to leave. They report that some prayed in these very terms. The passage sits inside a longer section on reluctance in Medina. It answers that reluctance not with a warning but by naming who was waiting. The reports agree on the general situation while differing over individual details.

keyTerms.note: A passive form, so the weakness is something done to them rather than something belonging to them. The grammar itself carries the accusation, naming a condition that somebody else produced.
The ordinary word for a settled place. The verse describes the town as one whose people are wrongdoers, locating the fault in the inhabitants rather than in the place itself.
From a root meaning nearness. The prayer asks for a protector and then, in a matched clause, for a helper, which are the two things a person with no standing actually lacks.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Those who could not emigrate were the ones with least: the poor, the enslaved, women without kin to travel with, the old. Leaving Mecca required money, an escort, and somewhere to arrive. Everyone in Medina knew people who had not managed it, and many had left relatives behind. The prayer quoted here was no abstraction to that first audience.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer here is built by repeating: appoint for us a protector, appoint for us a helper. The phrase from Your presence is used twice over. That doubling appears in several Quranic prayers. Early scholars read it as the shape urgency takes in Arabic prayer, not as a stylistic ornament.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reason given is the suffering of specific people, not doctrine and not command. That places the duty inside an encounter with a voice, which is a particular way of grounding a moral claim. It also lets the verse name the groups most easily overlooked. Men, women and children made powerless are exactly those with no means to press their own case.

crossReferences.why: Distinguishes those who genuinely could not leave from those who simply chose not to.
Reminds the community that they too were once few and considered weak in the land.
Describes the steep path as freeing a captive and feeding the destitute on a hungry day.

studies.applyIt: Find out the name of one person your community is currently failing, and say it out loud. Not a category, a name. The argument here runs through a voice rather than through a principle. A principle is a great deal easier to set aside than a person you could describe to someone else.
studies.explainEasier: Weak men, women and children are crying out to God. They ask Him to get them out of a town whose people treat them badly. They ask Him to send someone to protect them and help them.

studies.title: The Plot Is Weak
studies.meaning: Two causes are set opposite each other in one sentence. The second is named with the word for authority that has grown past every limit. The instruction that follows belongs to one particular conflict in history, and early scholars read it in that setting. What closes the verse is unexpected after such a face-off. It is an assessment of the other side's scheme as weak, offered as reassurance rather than as a boast.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the years of open conflict with Mecca. Early scholars place this among passages given while the community was small and outnumbered, and knew it. They read the closing words as speaking to that fear directly. The passage belongs to one clash in history. The tradition reads it in that setting rather than as a general rule.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to exceed every limit. The Quran applies it to idols, tyrants and arbitrary systems, and its breadth lets the verse name a cause without naming any particular party.
A word for a plan made quietly, without the connotation of cleverness a synonym might carry. The verse calls it weak rather than wicked, which is a claim about its effectiveness.
The same adjective used earlier in this surah of the human being as created. Its reappearance here, applied to a scheme, is one of the surah's quiet verbal links between distant passages.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A small settlement facing a larger alliance spent a great deal of time weighing the other side's plans. Who had joined whom, what a delegation had promised, where the next move would come from. Rumour did much of the damage before any encounter took place. To tell such a community that the scheme against it was weak addressed the nearer danger.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a scheme in this verse is used elsewhere in the Quran of God's own planning. So the term is not inherently negative in Arabic. Early scholars note this when explaining that the judgement here falls on the strength of the plan. It does not fall on the fact that a plan was made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does two different things at once. It names the loyalties lined up behind a conflict. Then it deflates the other side rather than puffing up its own. The reassurance offered is an assessment of weakness, not a promise of victory. That puts your confidence in the nature of the opposition rather than in the strength of your own side.

crossReferences.why: Describes a plot laid against the Prophet, and states that God is the best of planners.
Uses this same word for overreaching authority, there of a forum chosen for judgement.
Says their scheming will not harm at all those who are patient and mindful of God.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much energy you give to what someone might be planning against you: a colleague, a relative, a rival. The reassurance offered here is not that nothing is happening. It is that the plan is weaker than it feels. Spend a week acting as though that were accurate, and see what it frees up.
studies.explainEasier: People who believe fight for God's cause. People who do not believe fight for a false power. The verse tells believers to stand against the devil's side. The devil's plan is a weak one.

studies.title: Restrain Your Hands
studies.meaning: A reversal is traced here. People who were told to hold back, pray and give had found that restraint hard. When the situation changed, a group among them feared people the way God should be feared, and asked for the whole thing to be put off. Their words are quoted, including a question addressed straight to God. The answer given is not a rebuke but a measurement: the enjoyment of this life is little. Early scholars observe that the fear is named honestly rather than denied.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, early scholars explain that through the Meccan years the community was told to endure without fighting. Some found this restraint hard and wished for permission. When things changed in Medina, a portion of those same people asked for delay. The reports agree on that sequence. The verse presents it as one continuous account, not two separate episodes.

keyTerms.note: A phrase for holding back from action, using the hand as the instrument. It names the earlier instruction in physical terms, as a withholding rather than as a policy or a principle.
A word for fear mixed with reverence, usually reserved in the Quran for the fear of God. Applying it to the fear of people is what makes the comparison here so pointed.
A word for a fixed period whose end is already set. Asking for postponement to a nearer term is therefore asking to move something whose timing was never theirs to arrange.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Enduring insult and violence in Mecca without answering ran against everything Arabian honour asked for. It cost the early community in public. Restraint of that kind was read by neighbours as weakness. When things later changed, the same people who had chafed under restraint faced what they had wanted. That is the reversal this verse traces.
studies.didYouKnow: The verse quotes people putting a question straight to God, asking why something was ordained for them. The Quran keeps several such complaints in the mouths of its subjects without softening them. Early scholars note that the answer given here responds to the fear behind the question. It does not answer the question asked.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear is taken seriously enough to be measured rather than condemned. What is named is not cowardice but a misplacing: the awe owed to God has attached itself to people instead. The answer then works by proportion, setting a brief enjoyment against what follows. It closes with an assurance that nothing will be shortchanged. That speaks to the worry underneath the request.

crossReferences.why: Concedes the aversion an instruction like this provokes, and answers with the limits of knowledge.
Describes the same gap between what people say they would do and what they actually do.
Names those who kept what they had pledged, against those who asked instead for delay.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you asked for and then found harder than expected once it came: a role, a move, a duty. Do not treat the difficulty as proof that you were wrong to want it. The answer here is about proportion, not about going back. Honest measuring usually helps more than rethinking does.
studies.explainEasier: These people were once told to hold back, pray, and give to the poor. Later, when fighting was asked of them, some feared people as much as they feared God. They asked God to put it off a while.

studies.title: Even In Fortified Towers
studies.meaning: Two thoughts are joined here. Death reaches everyone wherever they are, even inside high towers built for safety. People then sort their fortunes by source, giving the good to God and the bad to a person. The reply comes in one sentence: all of it is from God. Early scholars discuss how this sits with being answerable for your own acts. They read the statement as being about ultimate source, not as removing what people do.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, within the section on those who had grown reluctant. Early scholars report that misfortune was being blamed on the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) after a setback in the field. They read this verse as answering that. The towers mentioned would have called to mind the strong towers around Medina, which several groups in the city kept.

keyTerms.note: A word for a raised tower, used also of the constellations. Its double sense means the sentence gestures at both the tallest structure people built and the sky standing above it.
A passive participle from a verb for building with lime plaster, the strongest construction then available. It specifies not merely height but expense, which is what makes the futility pointed.
A verb for comprehension that reaches the sense of a thing rather than its surface. The closing words say they scarcely grasp any statement, which is stronger than saying they disagree.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina held a number of strong towers, thick-walled places where families sheltered during raids. They stored there whatever they could not risk losing. Those towers were the most solid things anyone in the city had built. Naming them in a verse about the reach of death used the strongest local example of safety there was. Every listener could see one nearby.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for towers in this verse is the same one the Quran uses for the constellations of the sky. It also gives modern Arabic its word for a tower block. That double sense was there for the first audience. So a single word reaches from a strong building up to the heavens.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses a split people make by instinct. In it, good comes from one source and harm from another. Saying all is from God keeps a single origin for events. Early scholars carefully separate that from the question of who answers for an act. The closing complaint about understanding suggests the trouble is unwillingness rather than intellect.

crossReferences.why: Immediately qualifies this, saying whatever harm reaches you is from yourself instead.
States that the death you flee from will meet you, in nearly the same construction.
Says no misfortune strikes on earth or in yourselves without being recorded beforehand.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you narrate a setback. Most of us look immediately for the person who caused it, and the search feels like clarity. Try holding one recent setback for a day without assigning it to anybody. The point is not to excuse anyone. It is to see what the search for a source was doing for you.
studies.explainEasier: Death will find you no matter where you hide, even in the strongest tower. When good things happen, these people say it came from God. When bad things happen, they blame you. Say: it all comes from God.

studies.title: Good From God, Harm From Yourself
studies.meaning: Credit and blame are split unevenly here. Early scholars are careful about what the verse does not say: everything still lies under God's decree. The point is where a person should look. Good is received, so it points outward. Harm is traced to your own doing, so it points inward. Then the second verse takes the messenger out of enforcement altogether. Obeying him counts as obeying God, but refusal is not his to prevent.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, the verses before describe people who blamed their misfortunes on the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). They credited their good fortune to themselves. Early scholars read this passage as answering that habit directly. The defeat at Uhud had given the habit a recent and concrete case. By this point the surah is largely taken up with people who kept their distance from the community while claiming to belong to it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a thing hitting its mark, used of an arrow finding its target and of rain reaching land. It shows both good and harm as arriving rather than as being made.
The word covers a good deed and a good happening, both a kindness done and a piece of luck received. That breadth lets the verse move between morals and circumstance without changing terms.
One who keeps and watches over something, used of guarding property and of memorising. Denying this role to the messenger limits him to delivering the message rather than to its results.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs before Islam read fortune in omens. They watched the direction a startled bird flew, the day a journey began, the person met on the road. Bad luck was thought to attach itself to people. A newcomer who arrived in a year of drought could be blamed for it. Holding a stranger responsible for a failed harvest was ordinary reasoning. The surah is answering people who did exactly that in Medina.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical scholars debated the two halves of this verse at length, because they seem to sit awkwardly with the verse just before, which says everything is from God. The major commentaries settle it the same way. The earlier statement describes what causes an event. This one describes who answers for it. They are two different questions about the same event.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Credit and blame are handed out in the direction least flattering to you. That reverses the usual human accounting, and the one reversal does two things at once. It keeps thanks from turning into self-praise, and it keeps misfortune from turning into a complaint against God. Then the second verse adds a limit on religious authority. The messenger is owed obedience. He is not given charge of anyone's outcome.

crossReferences.why: Says the same thing about misfortune, and adds that much is pardoned.
Traces every blessing to God and describes the cry for help when harm touches.
Repeats the limit on the messenger's role, a reminder and not a controller.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing that went wrong for you recently and write the shortest honest sentence about your own part in it. Not a confession, an inventory. Then take one thing that went right and name someone or something outside yourself that made it possible. Do both, in that order, and notice which one was harder.
studies.explainEasier: When something good happens to you, it comes from God. When something bad happens, look at what you did. The messenger's job is to pass on the message, not to force anyone to listen.

studies.title: God Is Guardian Enough
studies.meaning: A pattern is described here in three stages. Agreement is given in person, a different plan is settled once out of sight, and a record is kept either way. The verb used for that planning is specific: it means working something out under cover of darkness. The response instructed is twofold and unexpected: turn away, and rely. Nothing at all is said about exposing them or acting against them.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing a passage about those who professed loyalty while working otherwise. Early scholars place it during the time of conflict, when the community's plans could leak and its unity be tested from inside. The instruction to turn away comes up in this surah in like situations. Early scholars read it as a policy given for one period, not as a general rule.

keyTerms.note: From the word for a house or for spending the night. The verb means arranging something under cover of darkness, so the deception is described by when it happens rather than by its contents.
A verb for coming out into open ground, from the root that gives the word for a plain. It marks the moment of leaving a presence, which is when the second version begins.
A word for someone appointed to manage affairs on another's behalf. It names God not as an observer here but as the one actually handling the matter, which makes turning away possible.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Word travelled by mouth in Medina. A plan discussed in one courtyard could reach another by morning. There were no secure channels and no written orders. Loyalty was judged by what people said in your presence. So a community under pressure had to live with knowing that agreement in a room proved very little about the night.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic verb for planning by night in this verse has no one-word match in English. Translations render it with a phrase. The Quran uses the verb in several places, always for something arranged in darkness. So the language itself tells planning apart from planning at night.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction given is striking for what it leaves out. Faced with people described as working against him, the Prophet is told to withdraw his attention and to rely. The verse closes by naming God as the one entrusted with the matter. Trust here is not a feeling but a handing over of responsibility. It is offered as the practical answer to a problem that watchfulness cannot solve.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the instruction to disregard them and to rely on God, who suffices as a trustee.
Gives a similar instruction earlier in this surah, to turn away and then to speak.
Records the community's answer under pressure: God suffices for us, an excellent trustee.

studies.applyIt: Pick a situation where you have been keeping watch on somebody: rereading messages, checking what they said elsewhere, building a case. Stop for a week. Not because they are innocent, and not because it does not matter. Do it to find out how much of your attention that watching had been eating without producing anything.
studies.explainEasier: They tell you they will obey. Then they leave and quietly plan something else. God writes down every word of it. So let them be, and put your trust in God. He is enough to look after you.

studies.title: Had It Been From Another
studies.meaning: A question comes first, and then a test, inside one sentence. The invitation is to reflect on the Quran all the way through. The argument turns on inner consistency. A text made across many years, under changing conditions, by a human source would show mismatch. The claim is that it does not. Early scholars note that this is put as an invitation to look, not as a statement to take on authority.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, among passages about people who spread rumours and questioned decisions. Early scholars read the placing as chosen. An argument about where the Quran comes from arrives in the middle of a section about how the community handled news. No specific occasion is reported. By this point the revelations had been coming for roughly twenty years.

keyTerms.note: From the root for the back or the end of a thing. It means considering something all the way to its consequences, so the verb asks for sustained attention rather than a first impression.
A word covering both difference and inconsistency. Early scholars read it here as inner contradiction rather than variety, since the argument concerns a text being checked against itself.
An adjective of quantity, and its presence is precise. The claim is not that no difficulty could ever be found, but that a human origin would leave a great deal of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was learned by heart and recited by people trained to catch a false line. Audiences competed at spotting where a poet had borrowed or repeated himself, and where he slipped. Holding steady across a long composition was a known measure of quality in that culture. An argument built on inner coherence spoke to the very skill its first hearers had spent their lives building.
studies.didYouKnow: Revelation came in pieces across roughly twenty-three years, answering events as they happened. That is unusual for a scripture. The argument in this verse rests on that fact. A text put together that way, under pressure and without revision, is exactly the kind you would expect to show strain across its length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage offers evidence rather than asking for assent, and the evidence is of a kind anyone can check. That is a particular way of grounding a claim. It rests not on a miracle and not on authority. It rests on a property of the text that is open to inspection. It also implies that careful reading is itself a religious act, since the invitation to reflect carries the argument.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the question about reflecting on the Quran, asking whether hearts have locks upon them.
Describes the Book as sent down blessed, so that people may reflect upon its signs.
Challenges humanity and the unseen together to produce anything like this Quran.

studies.applyIt: Read one page of the Quran this week twice. Once at your normal pace. Then once slowly enough to notice how a sentence is built. The verb in this verse asks for the second kind of reading. Most of us have done a great deal of the first and very little of the second.
studies.explainEasier: God asks people to think hard about the Quran. Suppose it had come from anyone other than God. They would have found lots of things in it that did not match up.

studies.title: News Of Security Or Alarm
studies.meaning: A particular failure with information is described here. News arrives, reassuring or frightening, and it is broadcast at once. The alternative offered is not silence but referral: taking it to those able to draw out what it actually means. Early scholars note the verb for that drawing out. It is used of reaching water underground, so weighing news is pictured as digging rather than as opinion. Only a few, the verse says, would have escaped the error unaided.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in a time of conflict. Reports about distant engagements arrived unchecked and moved through the city fast. Early scholars connect the verse to rumours going round after expeditions. Some announced disaster and some victory, before anything had been confirmed. It sits among passages about how the community handled pressure from inside as well as outside.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to scatter widely. The verb makes the fault the distribution rather than the belief, so a person who passes something on without accepting it is still being described.
From a verb used of the first water reached when digging a well. Assessment is pictured as bringing something up from below rather than as forming a view on the surface.
A phrase meaning those charged with the matter. Early scholars read it broadly, covering both those with responsibility and those with the knowledge to judge, and they record the range.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A rider arriving at Medina with news could empty a market in minutes. Families with men away needed to know. So an unchecked report about a battle spread faster than any confirmation could follow. There was no way to hold information while it was checked. A false report of defeat could set off choices that could not be undone.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb this verse uses for working out what news means comes from the words of well-digging. It describes the moment water is first reached. Arabic later took the same root as its technical term for drawing rulings from texts. So a whole method of study is named after finding water underground.
studies.theologicalSignificance: How you handle information is treated as a moral matter, not just a practical one. The verse closes by saying most people would have gone wrong in this without help. That is a striking judgement on ordinary human sense. It also puts the remedy in a process rather than in personal restraint. Referral comes first, then weighing by those able to carry it out.

crossReferences.why: Asks that a report brought by an unreliable source be verified before a community acts on it.
Describes people passing something on with their tongues while thinking it a light matter.
Names obedience to those in authority among believers, using the same phrase as this verse.

studies.applyIt: The next time something alarming reaches you, wait until you have spoken to one person who would actually know before you pass it on. Not a day, just one conversation. The remedy here is not silence but referral, and referral takes far less time than most people assume.
studies.explainEasier: When news comes about safety or danger, some people spread it right away. It would be better to take it first to the Messenger and to those who lead. They would work out what it really means.

studies.title: Responsible Only For Yourself
studies.meaning: An instruction is addressed to one person, in the singular, with a clause that limits it sharply: you are not held to account for anyone else. Then comes a second task, rousing others, which is influence rather than duty. What follows is a possibility rather than a promise, carried by a particle of hope. Perhaps God will restrain the force of the other side. Early scholars note that no outcome is guaranteed anywhere in the sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at a time when the community's willingness to act was uncertain and some were holding back. Early scholars describe an occasion on which few were ready to move. The instruction came addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) alone. The reports agree on that general setting.
