The passage sits inside a run of verses about reluctance and about who carries what.

keyTerms.note: From a root for imposing something heavy. The passive form means the burden is not placed on him, which limits responsibility rather than describing what he might choose to do.
An intensive verb for stirring someone into motion. It names encouragement as a distinct task from acting, given as a separate instruction within the same sentence.
A particle of possibility and hope. Its presence keeps the clause that follows from becoming a guarantee, which is the same function it performs elsewhere in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A leader in Arabia was expected to deliver his men. Command meant standing surety for a group. A chief whose people would not follow him lost his standing altogether. Telling one man that he answered only for himself cut against that whole structure. It would have landed as real relief for anyone who had carried such expectation.
studies.didYouKnow: The little word of hope used here turns up all over the Quran. It comes at just the points where a promise might have been expected. That includes passages about pardon and about relief. Early scholars treat the pattern as chosen. It leaves the outcome open, and it keeps hope alive for whoever is being spoken to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is separated from outcome, and also from what other people do. Those are two distinct limits set inside one clause. What remains is a task and an attempt to persuade. The possible result is then placed under a particle of hope rather than stated. So the person addressed is asked to act without being told what will follow.

crossReferences.why: States that God burdens no soul beyond what it can bear, the same principle put generally.
Says no bearer of burdens carries the burden of another, another statement of this limit.
Instructs the Prophet, if they turn away, to say God suffices him and to rely on Him.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you have been carrying that belongs to somebody else: their decision, their reaction, their choice not to change. Set it down for a week and keep only your own part. This verse separates the two in a single clause. Most people find their own part smaller and far more doable than the whole.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to go and fight for His cause. He is answerable only for himself. He should also urge the believers on. Maybe God will hold back the strength of those who refuse to believe.

studies.title: A Word Spoken For Someone
studies.meaning: The speaking up here is not the Day of Judgement kind. It is the everyday act of putting in a word for someone. The verse gives that act weight in both directions: a share of the good you made possible, a portion of the harm. Then comes a smaller case of the same rule. A greeting arrives, and it is to be answered with a better one or at least returned. Even the minimum is set. Both verses close with a divine name about counting.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside a passage about who stands with whom when a community is divided. Early scholars record no particular occasion for it. What they note is the placement. These two verses sit inside hard material about people who would not commit themselves. They describe the small exchanges that actually hold a community together. Those are set beside the larger loyalties, and treated the same way.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to make something even by adding a second to it. The one who speaks up joins himself to the person he speaks for, which is why he then shares in the result.
A word tied to the pad placed on a camel's back so a second rider can sit behind. It is chosen for the bad share, rather than the plainer word used for the good one.
From the root for life. The standard greeting was a wish for life, so returning one better than you received means adding to what somebody has just wished you.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access in that society ran through people who spoke for you. A man who wanted a debt forgiven, a captive released or a marriage agreed sent someone with standing to ask. The asker's reputation travelled with the request. Turning such a man down was a public act. Greetings worked the same way. They marked whether a person stood inside your circle, and passing someone in silence was a known form of hostility.
studies.didYouKnow: The second verse sets both a floor and a ceiling for a greeting. Answer with a better one, or with one exactly equal. The Quran rarely pins down a courtesy this closely. The classical commentaries note that the equal return is named as the lower limit, not as the expected reply.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speech is treated as taking part. A word said on someone's behalf makes the speaker a party to what follows. Influence is never neutral, and it cannot be disowned later. The greeting then carries the same logic down to the smallest social act there is. Nothing here is too minor to be counted. Both verses close with divine names drawn from keeping accounts, not from mercy or power.

crossReferences.why: Instructs the Prophet to open with peace when believers come to him, the same greeting.
Makes peace the greeting exchanged in the Garden, the same word used here.
Praises private talk that urges charity, kindness or reconciliation between people.

studies.applyIt: Answer the next message you receive with slightly more than you were given: one extra sentence, a question back, a name at the start. It takes seconds. The verse sets returning the same as the floor and going beyond it as the expectation. Most of what makes a person feel met is exactly that small margin.
studies.explainEasier: If you help someone by speaking up for them, you share in the good that comes of it. If you help them do wrong, you share in that too. When someone greets you, greet them back just as warmly or better.

studies.title: Who Speaks More Truly
studies.meaning: Three statements sit in one short verse, each of a different kind. First, that there is no god but Him. Then a promise, carried by an emphatic oath, that everyone will be gathered on a day about which there is no doubt. Then a question with no answer supplied. Early scholars note that the question closes the verse rather than opening it, so it seals what came before rather than beginning an inquiry.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, it arrives in the middle of a section about people who spread reports and whose loyalty was in doubt. Early scholars note the contrast the placing creates. A passage about unreliable speech is broken into by a statement about the most reliable speech there is. No specific occasion is reported for the verse itself in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: The verb for collecting scattered things together, carrying two emphatic markers in Arabic. Its ordinary use is of gathering a harvest or assembling people, which keeps the image concrete.
A word for doubt that disturbs rather than mere uncertainty. It names the kind of misgiving that keeps a person from settling, which is what is denied of the day described.
A comparative from the root for truthfulness, the same one that gives the word used for a dowry. It measures speech by its correspondence with reality rather than by sincerity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reliable speech was what that society ran on. Contracts, family lines, news from a distance and the terms of an alliance all rested on somebody's word. A man known to speak accurately was consulted far beyond his own family. In a city awash with unchecked reports, the question mattered. Asking who speaks most truly was anything but abstract.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this verse uses for truthful speech shares its root with the word for a dowry. That word appears earlier in the same surah. Arabic ties the bridal payment to truthfulness, because the payment is taken as proof of serious intent. So one root reaches from the language of marriage to the language of reliable reporting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Setting a statement about God's oneness beside a promise about the gathering makes the second follow from the first. If there is one authority, there is one accounting. The closing question then gives the ground for accepting the promise, and it does so by comparison rather than by claim. Nothing is demanded. A standard is offered, and you are left holding it.

crossReferences.why: Asks a nearly identical question later in this surah, about whose word is more truthful.
Opens with the same declaration of oneness and expands it through denial and possession.
States that God has decreed mercy upon Himself and will gather all to a day beyond doubt.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of what you believed this week came from a source you never checked and would not defend if asked. You do not need to become suspicious of everyone. Just pick one such source and hold what it tells you more loosely. That is what the closing question here quietly invites.
studies.explainEasier: There is no god but God. He will gather everyone together on the Day of Rising, and there is no doubt about that day. Nobody tells the truth better than God does.

studies.title: Divided Into Two Factions
studies.meaning: The community had split over how to treat one particular group. The verse addresses the split itself rather than either side of it. It says that the group's own conduct has already settled the matter. Then it asks a question about the limits of what any community can do for another. Early scholars are careful here. They read the closing words as being about God's judgement, not as leave for anyone to decide that some named person is beyond reach.
studies.historicalContext: In Medina, early scholars report an argument over how to treat people who said they believed and then pulled back. Some in the community took one side, some the other. The reports differ over which case is meant, while agreeing that the community had split. The passage speaks to the argument itself before it speaks to its subject.

keyTerms.note: The dual of a word for a group or a detachment. Using the dual makes the split precise: not scattered opinion but two organised positions facing each other inside one community.
A rare verb for turning something upside down or returning it to a former state. It appears only twice in the Quran, both times in this surah, describing a reversal already accomplished.
From the root for losing one's way. Early scholars discuss whether the causative here means active misleading or the withdrawal of guidance, and they record both readings side by side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A community deciding how to treat defectors had to weigh things pulling in opposite directions. There was kinship with the people concerned. There was the safety of the settlement. And there was the shame of turning on someone who had eaten in your house. Such disputes were not theoretical. They ran straight through families, since the people being discussed were often somebody's cousins.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing what happened to the group in this verse occurs only twice in the whole Quran. Both times fall in this surah, a few verses apart. Rare words clustered like that are one of the ways a long surah signals something. They show that two passages are handling a single situation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A limit is set on what one person's effort can do inside another. That is uncomfortable to hear. But it has a practical edge: it frees a community from a load it was never really carrying. Early scholars pair the verse with passages saying even the Prophet could not guide whom he loved. So the limit is on everyone, and it marks no one's failure.

crossReferences.why: States that even the Prophet cannot guide whom he loves, and that God guides whom He wills.
Uses the same rare verb of reversal a few verses later, of a closely related group.
Says guiding them is not upon you, in the middle of an instruction about giving.

studies.applyIt: Think of a person you have been trying to change, and count how many conversations you have spent on it. Then decide what you will still do for them once you stop trying. This verse sets a limit on one kind of effort. The useful question is what remains available after that limit is accepted.
studies.explainEasier: The believers had split into two groups. They argued about how to treat some people who had turned back. God says their own actions have already settled it. If God lets someone go astray, you cannot find a way for him.

studies.title: Wishing You Were The Same
studies.meaning: The passage concerns one specific group in a state of open war. They had professed belief, returned to the opposing side, and went on fighting from there. What is described is a wartime measure against combatants, and it is bounded at once. The very next verse removes from it anyone under treaty, anyone unwilling to fight either side, and anyone who withdraws and offers peace. Early scholars read the two verses together as one passage.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the years of open conflict between Medina and Mecca. Early scholars describe people who had joined the community and then left it, carrying what they knew and acting against it from outside. They read the passage as addressing that. The reports differ over which group is meant while agreeing on the wartime setting. The exception follows in the next breath.

keyTerms.note: From the same root as the word for affection used earlier in this surah. The wish described is for equivalence, that the difference between the two sides should disappear altogether.
A word for evenness, from the root meaning to make something level. The wish is not for conversion but for sameness, which would remove any ground for the community to stand apart.
The plural of the word for a close ally, used throughout this surah. In that society an alliance carried military obligation, so the term names a formal commitment rather than a friendship.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliance in Arabia was a declared and binding arrangement. It committed a group to fight alongside another and to shelter them. Switching sides during a conflict was a known risk. A party that had lived among you knew your defences and your numbers. The passage speaks to that risk in a setting where no neutral authority existed to judge.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction in this verse is qualified twice over in the verse right after it. That next verse names three separate groups it does not touch. They are those linked by treaty, those unwilling to fight either side, and those who withdraw and offer peace. The classical commentaries treat the two verses as a single unit for that reason.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage belongs to the Quran's treatment of one specific armed conflict, and its shape is instructive. A measure is stated and then bounded in the next breath. The bounds are drawn around anyone who steps back from fighting. That pattern recurs across the Quran's passages on war. There, dropping hostility steadily removes the ground for any response.

crossReferences.why: Immediately removes several categories from this, including anyone who withdraws and offers peace.
Instructs the community to incline to peace if the other side inclines to it, relying on God.
Sets a limit on fighting and warns against transgressing it in any circumstance whatever.

studies.applyIt: Read this verse together with the one after it, which is how the commentaries handle it. Notice what the second takes away from the first. Passages like this get quoted alone far more often than they are read in place. Getting into the habit of reading the next verse is a small discipline with a large effect.
studies.explainEasier: These people wish you would stop believing, so that you would be just like them. While they keep fighting you, God says not to take them as friends and allies. The next verse names those this does not cover.

studies.title: No Way Against Them
studies.meaning: War had already been declared on one group when this verse begins pulling people out of it. Some belong to a tribe you hold a treaty with, and that bond covers them. Others arrive with their chests tight at the thought of fighting you or fighting their own people. And anyone who steps back, stops fighting, and offers you peace is out of reach, because God "assigns no excuse for you against them." Early scholars treat those words as the ones that settle the matter.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina right after a wartime instruction, and it narrows that instruction at once. Early scholars describe a landscape where some tribes were tied to Medina by treaty, while others were caught between promises they could not square. The people this verse pulls out were real groups in that landscape, not imagined cases. That is how the classical commentaries read them, and it keeps the verse anchored to a war being fought.

keyTerms.note: A physical picture of reluctance, the tightness you feel facing something you cannot bring yourself to do. Naming an inner condition as grounds for exemption is unusual in a passage like this one.
The root means to separate yourself and stand apart. It describes a deliberate step back rather than a defeat, and that step back is what the whole exception rests on.
From the root that gives peace, safety and the greeting. The phrase is literally to throw peace toward someone, which pictures an offer tossed across the distance between two sides.

keyTerms.gloss: a way, a course of action
keyTerms.note: The ordinary Arabic word for a road. Saying God has made no road for you against them closes the possibility off entirely, rather than merely discouraging anyone from taking it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribal life produced men with duties on both sides of a fight. A mother's people here, a father's there, a treaty binding one and blood binding the other. Men like that often tried to stay out of a war entirely, and both sides distrusted them for it. This verse describes that man exactly, his chest tight at the thought of fighting either side, and it protects him.
studies.didYouKnow: A tight chest counts here as grounds for being left out of a war. An inner state is given real weight in a passage about fighting, and early scholars note how unusual that move is. The exception does not rest on a treaty or a public declaration. It rests on a reluctance that only the person feeling it could report.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse keeps narrowing a wartime instruction, and it says God is the one who did the narrowing. Nobody is handing down a favour from a position of strength. When someone stops fighting and offers peace, the way against them is simply not there, and that is put as a fact about the world rather than a kindness the stronger side chose. Peace offered is enough to close the matter.

crossReferences.why: States the wartime instruction this verse immediately narrows, and the two are read together throughout.
Tells the believers to lean toward peace whenever the other side leans toward it too.
Warns against denying the sincerity of someone who offers peace, out of desire for gain.

studies.applyIt: Think of a disagreement where the other person has already stepped back and you have not. Maybe they stopped replying, or conceded, or simply went quiet. Notice whether you are still building the case in your head. This verse closes a matter the moment the other side withdraws, and most private conflicts end long before we agree to stop.
studies.explainEasier: Some people are left out of this fight. That includes anyone tied to a group you have a treaty with, and anyone who comes to you unable to fight either side. If people step back and offer you peace, God leaves you no way against them.

studies.title: Security From Both Sides
studies.meaning: Here is a third group, and they are not like the two before them. They want to be safe with you and safe with their own people at the same time, so they keep both doors open. But every time the fighting pulls at them, they plunge back into it. The verse then names when they are treated as fighters, and each condition is something they failed to do: they did not withdraw, did not offer peace, did not hold their hands back. All three ways out stay open.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the middle of a real war, closing a run of verses about people caught between two sides. Early scholars identify those described as tribes who came to Medina asking for safety and then joined the other side whenever they were pressed. The reports vary over exactly who is meant, and they agree on the pattern. The tradition keeps this verse tied to that one conflict.

keyTerms.note: From a verb for testing metal in fire. The word covers persecution, temptation and internal conflict all at once, and early scholars read it here as the surrounding war these people kept being pulled into.

A passive form of a rare verb for overturning, used a few verses earlier of a different group. The passive hints at being carried along rather than choosing, though it does not excuse where they end up.
The same phrase used earlier in this surah for the instruction given during the Meccan years. Reusing it makes restraint the one standard being applied to both parties alike.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A small tribe standing between two larger powers was in a genuinely impossible spot. Playing both sides was a known way to survive, not some strange vice, and everyone understood it for what it was. So the problem this verse names is not confusion about right and wrong. It is a group that went back to fighting every time the pressure rose.
studies.didYouKnow: Every condition in this verse is stated as something not done: not withdrawing, not offering peace, not holding their hands back. Early scholars notice what that leaves behind. Three separate ways out stay open, and meeting any one of them would place a person outside what the verse describes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This verse is about a divided inside, and it shows that division in what a person keeps doing. What it describes is not quite lying. It is a failure to hold a position once the pressure comes. The verse records that plainly, without dressing it up, and its terms measure actions rather than feelings. What you do is the only part of you the other side can see.

crossReferences.why: Names the people placed outside this, including anyone who withdraws and offers peace.
Uses the same rare verb of reversal a few verses earlier, of a related group inside the city.
Sets limits on fighting and warns against crossing them under any circumstance at all.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you keep yourself safe with two groups at once by saying different things in each room. Everyone does some version of this, and from the inside it rarely feels like dishonesty. Pick the smaller of your two positions and say it out loud in the other room this week, then watch what happens.
studies.explainEasier: Some people want to be safe with you and safe with their own side too. But every time trouble starts, they jump back into it. If they will not step back, make peace, or stop fighting, they are treated as enemies.

studies.title: Unless By Mistake
studies.meaning: This should never happen, the verse says first. Then it turns to the case where it happens anyway, by accident. Three situations are told apart by who the person killed was. Each one carries its own mix of freeing someone held and paying the family, and the family may waive the payment. Where the means are simply not there, two months of fasting stand in their place. The whole of it is called a turning toward God, which changes what it is for.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Early scholars report a case where a man was killed by mistake during the fighting, at a time when you could not always tell which side a person was on. They read this passage as speaking into that kind of moment. The reports differ over the incident itself and agree on the setting. The surah is handling the practical fallout of a war fought between people who knew each other.

keyTerms.note: From a root for missing a mark, the opposite of hitting it. The word describes an act that went astray rather than one meant, and that is the whole basis of the difference being drawn.
A payment made to the relatives of someone killed, a practice already old in Arabia long before the Quran. Keeping it here sets a familiar custom inside a new frame of answering for what you do.
Literally the freeing of a neck. The Quran keeps attaching this to making amends, so that a wrong done is answered by ending someone else's bondage and not by payment alone.
The word for returning to God. Applying it to this whole set of measures makes them a movement in the person responsible, rather than the settling of a debt.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A killing in Arabia set off duties that could last for generations. The family who lost a man could demand blood, or take a payment instead, and the choice shaped ties between tribes for decades. Payment existed because feuds cost every side dearly, and they all knew the sums. This passage works inside that system rather than sweeping it away.
studies.didYouKnow: In one of the three cases here, no money goes to the family at all. That is when the person killed was a believer living among a people hostile to the Muslims, and only a freeing is asked. Early scholars explain that sending payment there would have strengthened the opposing side while the fighting was still going on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An accident is treated as carrying real weight here, without being treated as a crime, and that is a hard balance to hold. Something has to be done, and what is asked comes in three parts: a person freed, a family paid, and a turning back toward God. That last part keeps the whole thing from being a transaction. The person responsible is understood to have been changed by it.

crossReferences.why: States the completely different case of deliberate killing, in the verse right after this one.
Says that taking one life without cause is like killing the whole of humanity.
Addresses the family's option to give up retaliation, and calls that a lightening and a mercy.

studies.applyIt: Think of harm you caused without meaning to and settled with an apology. This passage asks for something past the apology: an actual act, costly enough that you feel it. Choose one and do it quietly, without telling the person concerned. The point is not to reopen anything, but to let the thing register somewhere.
studies.explainEasier: A believer should never kill another believer, unless it is a mistake. If it happens by mistake, he sets a believing slave free. He also pays money to the dead man's family. If he cannot do that, he fasts for two months in a row.

studies.title: Deliberately, And What Follows
studies.meaning: This is the other case, and it takes one sentence. Whoever kills a believer on purpose has Hell as his return. He stays there, God is angry with him, He curses him, and a terrible punishment waits. Early scholars say nothing else in the Quran gathers that much into one place. They also argued for ages over whether the staying means forever or is said for weight. The tradition kept a real range of views rather than one settled answer.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, right after the passage on killing by accident. Blood feuds and revenge killings were an ordinary part of Arabian life. Early scholars report that the first Muslims remarked on how severe this verse was. No occasion of revelation is reported for it. Scholars read it as a general statement rather than an answer to one event.

keyTerms.note: The root means a pillar or a support, so the verb suggests leaning on something on purpose. Intent is pictured as a thing you prop yourself against, not just something you happen to have.
A word for a return that matches what was given. It makes the punishment a match for the act rather than something added on top, which is how the Quran usually frames results.
The verb for anger, used of God only rarely across the Quran. Early scholars discuss what it can mean when said of God, and most read it as naming a relation of rejection.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Revenge killing was built into Arabian life, and many people thought it honourable. A man who did not avenge a relative lost standing among his own people. Killing inside a feud carried no shame at all. So a verse that put this much weight on killing on purpose spoke to something the first hearers had never treated as final.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where four results are stacked into a single sentence like this. Scholars of the classical period argued at length over whether the staying named here is absolute or said for force. The tradition holds several views on it and never settled on one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Killing on purpose sits at the far edge of what the Quran describes. The old argument around it matters as much as the severity does. Scholars held this next to the wide promise of forgiveness given earlier in this same surah. They refused to fold either one into the other. The tradition keeps that tension open instead of tidying it away.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the accidental case just before, with a completely different set of consequences.
Says earlier in this surah that God forgives anything short of setting up partners with Him.
Names killing among the gravest wrongs, then describes repentance and a changing of deeds.

studies.applyIt: Sit with how far this verse goes, and notice that the tradition never smoothed it out. Then think about the smaller cruelties you allow yourself, the ones that damage a person slowly rather than all at once. The distance between the two is real, and it is also shorter than most of us prefer to think.
studies.explainEasier: Killing a believer on purpose is one of the worst things a person can do. The Quran names a long and heavy punishment for it. Nothing else in the whole book is answered in quite that way.

studies.title: You Were Like This Before
studies.meaning: You are on the road, armed, and a stranger calls out a greeting of peace. The verse tells you to establish the facts, and it says so twice. The mistake it names is telling that man his belief is not genuine, and the motive it names is gain, "the goods of this world." Then the tone shifts entirely. You yourselves were like this once, and God favoured you. The case against the mistake is not a rule. It is a memory you have to go and find.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Early scholars report an incident on an expedition: a man greeted an armed party with a declaration of peace, and they killed him and took his goods, certain he had said it only to save himself. The reports differ over names and details, and they agree on the substance. They describe this verse as the answer to what happened that day.

keyTerms.note: The root means separating and telling apart, so the verb means making a thing clear by setting it apart. It turns up twice in this verse, opening the instruction and then closing it.
A word for something that passes across, used of things that do not last. Naming the motive with this word judges it in the same breath as naming it.
The word for peace, used here of the greeting itself. The man is killed for the very act by which he said he was not an enemy, and that is what the verse exposes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A traveller who met an armed party in open country had one tool. He called out a greeting, loud enough to be heard from a distance, and everyone knew it as the sign that a man came in peace. Treating that greeting as a trick took away the only guard an unarmed man had. That is why this verse speaks about the greeting itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The order to check the facts turns up twice inside one verse, once at the start and once at the end. Early scholars call that repeat unusual, even in a book that repeats often. They read the two as brackets around the whole argument, so everything between them sits inside a single insistence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument here runs through memory rather than through a principle. You once stood where the other person stands now, and from the outside you looked no different. Then you were given something you had not earned. So the failure is forgetting, not a failure to know the rule. Being thankful for your own past becomes the ground on which you hear another person's claim.

crossReferences.why: Tells the believers to check a report before acting, so no people are harmed in ignorance.
Removes any course of action against those who withdraw from fighting and offer peace.
Reminds the community that they were once few and weak, before God gave them shelter.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose sincerity you doubt, and try to recall a time when yours would have looked just as thin from outside. Most of us have been at that stage and forgotten it quickly. The argument here runs entirely through that memory, and it only works if you go and retrieve it.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people not to say that someone is lying about being at peace, just so they can take his things. Find out the truth first. Remember that you once looked the same way to other people.

studies.title: Not Equal, But Both Promised
studies.meaning: Some went out and some stayed home, and this verse says plainly that the two are not equal. Those who strive with their wealth and their persons stand one degree above those who sit. Then, in the middle of the sentence, an exception arrives: anyone who genuinely cannot go is taken out of the comparison. And God has promised good to both. Early scholars note that the verse ranks people without shutting anyone out of the promise.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the years of conflict. Early scholars report that the clause about being unable was added after a man who could not see asked whether the first part of the verse applied to him. The reports agree on the substance of that incident. The verse stands at the close of this surah's long stretch about those who went and those who stayed.

keyTerms.note: A participle from the verb to sit. It describes a position rather than passing a judgement, which is why the verse can go on to promise good to these people as well.
A word for damage or injury, used here of a condition that stops someone from acting. It covers limitation broadly rather than naming any particular kind of disability.
From the root for a stair or a rank. A single step is named, which measures the difference exactly rather than describing a gap that cannot be crossed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: When the community set out, it left behind the old, the ill, those with no mount, and those needed at home. The gap between going and staying was plain to see. Those who stayed watched the others leave, and then lived with how that had looked. A verse that both ranked and reassured was treating a real wound in a small town.
studies.didYouKnow: Early scholars report that the clause about being unable came only after a man who could not see raised the question. Views differ on the details, and the tradition keeps that order of events. The clause does sit in the verse as a break inside a sentence that otherwise runs straight through.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This verse ranks people without condemning anyone, which is rare. One step separates the two groups, and the same sentence promises good to both, so the ranking never shuts anyone out. The exception then lifts ability out of the comparison entirely. What is being measured is what a person did with what they actually had.

crossReferences.why: States that no blame lies on the blind, the lame or the ill, in a closely similar exemption.
Says there is no way against the weak or ill who are sincere toward God and His Messenger.
States that God burdens no soul beyond what it can bear, the idea behind such exemptions.

studies.applyIt: Compare yourself to someone else this week, as you probably will anyway. Then correct for what each of you actually had: time, health, money, a family that helped or did not. This verse makes that correction openly, in a clause dropped into the middle of a sentence. The corrected view is usually fairer and more useful.
studies.explainEasier: God says people who go out and give their time and money are not the same as people who stay behind. But anyone who is unwell or unable is not being compared at all. God promises good to both groups.

studies.title: Degrees, Forgiveness And Mercy
studies.meaning: This verse hands out three things, and the order they come in carries the weight. Ranks come first, then forgiveness, then mercy. What began as a comparison of effort ends in something nobody earns. Early scholars note that the plural for degrees is left open, since neither how many there are nor how far apart they lie is ever said. The two names of God that end it repeat the last two gifts, so the promise turns into a description of the one who makes it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This verse completes a statement about those who strove and those who stayed behind, which is why it runs so short. It finishes a sentence begun in the verse before, and early scholars treat the two as a single unit. It closes this surah's long stretch on how the community acted during the fighting, just before the text turns to migration.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a stair, left open here. The verse before named one degree, and this one opens into a number never stated, which early scholars read as a deliberate widening.
From a root meaning to cover something protectively, the way a helmet covers the head. Forgiveness in Arabic is pictured as the covering of a fault rather than its erasure.
From the root that also gives the word for a womb. The connection is old and deliberate, tying mercy to the bond between a mother and what she carries.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rank in Arabian society was public and finely graded. Where you sat in a gathering, whose name came first when a family line was recited, who spoke before whom. Everyone knew their own place and could name the people above and below them. A promise of degrees landed in a society that already measured itself that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names that close this verse, the Forgiving and the Merciful, end more verses together than any other pair in the Quran. Here they repeat, as names of God, the two things the verse has just promised. The promise and the one who makes it share a single set of words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ranks mean measuring and comparing, and the two words that follow them cut against that. Forgiveness deals with what falls short, and mercy is not earned at all. So a verse about striving ends by naming two things no striving can produce, which keeps the ranking from turning into a ledger. What you are given outruns what you can count.

crossReferences.why: Draws the distinction this verse completes, between those who strove and those who remained.
States that all have degrees according to what they did, and God is not unaware.
Says God raises in degrees those who believe and those given knowledge among you.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this short verse moves from ranking to forgiveness in three words. Whatever you are measuring yourself against right now, set beside it one thing you were simply given and did not earn. Hold both at once. The verse does not choose between them, and the discomfort of holding both is roughly the point.
studies.explainEasier: God promises people who tried hard for Him different levels of reward. He also promises to cover their faults and to be kind to them. Those last two are gifts, and not prizes anyone won.

studies.title: Was God's Earth Not Vast
studies.meaning: Death arrives, and the verse lets you hear the conversation. The angels ask these people what state they were in, and they answer that they were held down and could not act. The reply is a question about the size of the earth, whether God's earth was not wide enough to emigrate in. Early scholars are careful to read this beside the verse that follows, which excuses anyone who truly had no means. What is answered here is the excuse, not the hardship.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Early scholars identify those described as people who had accepted the message in Mecca and stayed there, and in some reports went out with the opposing side. The reports differ over which individuals are meant, while they agree that the passage concerns those who could have left and did not. The exemption in the next verse is treated as part of the same statement.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to receive something completely, used of collecting a debt in full. Death is described as the taking of what is owed rather than as an ending or a loss.
A passive form, so the weakness is done to them rather than owned. The same word is used a few verses earlier of people the community was being urged to act for.
An adjective for wide open space, from a root meaning to have room. Applied to God's earth, it answers a claim of being hemmed in by describing how much was available.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving Mecca meant giving up a house, a share in the family trade, and the safety of a clan. You arrived somewhere else with nothing, living off other people. It was neither romantic nor easy, and some who could have gone kept what they had instead. Everyone in Medina knew both kinds of people, and knew which relatives had chosen what.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of very few places in the Quran that report a conversation at the moment of death as direct speech on both sides. Early scholars note that the questions are left open. The excuse is spoken by the people themselves, in their own words, rather than summed up for them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The excuse gets an answer, which means excuses are looked at rather than waved away or simply taken. The reply asks what options there really were, and the next verse then excuses exactly those who had none. Put together, the two show that what you answer for matches what you could do. They also show that a claim of having no choice is itself checked.

crossReferences.why: Exempts those who genuinely had no means and no way out, and holds out pardon for them.
Tells those mindful of God that His earth is spacious, using the same argument about room.
Addresses believing servants directly: My earth is wide, so worship Me within it.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you have described to yourself as impossible, and write down what you would actually have to give up in order to do it. This is not to shame you into doing it. Some things really are impossible, and the next verse says so plainly. But writing it down is what separates the two cases.
studies.explainEasier: At death, angels ask people why they stayed where they could not live their faith. The people say they were held down and had no power. The angels ask if God's earth was not big enough to move to.

studies.title: No Means And No Way
studies.meaning: The verse before pressed hard, and this one carves out the people it does not reach. They are men, women and children who could arrange nothing and could find no route out. Two different lacks are named here: one is having no means, the other is not knowing where to go. Then comes pardon, worded with a particle of possibility rather than a flat promise. Early scholars discuss it and mostly read it as certainty said with restraint.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, and this qualifies the verse just before it. Early scholars report that some believers in Mecca truly could not leave: they had no money, or no escort, or no leave from the people who held them. This passage is about those people. Some reports name individuals and others describe the group, and they agree throughout on the substance of the exemption.

keyTerms.gloss: a means, a way of contriving
keyTerms.note: A word for a device or stratagem, from a root about turning something around. It names practical capacity, the ability to arrange something, rather than willingness or courage.

keyTerms.gloss: find a way, know the route
keyTerms.note: The verb for being guided, applied here to a road. It names a second and different lack: not only no means, but no knowledge of where the road actually runs.
An intensive form from a root meaning to erase a trace, as wind erases footprints in sand. It suggests removing the mark rather than merely holding back punishment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The road from Mecca to Medina ran for several days across desert. It took a mount, food and water, and someone who knew where the wells were. A person with no money and no standing could not simply set out, and a woman or a child could not travel alone at all. The two conditions named here describe exactly what that journey took.
studies.didYouKnow: The small word of possibility used here also opens other statements about God's forgiveness in the Quran. Early scholars note what happens when God is its subject: the tradition reads it as certainty put in the shape of hope. Nothing can place a condition on God, so the restraint belongs to the way we are addressed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The excuse here rests on being unable, not on what anyone meant. Nothing is said about what these people felt or wanted, and what counts is that no road existed. So what a person answers for stays inside what was possible for them. The pardon that follows arrives as a name of God rather than a decision taken once, which makes it a matter of who He is.

crossReferences.why: Presses the excuse this verse exempts, and the two are read together as one statement.
States that God burdens no soul beyond what it can bear, the idea behind this exemption.
Describes people in exactly this condition, calling out for a protector and a helper.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have quietly judged for not getting out of a situation: a job, a marriage, a country, a debt. List what leaving would actually require of them, item by item. This exemption turns on means and on knowing a route, and most judgements of that kind collapse once the list is written.
studies.explainEasier: Some people were too weak or too poor to leave, and they had no way to go. They are not blamed for staying. God may well pardon them, because He knows they had no real choice.

studies.title: Room Enough On Earth
studies.meaning: Leaving home is frightening, and this verse answers the fear with two promises: a place of refuge, and room. The first word is unusual. Its root is about forcing an opponent's nose into the dust, so what is promised carries a note of being set right, not shelter alone. Then the verse turns to the person who sets out and dies on the road, and says his reward has already fallen due upon God.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the passage on those who stayed and those who left. Early scholars report that a man set out from Mecca and died before he reached Medina. That was the occasion for the words about dying on the road, and this verse settled where he stood. The reports differ over his name and agree on the incident, which the tradition treats as well established.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning the nose in the dust. Early scholars read it as a place where you escape those who forced you to go, so it carries shelter and a reversal of humiliation together.
From the root for width, used of room and of ample provision at once. It answers the fear behind staying, which was that leaving would mean arriving with nothing at all.
A verb for something falling into place, used of a payment becoming due. The reward is described as settled at the moment of setting out, before there is any arrival.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Emigrants reached Medina with nothing, and local families took them in and shared what they had. Some never got their old standing back, while others did well within a few years. Both outcomes were there to see in the streets of the city. So a promise of room was given to people who knew for themselves how uncertain leaving really was.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this verse uses for a place of refuge appears nowhere else in the Quran. It comes from an image of forcing an opponent's face into the dust. Translators usually give it simply as refuge, which loses the note of being set right that the classical commentaries record in it again and again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reward here is tied to setting out, not to arriving, which cuts it loose from the outcome altogether. A person who dies on the road has already done what was asked of him. That says something about how what you intend and what you do are weighed. Early scholars link it with other passages where God rewards what was taken up rather than what was reached.

crossReferences.why: Presses the question of why they did not emigrate, which this verse answers with a promise.
Promises good in this world to those who emigrated after being wronged, and more beyond.
Tells believing servants that God's earth is wide, so they may worship Him within it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a change you have not made because you cannot see how it would work out. This verse attaches the reward to leaving rather than to arriving. Take the first step of that change this week, the smallest one available, and do it without requiring yourself to know what follows.
studies.explainEasier: Anyone who leaves home for God will find many places to go, and plenty of room. If someone dies on the way, God still gives him his full reward.

studies.title: When You Travel The Land
studies.meaning: You are days from home, watching the horizon, and the prayer still has to be made. The verse says there is no blame on you for shortening it, which is a gift rather than an order. It also attaches a condition about fearing harm from those who reject the message. Early scholars discussed that condition at length: some read travel on its own as enough, while others tied the shortening to the danger named. The verse names the situation and leaves the discussion open.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at a time when leaving the city carried real risk. Early scholars report that the community went on shortening prayers on journeys after the danger had passed, until someone raised the question. The answer described the shortening as a gift given to them. The reports agree on the substance and differ over the exact wording.

keyTerms.gloss: travel, strike out in the land
keyTerms.note: The verb literally means to strike. Arabic uses it of setting out on a journey, picturing travel as striking the ground with your feet across a long distance.
From a root meaning to lean or tilt, the same one that gives the word for a wing. A fault is pictured as a leaning away from straightness rather than a broken rule.

keyTerms.gloss: harm you, put you to trial
keyTerms.note: From the verb for testing metal in fire. It covers attack, persecution and disruption together, which is why early scholars discuss what kind of danger the condition really names.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A journey out of Medina meant days in open country. A party could be seen from far off, and stopping made you easier to spot. Travellers moved from well to well on a schedule set by their water, so anything that made a halt shorter cut the time they stood exposed. This concession meant something plain and immediate to anyone who had made that trip.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase this verse uses for travel is literally about striking the ground. The same wording appears elsewhere in the Quran for journeys made to seek provision. Arabic keeps that physical picture inside its ordinary word for travelling, so setting out and striking are named by one verb.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse lifts blame rather than giving an order, and that shape matters. Nothing is being required of you here; a weight is being taken off. The same shape comes back across the Quran wherever hardship is being met. It means the relief is described from where the person carrying the difficulty stands, not from where rules are made.

crossReferences.why: Continues into the arrangement of prayer under direct threat, in much greater detail.
Uses the same shape of relief for the sick and the traveller during the fast.
States that no hardship has been placed upon this community in matters of religion.

studies.applyIt: Notice how reluctant you are to accept something offered to make things easier: the shorter route, the lighter version, the help someone volunteered. Many people find it easier to be strict than to be met halfway. This verse lifts a weight rather than adding one, and accepting that is its own small discipline.
studies.explainEasier: When you are travelling and afraid that people may harm you, you can make your prayers shorter. God says no one will blame you for that.

studies.title: Prayer With Weapons Held
studies.meaning: An enemy is close, and the prayer still happens. One group stands with the leader while the other faces outward, weapons in hand, and then the two change places. The verse then lets weapons be set down in rain or illness, and it repeats the order about caution right after. Early scholars note how much of this is practical detail. The prayer is never stopped here, only rearranged around the danger.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at a time when the community expected attack while out in the field. Early scholars tie this arrangement to particular expeditions. They record that it was done in more than one form, and pass on several accounts of how the two groups changed over. They treat those differences as signs of adapting, not as a quarrel about the passage.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to go around, the same one behind the word for circling. It names a group defined by its movement within the arrangement rather than by who belongs to it.
The plural of a word for a weapon or an instrument. Repeating it several times in one verse keeps the practical situation present inside a passage about prayer.
The noun for wariness, treated as something you take up. It appears twice here, at the start of the arrangement and again after the concession, closing on caution rather than relief.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An armed party in open country was at its weakest the moment it stopped. Laying weapons aside, kneeling, turning your eyes from the horizon: that was exactly when a watching enemy would come. Anyone who had travelled with a caravan knew it in his bones. So this arrangement reads as tactics rather than ceremony.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the longest passage in the Quran on how to arrange a prayer in practice, longer than anything said about prayer in ordinary times. Early scholars note that imbalance. The way of praying is spelled out in detail only where praying is hard.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This passage assumes the prayer goes on in conditions that would stop almost any other activity. It arranges the danger around the prayer, rather than the prayer around the danger. And it takes the danger completely seriously, since the order about weapons and caution comes twice. Neither side is allowed to push the other out, and that refusal is the heart of it.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with what happens once safety returns, restoring the ordinary form.
Gives a briefer provision for prayer in fear, on foot or mounted, in another surah.
Uses the same word for taking precaution earlier in this surah, in a different setting.

studies.applyIt: Think of the thing you drop first when life gets hard. For most people it is not the urgent thing but the quiet one that holds everything else together. This passage rearranges the difficulty around the practice, instead of the practice around the difficulty. Try that once this week, with whatever your own version is.
studies.explainEasier: Even when an enemy is close, the prayer still happens. One group prays while the others keep watch with their weapons, and then they change over. God does not want the group caught off guard.

studies.title: Standing, Sitting, Lying Down
studies.meaning: The prayer ends, and the verse keeps you going. Remember God standing, or sitting, or lying on your sides, and between them those three cover every position a body can take. That is the point: remembrance runs on, while the prayer has edges. Once you feel secure, the ordinary form comes back. And the prayer is called fixed at set times, in a word borrowed from the vocabulary of timekeeping, which early scholars read as the source of its regularity.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, right after the arrangement for praying under threat, and the order is deliberate. First the special form is described, and then what happens once the exception ends. Early scholars read this verse as finishing that passage rather than opening a new subject. They also note that it states the general point about set times, which is rarely put so directly anywhere else.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers both calling to mind and saying aloud, which Arabic does not separate. Remembrance in the Quran is therefore never purely inward, and never merely spoken either.
From a root meaning to come to rest, used of ground that stops shaking and of a heart that stops fearing. It names the return of calm rather than the removal of danger.
A passive participle from the root for time, appearing only here in the Quran. It describes something appointed to specific hours rather than merely regular or often repeated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in that world was read from the sky and the ground. People watched the length of a shadow, the position of the sun, the first light on the horizon. There were no clocks, and appointments were made by naming a moment of the day everyone could see. A practice fixed to times was tied to the same signs that governed travel, work and rest.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this verse uses for something fixed to set times occurs only here in the whole Quran. Modern Arabic took the same root for its everyday words for timing and schedule. A term used once in scripture became the ordinary vocabulary of clocks and calendars.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things sit side by side here. One is bounded by hours, and the other is not bounded by posture at all. Remembrance in every position covers the whole of a life, while prayer is fixed to set moments inside it. Neither takes the place of the other. The shape suggests that the bounded practice is what keeps the unbounded one going, rather than competing with it.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who remember God standing, sitting and on their sides, using the same postures.
Contrasts this with those who remember God only a little when they stand for prayer.
Names the times of prayer by the movement of the sun and the recitation of dawn.

studies.applyIt: Pick one posture you are often in and rarely think in: waiting in a queue, lying awake, sitting in traffic. Attach one short remembrance to it this week, the same words each time. This verse names postures rather than occasions, which is a practical hint about where remembrance actually fits.
studies.explainEasier: After you finish praying, keep God in mind while standing, sitting or lying down. When things are calm again, pray the normal way. The prayer is set for certain times of the day.

studies.title: They Ache As You Ache
studies.meaning: You are wounded and exhausted, and the verse tells you not to weaken in the pursuit. Then it argues, and the argument is built on sameness. If you are aching, they are aching just as you are, and the Arabic verb for pain repeats three times in one clause so that you hear it. One thing is not the same: you expect something from God that they cannot expect. Early scholars note that the verse grants the pain rather than denying it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, after a costly battle, with the community worn out. Early scholars tie this verse to a pursuit made while men were still carrying wounds. They describe the instruction as reaching a group who had every ordinary reason to stop. The reports agree on the setting and differ over which occasion is meant.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be feeble or thin. It describes strength draining away rather than a decision to stop, which is why the instruction addresses a process rather than a choice.
The ordinary verb for suffering pain, in the body or otherwise. It occurs three times within one clause here, applied to both sides, and that is what builds the sameness.
A verb combining expectation with hope, used of awaiting something you have reason to look for. It names the one difference the verse offers, and it is not about strength.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: After a battle both sides pulled back with wounded men and made camp within a day's ride of each other. Everyone knew the other side was in the same state. But you feel your own exhaustion from the inside, and can only dimly picture what anyone else feels. This argument spoke to men who could see their own losses and not the losses across the field.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic verb for feeling pain turns up three times inside one short clause here. That is unusually dense, even for a book that repeats on purpose. Early scholars read the density as doing the work of the argument, so you hear the sameness before you reason it out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Endurance here rests on seeing the situation clearly, not on an appeal to strength. Both sides suffer the same, so pain is no evidence about who is failing. The one difference named is what you expect from God. That says hope, rather than capacity, is what separates people under the same pressure. Nothing at all is promised about the outcome.

crossReferences.why: Tells the community not to weaken or grieve, since they are the higher if they believe.
Attaches the same reward to both possible outcomes, taking results out of the reckoning.
Describes those who did not weaken at what befell them, nor lose heart, nor give in.

studies.applyIt: When something is hard, you compare your inside to other people's outside. Take one situation where you feel you are struggling more than everyone else. Ask honestly what you can actually see of their condition, which is usually very little. That correction alone changes how long you can keep going.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the believers not to give up when chasing the enemy. Yes, it hurts, but the other side hurts just as much. The difference is that you are hoping for something from God, and they are not.

studies.title: Judge By What You Are Shown
studies.meaning: A case is in front of you, and one side has told its story well. This verse says why the Book came down: so that judgement between people follows what God has shown, not what one side presents. Then it draws a line. Do not be an advocate for those who deceive. Early scholars note that the warning is about taking a side, not about getting it wrong. The risk named is arguing on the wrong side of a case.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. The classical commentaries tie this verse and the ones after it to a theft in the city. The man who did it tried to push the blame onto an innocent neighbour, and at first the community took his side. The reports agree on the substance and differ over the details. They treat this passage as the correction.

keyTerms.note: A word covering truth, reality and a rightful claim together. Its breadth means the Book is described as sent with what is real and with what is owed, inside a single phrase.
A causative from the verb to see. Judgement is grounded in something shown rather than worked out, which early scholars discuss carefully in relation to how a judge reasons.
From the root for arguing against someone. It names a person who takes a side and argues it, which is exactly the role this verse warns against taking.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dispute in Medina was argued in public. Whoever had standing to speak for a family spoke for it, and fine speech often decided a case as much as evidence did. A well-connected family could put up speakers a poor man had no way to match. The warning here addresses a system in which that was exactly what the powerful wanted.
studies.didYouKnow: These verses are among the very few in the Quran that answer one actual crime in Medina, and they run on for several verses rather than one. Early scholars note that the passage corrects the community, not the accused. That is unusual for a text that grows out of a wrong done.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse pulls apart two things that feel the same from the inside. One is judging by what is true. The other is arguing for someone you already lean toward. The second can spoil the first without the person noticing, because a man who argues a case comes to believe it. Grounding judgement in what God has shown puts the standard outside the person using it.

crossReferences.why: Instructs standing firmly for justice even against yourselves, your parents and your relatives.
Continues the warning, against arguing on behalf of those who deceive themselves.
Warns that hatred of a people must not lead you away from being just toward them.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last argument you took part in where you were, in effect, someone's advocate. Ask what you would have concluded if you had heard those same facts about a stranger. The line here falls between judging and taking a side, and most of us slide from one to the other without ever deciding to.
studies.explainEasier: God sent the Book down with the truth, so that people would be judged by what God has shown. The Book also warns against taking the side of people who cheat.

studies.title: Do Not Argue For Them
studies.meaning: Two short instructions follow the correction, and both land on the reader rather than the wrongdoer. First, ask God for forgiveness. Early scholars read that as covering the community's own readiness to take the wrong side. Second, do not argue for those who betray themselves. The wording is exact: the deceit is aimed at the deceivers, not at anyone else, and that is where the harm is placed.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This continues the passage that arose from a theft in the city, where suspicion was pushed onto an innocent man. Early scholars describe a community that closed around one of its own before finding out what had happened. These two verses address that reflex head on, moving from correcting the judgement to correcting the impulse behind it.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb meaning to ask for covering. The request is for a fault to be covered rather than argued away, which is the opposite of what the verse has just warned against.
A reflexive form of the verb for betrayal. It makes the deceiver into the person deceived, which places the injury inside the one committing the act.
An intensive form describing a settled pattern rather than a single act. That intensity is what keeps the statement from covering anyone who has betrayed a trust only once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Family and tribe closed around an accused member almost at once. Failing to do so was itself a kind of betrayal in the eyes of your relatives. Standing back while your own man was looked into cost you standing with everyone who shared your name. That reflex is what these verses work against, and it was very strong.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for betrayal here is turned back on the people doing it, so they are betraying themselves. The Quran uses that construction for several wrongs, among them the phrase about wronging your own soul. The grammar keeps putting the injury back onto the person who did the act.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Asking forgiveness comes first, before the instruction not to defend the guilty. Correction starts with the person being corrected, not with the offender. Then habitual treachery is named as what God does not love, in an intensive form that marks a settled character rather than a single failure. That leaves room for the person who has betrayed a trust once.

crossReferences.why: States the standard this passage applies, judging by what God has shown rather than by loyalty.
Asks who will argue on their behalf when the Day of Resurrection actually comes.
Follows with the promise that whoever does wrong and seeks forgiveness will find God forgiving.

studies.applyIt: Notice the moment you start defending someone before you know what happened, usually because they are yours. That instinct is loyalty, and it is not worthless. But hold it for one day before you speak, and use the day to find out. Most of the harm here is done in the first hour, by people acting on a good motive.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the believers to ask Him for forgiveness. He also tells them not to speak up for people who lie and cheat. Those people are really only cheating themselves.

studies.title: Hidden From People, Not God
studies.meaning: People hide what they are doing, and this verse lets that hiding stand for a moment before it falls apart. They hide from other people and cannot hide from God, and He is with them while they plan their words in the night. The Arabic verb for that planning is the same one used earlier in this surah of a different group. And God is named as encompassing what they do, surrounding it rather than watching from outside.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the passage that arose from a theft in the city where suspicion was pushed elsewhere. Early scholars describe the plan being made at night, among people who had counted on the community believing them. The picture of arranging things by night matches those reports exactly. The same verb has already appeared earlier in this surah for a similar situation.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to try to become hidden, so effort is built into the verb. Concealment is described as something attempted rather than achieved, which the rest of the sentence confirms.
From the word for a house or for passing the night. The verb was used earlier in this surah of a different group, linking the two passages by vocabulary rather than by subject.
From a root meaning to enclose on all sides, used of a wall around a garden. It describes knowledge as containment rather than as watching from some distance away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Houses in Medina stood close together and had thin walls, so privacy meant waiting until everyone slept. Talk that could not be held in daylight was held after the last prayer, in a courtyard or an inner room. The picture in this verse is exact. Night was when people in that city actually arranged things they did not want overheard.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing God as encompassing comes from the same root as the Arabic for a wall or an enclosure. The image is about space rather than sight. So the verse describes knowledge as something a person is inside of, which is a different picture from simply being watched.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse names the illusion that makes hiding feel like it works. The audience you hide from is human, and getting past them feels like getting away with it. What follows is not a threat but a description of where everyone is standing. If God is with them while they plan, the hiding was never even tried on the party that mattered.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for planning at night, of a different group earlier in this surah.
Says God is with them wherever they are, present as a fourth to any three conferring.
Names God as knowing the treachery of the eyes and whatever the breasts conceal.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you would adjust if one particular person could see it. Not something shameful, necessarily, just something you set for an audience. Then ask which audience you are actually working for. The point here is not surveillance. It is that most concealment is aimed at the wrong party entirely.
studies.explainEasier: People can hide what they are doing from other people. They cannot hide it from God. He is right there with them while they plan at night, and He knows all of it.

studies.title: Who Will Argue For Them
studies.meaning: The passage turns the community's own behaviour into a question. Here you are, arguing for them in this life, while the case is still in front of you. Then it asks who will argue with God for them on the Day of Resurrection, and who will stand as their representative. Neither question is answered. Early scholars note the shift in scale, and one verb for arguing covers both settings, which is what makes the comparison land.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This closes the sequence that arose from a theft in the city and the community's readiness to defend the accused. Early scholars describe the passage as addressed to those who had spoken up before finding out the facts. The verse completes the correction by throwing the same behaviour forward into the next life. The reports treat the episode as well established.

keyTerms.note: A construction placing two demonstratives together, an emphatic address that points straight at the hearers. It has the tone of turning to face somebody in the middle of a conversation.
From a root meaning to twist a rope tightly. Argument is pictured as two strands wound against each other, which suits a word used here of contesting somebody's case.
A word for someone appointed to act on another person's behalf. It is used of God elsewhere in this surah, and the question asks who else could possibly fill that role.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Legal standing in Arabia ran through representation. A person without a strong advocate had no real way to press a claim, and families spent effort on producing men who could speak well. This verse asks who will speak for someone on the Day of Resurrection. It takes the most familiar shape of justice they had and removes it, leaving a person standing alone.
studies.didYouKnow: The same verb for arguing on someone's behalf turns up twice within a few verses here. Once it closes off the act in this life, and once it asks who could do it in the next. Early scholars note that the repeat ties the passage together, so a warning and a question turn on one word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse throws a present behaviour into a setting where it is plainly useless. Speaking up for someone is real and it works in this world, which is exactly why people invest in it. The question shows what it can reach and what it cannot. Then the question about a representative takes away the last structure a person might lean on. The case is left standing alone.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction this verse enforces, against arguing for those who deceive themselves.
Describes a day when no soul helps another and no one is allowed to speak up for it.
Pictures people arriving alone, without the go-betweens they had claimed would stand beside them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a favour you have relied on being able to call in: someone who would speak for you, smooth something over, vouch for you. Notice how much of your sense of safety rests on it. This verse is not saying such people are worthless. It asks what remains when they are not in the room.
studies.explainEasier: Right now some people are speaking up for those who did wrong. The passage asks who will speak up for them in front of God. It asks who will stand there for them on the last day.

studies.title: Whoever Wrongs His Own Soul
studies.meaning: Two sentences here, and they pull in opposite directions on purpose. The first begins with a wrong done, to anyone or to your own soul, and ends with finding God forgiving and merciful. Nothing at all is placed between the seeking and the finding. Early scholars point to the verb: a person does not so much receive forgiveness as discover it was already there. Then comes the line that shuts an easy way out, since a sin is earned against yourself and nobody else carries it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, following the passage about a man who stole and then tried to push the blame onto an innocent person. Early scholars report that case in detail, though their accounts of the names and details differ. These two verses draw the general lesson out of it. The door back is open, and moving a wrong onto someone else is exactly what the verses around them have just refused.

keyTerms.note: The root means to put something where it does not belong, and it also gives the word for darkness. Wrongdoing is a misplacing, and the first party damaged is the one who does it.
A verb of discovery rather than of receiving. It suggests the forgiveness was there to be found, and that the seeking is what brings a person to where it already was.
Trade vocabulary for gain made through effort. Using it of sin makes wrongdoing something worked for and piled up, held in an account belonging to whoever did the work.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Guilt in a clan was rarely private. A theft stuck to a whole family, and blood money for a killing was raised across the kin group, so a wrong was shared out by default. Moving blame onto an outsider or a weaker household was practical, not just dishonest. These verses cut against a habit everyone listening knew from the inside.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of names for God at the end of each verse is doing work. The first ends with forgiving and merciful, the second with knowing and wise. So the sentence that offers pardon and the sentence that fixes responsibility are sealed with different qualities. Matching those closing names to the content runs right through these Medinan passages.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness is described as available before it is asked for, and that changes what asking is. You are not talking God round. You are locating something. The second verse then refuses to let mercy blur who answers for what, since a wrong stays attached to whoever did it and cannot be passed to a scapegoat or soaked up by a group. The open door and answering for your own acts sit side by side, with no strain between them.

crossReferences.why: Extends the same offer at its widest, addressing those who have wronged themselves greatly.
Says that no bearer of burdens carries the burden of another person.
Continues the passage, describing the person who throws his own fault onto someone innocent.

studies.applyIt: Think of a fault you have always told with a reason attached, where circumstances or another person explain most of it. Try telling it once, silently, without the reason. The verse puts nothing between asking and finding. What usually stands in the way is the account we have practised.
studies.explainEasier: If you do something wrong, even to yourself, you can ask God to forgive you. You will find that He is ready to. But if you keep doing wrong, the harm lands on you, and not on anyone else.

studies.title: Blaming An Innocent Person
studies.meaning: Something goes wrong, and the easiest thing in the world is to let it land on someone else. The verse describes exactly that. A person commits a fault, then throws it at someone who did nothing. The Arabic verb for the throwing is physical, the one used of hurling a stone. And what he carries away is named twice over, as a barefaced lie and as plain wrongdoing. So the deflection counts as its own offence, not as the first one made worse.
