studies.historicalContext: Medina. This closes the passage that arose from a theft in the city, where the man responsible pointed suspicion at a neighbour. Early scholars read this verse as stating the principle behind the whole episode and lifting it clear of that one case. Its wording is general, with no names and no details, which is how the classical commentaries treat its role.

keyTerms.note: The verb for throwing a stone or a spear. Applied to accusation it makes the act physical, something launched at a person, and the same root gives Arabic its word for slandering.
From a root meaning to be free of something, also used of recovering from illness. Innocence is described as being clear of a thing rather than as a quality a person owns.
A verb for shouldering a load and bearing it away. It pictures the wrong as weight moved onto the person's own back at the very moment he tried to shift it elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a city where a theft was looked into by asking the neighbours, an accusation moved fast and left a mark no later finding could remove. There were no records with which to clear a name. A man wrongly named carried it in how people traded with him, married into his family, and spoke of him for years.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a barefaced lie here already appeared earlier in this same surah, where it described a husband taking back a dowry after a separation. The reuse links two very different situations by one term. That is a pattern in this surah: shared words mark two passages as one underlying failure.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse separates the wrong from the covering up, and weighs the covering up on its own. That matters, because deflection usually feels like protecting yourself rather than attacking anyone. The verse insists that it is aimed at somebody. And the picture of shouldering a load makes the transfer fail, since what was pushed onto another ends up carried by the one who pushed.

crossReferences.why: Opens the passage this verse closes, warning against advocacy for those who deceive.
Asks why believing men and women did not think well of one another when an accusation circulated.
Says those who injure believing men and women without cause bear slander and clear sin.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you let someone else absorb the consequence of something you did, even partly, even by staying quiet while they were blamed. Go back to it this week, at least in words, with the one person who would need to hear it. This verse counts the silence and the accusation as one act.
studies.explainEasier: If someone does something wrong and then puts the blame on a person who did nothing, that is a second wrong. The Quran counts the lie on its own, sitting on top of the first fault.

studies.title: Taught What You Did Not Know
studies.meaning: A group had made up its mind to lead the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) astray. The verse describes that near miss and then sets it aside. They mislead only themselves, and they cannot harm him in any way. Then it gives the reason, and the reason is not watchfulness but what he was given: the Book, wisdom, and knowledge he did not have before. Early scholars note that the protection is described as teaching rather than as a shield.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This closes the passage about the theft, where suspicion was pushed onto an innocent man and the community briefly took the wrong side. Early scholars read the verse as addressing that episode directly: an attempt was made to win a judgement by twisting the facts, and it did not succeed. The reports agree on the setting, which the tradition treats as well attested.

keyTerms.note: A verb for an intention that has formed but not yet acted. It describes the group at the point of decision, which is exactly where the verse says the grace came in.
From the root for judgement and restraint, connected with a bridle. Paired with the Book, it names the ability to apply what was given rather than the content of it.
From a root meaning what is left over and abundant. The word frames what was given as excess rather than as something owed, and it both opens and closes this verse.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A judge in Arabia had no investigators and no records. He heard both sides, weighed their standing, and decided. A well-made case put by respected men was very powerful, while a person with fewer ties could be talked into a corner. Everyone who heard this verse knew how a united family could steer a result.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for grace opens this verse and closes it, framing everything between. Arabic uses that kind of bracketing often. Early scholars note it here because of what sits inside the frame: an attempt to deceive, and the gift of knowledge, held by one word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection here is described as knowledge rather than as prevention. What kept the outcome right was not that the attempt fell apart on its own. It was that the person judging had been taught. That gives revelation a practical job to do. It also implies that misleading someone is possible in principle, which is why the outcome is credited to what was given rather than to natural insight.

crossReferences.why: States the standard of judgement this verse says was protected, judging by what God showed.
Says God found him unaware and guided him, another statement of knowledge given.
Says he did not know what the Book or faith were, before it was made a light.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision you got right and quietly credited to your own judgement. Trace it back and find the person, the book or the accident that put the knowledge into your hands. Naming that is not false modesty. It is accuracy, and this verse does it about the one person who could most easily have claimed otherwise.
studies.explainEasier: Some people tried hard to lead the Prophet the wrong way. They only led themselves astray, and they could not hurt him. God had already given him the Book and taught him what he did not know.

studies.title: Except Three Kinds Of Talk
studies.meaning: Most of what people say to each other in private has no good in it, the verse says. Then it makes room for three things that do. Urging charity, urging what is known to be good, and setting things right between people. Early scholars note that all three face outward, since each one is about what happens to somebody else. And a condition is tied to the reward: the person did it seeking God's approval.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the passage about talk held out of sight, where a plan was made at night. The verse widens from that one episode to private counsel in general, and then rescues the practice by naming its proper uses. Early scholars observe that this surah has been dealing all along with what is said where others cannot hear.

keyTerms.note: A noun for talk held apart from others, from a root about being alone with somebody. It names the setting rather than the content, which is why the exception has to specify what is said.
From the root for repair. It names restoring a relationship between people rather than fixing an opinion, and the Quran uses it again and again of mending what has broken between parties.
A noun from the verb to be pleased, used of God's satisfaction. It names the intended audience of the act, which is the condition the promised reward depends upon.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A quiet word between two people in a small city carried real power. Marriages were arranged in such talks, feuds were settled, reputations were made or broken. Everyone understood that the big decisions of Medina were made in courtyards rather than in public. That is part of why a judgement on private talk mattered so much.
studies.didYouKnow: The three exceptions widen as they go. First giving to one person, then doing what is known to be good, then bringing two parties back together. Early scholars often pair this verse with a well-known report. It describes setting people right with each other as standing above extra fasting and prayer in what it achieves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speech is judged here by what it is for, not by whether it is hidden. Privacy itself is neutral, and the question is whose interest is served inside it. Then a further condition is added, since even the three good uses draw a reward only where God's approval was sought. That puts the motive above the outcome, even in acts whose outcome is plainly good.

crossReferences.why: Instructs that private conferring be about righteousness and mindfulness rather than about sin.
Describes reconciliation between believers as something a community owes its own members.
Warns against using oaths as an obstacle to doing good and reconciling between people.

studies.applyIt: Take one conversation this week that you would normally have about somebody, and have it with them instead. Or spend the private word you were going to use for complaint on setting something right between two people you know. This verse does not condemn quiet conversations. It asks what yours are for.
studies.explainEasier: God says most quiet talk between people does no good. There are three things that do. Telling someone to give to the poor, telling them to do good, and making peace between two people who have fallen out.

studies.title: The Path Of The Believers
studies.meaning: The verse names a condition in two parts, and early scholars discuss whether they are one thing or two. One is breaking with the Messenger after the guidance has become clear to you. The other is following a path other than the one the believers walk. Then comes an unusual picture of what follows: a person is turned toward what he had already turned toward. Nothing new is imposed on him. The direction he chose is confirmed, and he is left holding it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This closes the passage about the theft and the attempt to shift blame, after which the man responsible left the community. Early scholars tie the verse to that departure while noting that its wording is general. The mention of the believers' path has been discussed at length in the tradition, as bearing on the weight of what scholars agree on together.

keyTerms.note: From the root for splitting in two, the same one used earlier in this surah of a marriage coming apart. It pictures separation as one thing tearing rather than as two parties disagreeing.
From the root for separating one thing from another. Clarity is a condition of the whole sentence, so what is described is someone who saw the difference before crossing it.
The same verb appears twice in the clause, once of God and once of the person. That makes the outcome a confirmation of a choice rather than a separate response to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving a community in Arabia was not a private decision. A man who broke with his group lost protection, standing, and the right to be avenged. He had to attach himself somewhere else or live fully exposed. The word for splitting used here carried all of that weight, which is why the verse pairs it with following another path.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the path of the believers became one of the most discussed lines in the surah. The classical tradition took it as bearing on the weight of what scholars agree on together. One short clause, sitting inside a passage about a theft, became the base of a large later literature.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What follows is a confirmation rather than something imposed, and that shape is unusual. A person is turned toward the way he was already facing. So part of judgement is being handed what you chose, rather than having something arrive from outside. The words about clarity then keep the whole thing from touching anyone who never saw the line.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with the boundary of forgiveness, restating a verse from earlier in the surah.
Describes those who turn back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them.
Describes this community as a middle one, appointed as witnesses over other people.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often a consequence you resented turned out to be simply more of what you had chosen. This verse describes that shape, not a punishment arriving from elsewhere. Look at one direction you are facing now, and ask honestly whether you would want more of it. More of it is generally what comes.
studies.explainEasier: If someone breaks away from the Messenger after the right way has been made clear, God lets him go. He takes a different road from the believers, and God leaves him on it. It ends badly for him.

studies.title: Strayed Into Far Error
studies.meaning: This verse repeats one from earlier in the surah with a single change, and the change carries the point. The earlier one closed by calling it a great lie to set up partners with God. This one closes by calling it a straying that has gone a long way. The same boundary is described first as something done and then as a place you end up. Early scholars read the two endings as fitting together rather than as a choice between them.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This closes the long stretch that the earlier occurrence opened, and early scholars note how much of the surah runs between the two. What lies between covers argument about God, conflict, and a case of false accusation, and the repetition brackets all of it. No separate occasion is reported for this second occurrence.

keyTerms.note: The verb for losing your road in open country. It describes a condition rather than an act, which is exactly what sets this ending apart from the earlier one.
An adjective of distance applied to the straying. It measures the error by how far from the road a person now stands, not by the size of the step that took them there.
A clause leaving the forgiveness of everything else under God's will. Early scholars stress that it neither promises nor withholds, holding hope and seriousness together in one phrase.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Losing the track in the desert was the most ordinary disaster of that world. A person did not usually stray by a sharp turn. They strayed by a small drift held too long, until the landmarks no longer matched. Distance from the road, rather than the size of the first error, decided whether anyone could get back.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse and one earlier in the same surah are almost identical, and they differ only at the very end. Repetition that close inside a single surah is rare in the Quran. Early scholars read the pair as a frame around the material between them, rather than as a simple restatement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Describing one thing first as a lie and then as a distance says how a wrong turn works. It starts as something you do. It becomes somewhere you are, and that is harder to deal with. The words about God's will then hold the door open rather than shutting it. A distance is a description, not a verdict.

crossReferences.why: States the same boundary earlier in this surah, ending on fabrication rather than on distance.
Uses the same phrase for a straying that has gone far, there of a different failure.
Calls associating partners with God a great wrong, inside a father's counsel to his son.

studies.applyIt: Think about the small drifts rather than the dramatic turns. Nobody sets out to end up far from where they meant to be. Pick one habit you have been holding at a slight angle for a long time, and correct it a little this week. Distance builds from angles, which is the picture this verse uses.
studies.explainEasier: God says He will not forgive someone who puts another god beside Him. Anything smaller than that, He can forgive for whoever He wants. Setting up partners with God takes a person very far off the road.

studies.title: A Share Of Your Servants
studies.meaning: These two verses ask what is really being called on when God is not. The first names female figures. Early scholars explain that by the goddesses of the region and by the feminine names given to certain objects of worship. Then the whole practice is recast: what is called on is something else entirely. And the second verse quotes a claim, a fixed portion of God's servants, said in the very word this surah used of inheritance shares.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This follows the boundary drawn around forgiveness and turns to what stands on the other side of it. Early scholars explain the reference to female figures by the names of deities honoured in Mecca and the country around it before the community began. The passage then moves from that one practice to a general account of how such devotion is produced.

keyTerms.note: The plural for female beings. Early scholars explain it by the feminine names of pre-Islamic deities and by the objects venerated alongside them, and they record more than one reading of the word.
From a root meaning smooth or bare, used of a tree stripped of its leaves. It suggests something rendered down to pure defiance, with nothing else remaining on it.
The exact phrase this surah used of inheritance shares. Its reuse is pointed, since a claim upon people is being stated in the language of a legal entitlement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shrines across the region held named gods, several of them female. Each had its own keepers, its own offerings, its own pilgrims. Families had ties to one shrine or another going back for generations. Worship there was neither strange nor rare. It was the ordinary furniture of that world, which is what makes the turn here so sharp.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a fixed share here is the same one used earlier in this surah, where it named the set portions of an inheritance. Putting a claim on people into the language of legal right is a deliberate echo. This surah reuses its own terms across very different subjects in several places.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage moves the object of worship without doubting that the worship is sincere. People believe they are calling on one thing, and they are described as calling on another. So what a person actually worships is a different question from what they mean to worship. The claim to a fixed share then presents this as an arrangement with a shape, not as random temptation.

crossReferences.why: Names the deities of the region directly and asks whether such attributions carry any authority.
Records the same claim in fuller form, with the directions from which the approach comes.
Continues the quoted claim into specific practices, and closes on what is lost by it.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you actually turn to first when something goes wrong: a person, a screen, a substance, a plan. Not what you would say you rely on. The passage separates the two, and naming your own first reflex accurately is most of the work it asks for.
studies.explainEasier: When people pray to things that are not God, the Quran says they are really praying to something else. It quotes that thing. It says it will take a set share of God's servants for itself.

studies.title: Altering What Was Made
studies.meaning: The quoted claim runs on through four verbs, each one made emphatic in Arabic. There is misleading, then filling people with wishes, then two promptings that end in actual acts. Slitting the ears of cattle points to a known practice of marking animals given to a shrine. Altering the creation of God is far wider than that. Early scholars record a real range of readings for it, and they do not settle on one.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Early scholars explain the mention of cattle by a practice from before Islam: certain animals were marked by cutting their ears and then set aside from ordinary use, given to a shrine. The Quran addresses that custom elsewhere as well. Here it quotes a claim rather than telling a story, which is how the classical commentaries read the passage.

keyTerms.gloss: I will fill them with wishes
keyTerms.note: An intensive verb from the root for a wish or a hope. It names the manufacture of expectation, which the next verse then calls delusion, and the two are linked deliberately.
An intensive verb for cutting through something. It refers to marking livestock by cutting their ears, a practice by which an animal was dedicated and removed from ordinary use.
A phrase covering both the act of creating and the thing created. Early scholars record a wide range of readings for what altering it means, and they preserve that range rather than resolving it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Livestock were the visible wealth of a family, and marking them was ordinary. A cut in the ear showed who owned an animal across shared grazing ground. Giving an animal to a shrine used the same technique for another purpose. The animal then could not be ridden, milked or slaughtered. Wealth was taken out of use by a single cut.
studies.didYouKnow: The four verbs in this quoted claim all carry the same emphatic ending in Arabic, one after another, which makes the passage sound like a formal oath. Early scholars note the construction. What is reported is not a plan described but a vow spoken, and the grammar keeps that tone exactly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sequence moves from inward states to outward acts. It begins with misleading and wishes and ends with things done to animals and to creation itself. That order is the claim's own logic: what people do follows from what they have been led to expect. The outcome is then named as loss, in the language of trade, rather than as punishment.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same practices of setting animals aside, and says God ordained none of them.
Continues immediately, naming the promises as delusion and their end as no escape.
Names the original disposition on which people were made, and says it does not change.

studies.applyIt: Notice something you have been told to want that you never actually chose: an expectation about a house, a body, a career, a date by which things should have happened. Trace where it came from. This passage puts the making of expectation before any action. Most of what follows is easier to see once the source has a name.
studies.explainEasier: The quoted voice says it will lead people off the path. It says it will fill them with false hopes. It says it will push them to cut the ears of their animals and to change what God has made.

studies.title: Promises That Are Delusion
studies.meaning: Two verbs gather up everything before them: he promises, and he fills people with expectation. Then the whole thing is named with a word for something that deceives by looking better than it is. Early scholars note that the word covers being taken in by an appearance rather than by an outright lie, which is why nothing here is called false. And the next verse gives the end point, adding that no escape is found.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This closes the passage that began with the boundary around forgiveness and ran on through a quoted claim. Early scholars treat these two verses as the summary rather than as new material. They also note that the surah follows them at once with the matching description of those who believe, so the pair is never left standing alone.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for making a promise, used across the Quran of God's promises as well. Because it is neutral, the judgement falls in the words that follow rather than in the verb itself.
From a root about being taken in by how something looks. It names deception that works through the appearance of a thing rather than through any false statement about it.
A noun of place from a verb meaning to swerve away from something. It names a route out that a person looks for and does not find, rather than a door that has been closed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A mirage in that landscape was a daily fact, not a poetic image. Travellers saw water where none was. Experienced guides learned to distrust their own eyes at certain hours of the day. The words for being deceived by appearance came out of that, and nobody hearing them needed the comparison explained.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for delusion used here turns up throughout the Quran, often in the phrase that calls this life the enjoyment of deception. Its root is about being taken in by how something looks. So the Quran's ordinary term for a false promise is a word about appearance, not about lying.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not say the promises are broken. It says they deceive, which is a finer point, and early scholars keep it. What is offered may even arrive and still fail, because the appearance that made it attractive was never accurate. The next verse then sets the matching promise from God beside it, so the two are meant to be compared.

crossReferences.why: Sets the matching promise beside this one and asks who is more truthful in speech.
Warns that worldly life should not deceive you, nor the deceiver deceive you about God.
Records a speech at the end admitting that a promise was made and then not kept.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you are working toward. Describe, in concrete detail, what the day after getting it will actually look like. Not the feeling, the day. This passage separates a promise from an appearance, and that description is the simplest test there is for telling which one you are holding.
studies.explainEasier: This voice makes promises and gets people's hopes up. But the promises only look good, and they are not real. In the end those who follow them find no way out.

studies.title: The Promise Of God Is True
studies.meaning: Here is the matching picture, set on purpose against the one before it. Gardens with rivers running beneath them, and a life that lasts, all in familiar words. What marks this out is the ending: the sentence stops to call the promise itself true, and then asks who is more truthful in speech than God. So the argument is about how far the promise can be trusted, rather than about anything added to it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, right after the description of promises that deceive, and early scholars read the two as one construction. A false promise is named, and then a true one is set beside it with its truthfulness made plain. The surah has used this technique earlier, giving two outcomes in verses side by side. Here the comparison is between promises rather than destinations.

keyTerms.note: A construction that restates the sentence before it and then affirms it, a form Arabic uses to close an argument. It halts the description in order to say what kind of thing has just been described.
One word covering truth, reality and a rightful claim together. Applied to a promise it means both that it matches what will happen and that it is genuinely owed.
A verbal noun from the verb to say, used rarely in the Quran. Its choice makes the closing question about the act of speaking rather than about the content of what is said.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Promises in a world without writing rested on reputation alone. A man's word was judged by his record, and people traded on that judgement much as we now rely on a contract. Asking who is more truthful in speech was a practical question then. It was put in the very terms people used to decide whom to trust.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing question of this verse appears earlier in the same surah in almost the same form, with one word swapped for a near synonym. The tradition notes such paired questions. Here the repeat applies one test twice: once about a report, and once about a promise.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The weight of a promise hangs on the character of whoever makes it, not on its content. Anyone can describe a garden. The question is whether the description is backed by anything. That is a claim about where hope stands. It puts hope in the speaker rather than in how attractive the offer looks, which is exactly how the false promise before it failed.

crossReferences.why: Describes the promises this verse is set against, and names them as delusion.
Asks the same closing question earlier in this surah, about a report rather than a promise.
Names the promise of God and states that God does not fail in what He has promised.

studies.applyIt: Think about how you actually decide to trust a promise. Usually it is the person's record rather than the offer itself. Apply that same test on purpose to something you were promised recently and are hesitating over. This verse does exactly that, in public, and the method it uses is the one you already have.
studies.explainEasier: People who believe and do good will be let into gardens. Rivers will run under them, and they will stay there for ever. God's promise is true, and no one speaks more truly than God.

studies.title: Not According To Wishes
studies.meaning: Everyone likes to believe their own side is covered, and this verse takes that away from both sides at once. One set of expectations belongs to the community being addressed, the other to those who received earlier scripture. Neither claim of standing settles anything. What follows is a plain statement of what wrongdoing costs, and of the absence of any protector besides God. Early scholars note the even hand here: the verse levels a claim made by its own audience before it levels the claims of anyone else.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in a stretch of the surah arguing about who stands where before God. Early scholars report that the verse arrived amid competing claims of favour between religious communities in the city. Both are addressed inside one sentence. The reports describe an atmosphere of such claims rather than one occasion, and the tradition treats that as its setting.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a wish, from the root used a few verses earlier of manufactured expectation. Its reuse ties this verse to the passage about false promises just above it.
A passive form from the root for a matched return. The passive leaves the agent unnamed, which puts the weight on the certainty of the return rather than on who delivers it.
The same pair used earlier in this surah inside a prayer asking God for both. Here their absence is stated, which turns that earlier request into the measure of what is lacking.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in Arabia was passed down and claimed out loud. A family's claim to rank was recited, defended and believed, and it really did change how a person was treated. Groups in Medina held claims of the same shape about their tie to God. This verse speaks to a habit of mind that was common, not to rare pride.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for wishes here comes from the same root as a verb used a few verses earlier, where it meant filling people with expectations. The surah is building a vocabulary across the passage. A word first applied to deception is then applied to a community's own assumptions about itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse denies that belonging settles anything, and it does so evenly, naming its own audience's expectations first. That order matters. What is being made is not a claim about another community but a claim about claims. What replaces them is a plain account of consequence, with no protector named besides God. The question goes back to what a person actually did.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with what does count, and specifies that it applies to male and female alike.
Answers a claim about who enters the Garden by asking for the evidence behind it.
States that whoever does good does it for himself, and your Lord is not unjust to servants.

studies.applyIt: Notice the claim you quietly rely on: that you are basically a good person, that your family is decent, that your community is on the right side. None of those are lies. The verse simply removes them from the accounting and asks what you did, which is a narrower and far more useful question.
studies.explainEasier: Wanting something does not make it happen, and that goes for everyone. Whoever does something bad will pay for it. No one but God can protect them or help them.

studies.title: Abraham, Taken As A Friend
studies.meaning: What actually counts is put in a plain clause. Good work, from male or female, joined to belief. Nothing else is let in, and nothing is taken away. Then comes a question about who is better in religion. The answer names three things: turning your face wholly to God, doing good, and following the way of Abraham. It ends with a name for Abraham that the tradition treats as his defining title.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, right after the verse that set aside competing claims of standing. The mention of Abraham does particular work there, since the communities in dispute traced themselves back to him. Early scholars note this as the surah's second return to Abraham. They read both places as answering claims of inherited precedence by pointing to a shared ancestor.

keyTerms.note: The face stands for the whole person and for the direction one is turned. Submitting it means orienting everything, which is why the phrase is stronger than any English word for belief.
A word for turning aside from what surrounds you, toward what is straight. The Quran uses it almost only of Abraham, and it describes a stance rather than a doctrine.
From a root about something entering into every gap, so the friendship is described as having gone all the way in. It is rarer and warmer than the ordinary Arabic word for a friend.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Friendship in Arabia was a formal bond with duties attached, closer to alliance than to affection. A man's close friends were expected to defend him, house him and speak for him. Naming Abraham as God's friend used a word that carried all of that. In that society such a bond was declared in public and long remembered.
studies.didYouKnow: The title given to Abraham at the end here, God's close friend, became the name of a city. It is still the ordinary Arabic name for Hebron. A single word from this verse passed into geography, and people use it daily without always knowing where it came from.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Gender is taken out of the account entirely. The condition is stated and then both are named, which early scholars read as answering an assumption rather than making a new claim. Religion is then defined by three things, and all of them are stances or actions. None of them is membership. A question about standing is answered by describing conduct.

crossReferences.why: Sets aside the claims of standing that these two verses replace with conduct instead.
Describes Abraham as a community in himself, upright and not among those who associate.
Names believing men and believing women in parallel across a long list of qualities.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you do well. Ask whether you would still do it if nobody could tell which group you belonged to. The passage strips membership out of the question entirely and leaves conduct standing. That is uncomfortable in a useful way, because it removes the part of an identity that takes no effort.
studies.explainEasier: Anyone who does good and believes will go to the Garden, man or woman. Nothing will be taken off what they earned. The best way to live is to give yourself fully to God and do good, as Abraham did.

studies.title: Encompassing Every Thing
studies.meaning: A short verse with two things in it. Everything in the heavens and on earth belongs to God, and God encompasses everything. Early scholars note the pairing of owning with encompassing. One is a claim about whom things belong to, the other about a knowledge that surrounds rather than watches. Coming after a long argument about standing, the verse answers it by naming the scale on which such questions get settled.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the stretch that dealt with competing claims of favour and with what actually counts. Early scholars read short verses of this kind as punctuation inside a long surah, marking the end of an argument by lifting the frame. No specific occasion is reported for it. The same statement comes back several times in the later parts of the surah.

keyTerms.note: The preposition of possession placed first in the sentence, which Arabic uses for emphasis. Putting the owner before what is owned makes the ownership the point rather than the inventory.
From a root meaning to enclose on all sides, used of a wall around a garden. It appears earlier in this surah too, there describing knowledge of what people arrange in secret.
A phrase using the word for a thing in its widest sense, covering objects, events and states alike. Its openness is what makes the encompassing total rather than a long list.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ownership in that world rested on holding a thing and on what the neighbours remembered. A man held land because his father had held it and everyone said so. There was no register, so ownership was really a matter of what a community knew. A statement joining ownership to complete knowledge used exactly that logic, at the largest scale.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God comes back several times later in this surah. It works almost as a refrain. Long surahs in the Quran often mark their parts this way. A short, sweeping statement is set between passages on very different subjects.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Joining ownership to encompassing answers a particular worry. An owner might not know what he owns, and a knower might have no claim on what he knows. Putting the two together closes both gaps. After a long argument about who stands where, the verse moves the question. Standing is not settled between parties. It is held inside a single knowledge.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for encompassing, there of God's knowledge of what is arranged in secret.
States the same ownership and adds that God will call to account for what is within you.
Closes by saying that God has encompassed every single thing in His knowledge.

studies.applyIt: When you next feel your situation is unseen, take the second part of this verse literally. The picture is not of being watched from a distance but of being inside something. Sit with that for a minute rather than reasoning about it. The difference between those two pictures is most of what the verse offers.
studies.explainEasier: Everything in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. Nothing at all sits outside that. And God holds every single thing inside what He knows.

studies.title: They Ask You About Women
studies.meaning: People keep bringing the same question, and the answer sends them back to what they already have. God answers about women, and so does what is already being recited in the Book. Early scholars read that as pointing back to the verses that open this surah, about orphan girls. Three groups are then named together: women whose due is held back while marriage to them is wanted, children left powerless, and orphans in general. And the ending turns from what is owed to whatever good is actually done.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Early scholars report that questions about the arrangements set out at the start of this surah kept being brought forward. This passage answers them by turning attention back to what had already been given. The situation described, a guardian holding a ward's property while wanting to marry her, is the one the surah opened by addressing.

keyTerms.note: A verb for requesting a formal opinion on a difficult matter. Its use marks the question as one people had genuinely puzzled over rather than a casual query put in passing.
The passive of the verb to write, used of what has been appointed. Describing a woman's due as written places it outside the discretion of whoever happens to be holding it.
From the root for giving each party its due portion. The same root appeared in the third verse of this surah, so the answer closes on the word the whole question began from.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A guardian who held an orphan girl's wealth faced a real pull, with nobody checking on him. Marrying her kept the wealth in the house and saved him from handing it over. Everyone knew such deals went on. The community kept asking where the limits were, which is just what the verb that opens this verse records.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse sends the questioners back to what is already being recited in the Book, and early scholars identify that as the surah's own opening verses. It is one of the places where the Quran points at itself as an existing text with earlier passages. That happens in the middle of a surah still coming down.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The shape of the answer teaches something. A question about who is owed what is answered by naming the people most likely to be passed over. Then it widens to any good done at all, which keeps the matter from settling into a technical fix. It also treats a repeated question as a sign that something already given had not been acted on.

crossReferences.why: Opens the surah with the same situation, guardians and the orphan girls in their care.
Establishes that an orphan's property must reach the orphan, which this question circles back to.
Names the powerless among men, women and children in the same grouping used here.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you keep asking a question you have already been answered. It usually means the answer asks something of you that you would rather not do. Pick the one you have been circling and act on the part you already understand, which is generally most of it.
studies.explainEasier: People kept asking about the rights of women and orphans. The answer sends them back to what God had already said in the Book. It says to give the women what is theirs and to treat the orphans fairly.

studies.title: Reconciliation Is Better
studies.meaning: A wife senses her husband pulling away, and this verse takes her fear seriously. She may fear a breach, or a quiet withdrawal that is harder to name. What follows is not a procedure but a permission: the two of them may settle matters between themselves, and settling is called better. Then comes an unusual remark about people in general, that souls are made present to grasping. Early scholars read that as explaining why settling is so hard.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, near the close of this surah's long treatment of marriage. Early scholars report cases of women whose husbands had withdrawn from them and who preferred an arrangement to a separation. They read the verse as making room for such settlements. The reports describe more than one case, and agree that the passage came out of real arrangements rather than an imagined one.

keyTerms.note: The same word used earlier in this surah of a wife. Its use here of a husband is what lets the tradition read the two passages as one subject seen from both sides.
From the verb for averting the face. It names something less than a breach: the quiet removal of attention a marriage can survive on paper while failing in fact.
A word for holding tightly combined with wanting more, stronger than ordinary miserliness. The verse says souls are brought into its presence, describing it as a condition rather than a choice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman whose husband had withdrawn had few options. Separation sent her back to her father's people, often with children and always with less standing, and a second marriage was harder to arrange. A deal in which she kept the household while giving up something was often the outcome she herself wanted. This verse makes room for it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about souls being made present to grasping is quoted widely in Arabic as a description of people. It is passive in the grammar, so the tendency is described as something brought to the soul rather than made by it. Early scholars read that as diagnosis rather than blame.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse does something unusual. It names the obstacle in the same breath as the advice: settling is better, and here is why you will resist it. That treats moral teaching as needing a picture of the mind, not only a standard. It also refuses to pretend that what is advised will feel natural to either party.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a breach when the fear is a husband's, earlier in this surah.
Sets out arbitration by both families, another route through the same difficulty.
Names those protected from their own grasping as the ones who genuinely succeed.

studies.applyIt: Think about a relationship you have kept in place while quietly taking your attention out of it. This verse names that withdrawal as its own thing, apart from open conflict, and treats it as something the other person can feel. Give an hour of real attention back this week, without saying that you are doing it.
studies.explainEasier: If a wife is afraid her husband is turning away from her, the two of them can work something out between themselves. That is better for both. People tend to hold on tightly to what is theirs.

studies.title: Left Hanging In Between
studies.meaning: This verse begins by conceding something honest. You will not be able to treat women with equal fairness, however much you want to. Early scholars read that as about the heart rather than conduct. What is asked instead is not to lean so far that someone is left hanging. She is then neither held nor released. And the next verse turns to separation, promising provision to both out of God's abundance.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing this surah's treatment of marriage. Early scholars read the first of these two verses alongside the third verse of the surah, where fairness was made the condition, and note that this one concedes the limit of what fairness can mean. No specific occasion is reported. The passage completes a sequence that began at the very opening of the surah.

keyTerms.note: From a root for eager desire and greedy effort. The concession is made against maximum effort, so what is called impossible is impossible even for someone genuinely trying at it.
A passive participle from the verb to suspend. It pictures a person hung between two states, neither in a marriage nor out of one, unable to move in either direction.
From the root for width and room. Closing on it answers the fear behind staying in a failed marriage, which is that separation would leave someone with nothing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman neither divorced nor attended to had no standing anywhere. She could not remarry, and she could not go back fully to her father's house. She had no claim she was able to press. The word this verse uses for hanging described exactly that spot, and it was common enough that the language already had a term for it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for being left suspended appears only here in the Quran, and it became the standard term in later Arabic for a woman in exactly that position. A single word from this verse gave the language a name for that state. Before it, the state could only be described by circumstance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates feeling from conduct and asks only for the second. That is a precise claim about what can be required of a person. It concedes that the heart is not even, then draws a line where that unevenness harms somebody. The promise of provision after separation then removes the fear that most often keeps such situations frozen.

crossReferences.why: Makes fairness the condition at the surah's opening, whose limit this verse then defines.
Asks for good company, and warns that dislike may conceal something genuinely good.
Addresses provision at separation, another passage assuming responsibility continues past an ending.

studies.applyIt: Look for a situation you are keeping suspended: a decision half made, a person half included, a job you have neither committed to nor left. The harm this verse names is not the failure. It is the hanging. Resolve one of them this week, in either direction, and notice which way you actually went.
studies.explainEasier: A man cannot feel exactly the same about two wives, however hard he tries. But he should not lean so far that one of them is left hanging. If they split up, God will provide for both.

studies.title: God Is In No Need
studies.meaning: Everything in the heavens and on earth belongs to God, and the verse says it, gives one instruction, then says it again. The instruction went to the communities who received scripture before, and it goes to this one too: be mindful of God. And if people refuse, what comes back is not a threat, because the ownership stands either way. The verse closes by naming God as in no need and worthy of praise, in the same breath.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the run of short universal statements that punctuate the later parts of this surah. Early scholars note that the instruction is described as having been given to those who received scripture before. That places this community inside a line rather than at a start. No specific occasion is reported for the verse itself.

keyTerms.note: From the root for making a bequest, used earlier in this surah of inheritance. The same verb covers a will and a divine charge, both being something entrusted to be carried out.
From a root meaning to be free of need, which also gives the word for wealth. Applied to God it removes any suggestion that the instruction serves the one who gave it.
A form meaning worthy of praise, which is not the same as praised. It describes a quality holding whether or not anyone actually offers the praise, which suits the argument here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A patron in Arabia gave in order to be praised, and praise was the return he expected. Poets were paid to deliver it, and its absence was an insult. Naming God as both in no need and worthy of praise split apart two things that always travelled together in that world. The split would have been noticed at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement about the heavens and the earth appears twice inside this one verse. It comes once before the instruction and once after the refusal. Early scholars note that repeat as the argument itself. Nothing about the ownership changes, whatever anybody decides to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse removes any hint that God gains from being obeyed. Ownership is stated before the instruction and again after refusal, unchanged. So the instruction cannot be a demand made for the sake of the one who gave it. That moves the whole matter. Being mindful is described as given for the good of whoever practises it.

crossReferences.why: States that if all on earth were ungrateful, God would still be free of need and praiseworthy.
Uses the same statement of ownership a few verses earlier, inside a different argument.
Names people as those in need of God, and God as free of need and praiseworthy.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your practice is quietly a trade, done expecting something back. This verse cuts that wire twice inside one sentence. Try one act of devotion this week expecting nothing at all from it, and watch how strange that feels. The strangeness tells you something.
studies.explainEasier: Everything in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. He told the earlier peoples, and He tells you, to keep Him in mind. If people turn away, it takes nothing from Him.

studies.title: The Reward Of This World
studies.meaning: Three short verses, each cutting from a different angle. Ownership again, with God named as the one entrusted with affairs. Then the power to remove a whole people and bring others, stated flatly. Then the sharpest of the three: whoever wants only the reward of this world should note that both rewards are with God. Early scholars read that as exposing a bad trade rather than condemning the wanting itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the run of short statements that break up the later parts of this surah. Early scholars read the three together as one movement. Each verse widens the frame further from what the community was dealing with day to day. The section follows a long passage on marriage. It comes just before one about those whose loyalty was divided.

keyTerms.note: A word for someone appointed to handle affairs on another's behalf. Used of God it describes an active role rather than watching, which is why it closes a statement about ownership.
A causative from the verb to go. It describes removal with no violence in the word itself, which makes the statement one about capacity rather than about anger.
From a root meaning to come back, related to the word for a garment one returns to wearing. Reward is pictured as something that comes back rather than something handed over.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A trader who took a small sure profit rather than waiting for a bigger one was making a call everyone in Mecca and Medina understood. Caravans were financed on exactly that sum. The argument in the third of these verses is put in the terms of that trade. The smaller return was inside the larger one all along.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for reward here is related to the Arabic for a garment, through a root meaning to return. Clothing was what a person came back to at the end of a day. The same root gave a word for what comes back to someone as a result of what they did.
studies.theologicalSignificance: These three verses build by scale: ownership, then being replaceable, then a choice about what to want. Putting the power to replace a people in the middle makes the last point land differently. Someone choosing the smaller reward does so from a place that was never as safe as it felt. The wanting is not condemned, only its aim.

crossReferences.why: Opens this sequence with the same statement of ownership and the same self-sufficiency.
Says whoever desires the harvest of the hereafter is increased in it, and gives the contrast.
Distinguishes those who want the fleeting from those who strive for the hereafter as believers.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you are chasing and ask what you would be giving up by aiming higher with the same effort. Not sacrifice, aim. The argument in the third of these verses is about a trade made badly, and most such trades are made without anyone noticing they were trades.
studies.explainEasier: Everything in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. He could take people away and bring others instead. Whoever only wants the reward of this world should know that God holds both rewards.

studies.title: Witnesses Even Against Yourselves
studies.meaning: The call is not simply to be just. The Arabic word describes someone who keeps standing up for justice, a posture held rather than a single act. The hard cases come in order of difficulty: yourself, then your parents, then your relatives. A second pull is named too, the lean toward whichever side seems to deserve more sympathy. That is refused by the words saying God is nearer to both. The obstacle here is desire, not ignorance.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the same stretch of the surah as a theft that was blamed on an innocent man. The community's first instinct then had been to shield one of its own, and early scholars read this verse as drawing the wider lesson from that case. Medina was a town of clans, where testimony was shaped by loyalty as a matter of course. An oath sworn for a kinsman felt closer to a duty than to a lie.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the verb to stand. It names a standing role, not one stand. The same word is used of keeping up prayer, so it carries the sense of holding something up over time.
A word tied to portions and shares. The justice it names is the kind that divides things fairly. Its root can also carry the sense of straying, and the form used here turns that sense around.
From a root for falling and for empty air. It names the pull of what a person wants, pictured as a fall. That is why the verse treats it as what makes testimony swerve.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Justice in Arabia worked by tribal arithmetic. A killing was answered by a killing from the other clan. A man who spoke against his own people cut the branch he sat on. Protection, marriage prospects and trade all ran through kin, and there was no state to appeal to if your family cast you off. Standing as a witness against a relative was nearer to exile than to a small cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran makes this demand twice, with the terms swapped. Here people stand up for justice and bear witness to God. At 5:8 they stand up for God and bear witness with justice. Early scholars note the mirroring, and the second passage names a different obstacle: hatred rather than desire.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice here rests on something other than what a group gains. The witness testifies to God, which makes accuracy a form of worship and drops the question of who benefits from the answer. The line about rich and poor is the sharpest part. Pity for the weak is no licence to bend a fact, and neither is deference to the strong. God is said to be nearer to both sides than the witness is.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same demand with the terms swapped, and names hatred as the pressure to resist.
Calls for just speech even when a relative is involved.
Warns the Prophet against arguing for the treacherous, in the episode behind this passage.

studies.applyIt: The next time you retell an argument you were in, include the strongest thing the other person said. Use their words, not your summary of them. Nothing is being conceded by that. The verse opens with testimony against yourself, and the smallest form of it is refusing to edit someone else's case when nobody would notice.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to stand up for what is fair, even when the truth hurts them or their own family. Rich or poor, it makes no difference. God knows what you do.

studies.title: Believe In All Of It
studies.meaning: The address is to people who already believe, and the command is to believe. Early scholars offer a range of readings: stay firm on it, deepen it, or accept what you have not yet owned. The content comes as a chain, this Book and the Book sent before it. Then the words about denial widen out to angels, messengers and the Last Day. What is described is not a set of separate beliefs but one thing with parts, which is why rejecting any of them is called straying far.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. The surah is much taken up with people whose commitment was partial, and with argument between communities holding earlier scriptures. In that setting, the stress on the Book sent before is not a side note. Early scholars record no single occasion for the verse. They read it as aimed at the community itself, whose belief was being asked to become more than a stated position.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form suggesting descent in stages, used of the Quran coming down over years. A plainer form appears in the same sentence for the earlier scripture, and early scholars note the difference.
Classical grammarians connect the word with a root for a message or an errand. Angels appear in the list of what may not be rejected, placed between God Himself and the scriptures He sent.
The verb for losing your road in open country where there are no landmarks. It is paired here with a word for distance, so error is measured as a length walked rather than one wrong turn.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was a town where scriptural religion was already familiar. Jewish tribes had lived there for generations and kept their books, and their scholars were asked about the past. Arabs in the oasis had grown up hearing of earlier prophets, and of one still expected. A claim to carry on that line made sense to everybody there, in a way it had not in Mecca.
studies.didYouKnow: Five things are named here as objects of belief, and the same five are gathered in the long verse on righteousness in surah 2. There it is defined as belief in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets. The order differs between the two, and neither passage presents its list as complete.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief is put here as something that can be asked of believers. So it is not treated as a state already finished. The list also refuses a faith that starts with this messenger. Earlier scripture is part of the content, not a polite nod to others. The closing image measures rejection as a distance walked. That suggests positions are reached step by step, and can be walked back.

crossReferences.why: Gathers the same objects of belief, defining righteousness by them rather than by direction of prayer.
Shows the response, believers making no distinction between any of His messengers.
Names the same religion as laid on Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus alike.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the things you say you believe and ask what you did about it this month. Not whether you affirmed it, what you did. The verse addresses people who had already said the words and asks them for the thing itself. The gap between saying and holding is normal, not a scandal.
studies.explainEasier: God is telling people who already believe to believe for real. That means God, His angels, all of His books, all of His messengers, and the Last Day. Turning any of it down means going far off the road.

studies.title: Then Believed, Then Refused
studies.meaning: The verse recites a sequence: belief, refusal, belief, refusal, and then an increase in refusal. Early scholars note that what closes the door is the last stage, not the swinging back and forth. The Quran elsewhere describes repentance as open after any single turn. What is described here is a pattern that has settled into a direction. And the two things withheld are forgiveness and guidance to a way.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, opening a long section on those whose loyalty was divided. Early scholars connect the verse to people who moved back and forth as the community's fortunes rose and fell. They read the increase at the end as describing where such movement finally arrives. No single occasion is reported, and the description is read as a pattern rather than a report.

keyTerms.note: A connective indicating sequence with an interval, unlike the ordinary word for and. Repeated four times here, it makes the verse a chronology rather than a list of possible alternatives.
A reflexive form of the verb to increase, so the movement is described as self-generated. It marks the exact point where swinging back and forth stops and a settled direction begins.
The ordinary word for a road. What is withheld is described as a route rather than as an outcome, so the loss named is the loss of a means rather than of a destination.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a city where the community's fortunes changed with each battle, people kept reassessing where to stand. They shifted position quietly and often, and everyone could name someone who had. That constant weighing up is the behaviour this verse traces. Its first hearers would have followed the sequence as a description of people they knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The word marking each stage of this verse points to a gap in time, not merely to a sequence. Arabic tells apart events joined at once and events split by an interval. The choice here means the verse describes a whole life rather than one episode of confusion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The trouble is placed in a settled direction rather than in changing your mind as such. Four reversals are recited without comment, and it is the fifth stage that changes the sentence. That keeps open the wide promise of repentance stated earlier in the surah. What is described is not a person who wavered, but one who stopped wavering in a particular direction.

crossReferences.why: Names the exit from this passage: repentance, reform, holding fast, and sincerity of religion.
Describes the wavering itself a few verses later, as being with neither one party nor the other.
Says they believed and then rejected, so their hearts were sealed and they do not understand.

studies.applyIt: Notice a pattern you have repeated more than twice: the same resolution, the same collapse, the same restart. The verse does not condemn the cycle. What it marks is the point where a person begins arguing for the collapse rather than resisting it. Check honestly which of those two you are doing now.
studies.explainEasier: Some people believe, then stop, then believe, then stop again, and they keep going further away. God does not forgive them, and He does not show them the road back.

studies.title: Where Glory Is Sought
studies.meaning: The announcement is made with the word used for good news, and a painful punishment follows it. The reversal is deliberate. Then the people are named by one behaviour: taking allies outside the community rather than inside it. And a question is asked about the motive, whether they are looking for standing there. The answer given is that all standing belongs to God, which moves the object rather than condemning the wish.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the section on those whose loyalty was divided. Early scholars describe people in the city keeping ties with the community's opponents as insurance. They read the question about honour as naming what such ties were really for. The setting was one where standing depended on visible association, which the passage addresses head on.

keyTerms.note: A verb used across the Quran for glad tidings, from a root about the skin showing a change. Attaching it to punishment is a deliberate inversion that early scholars discuss at length.
From a root meaning rare, precious and out of reach. It names the standing of someone who cannot be touched or humiliated, which is exactly what alliance was being sought to provide.
The plural of the word for a close ally used across this surah. It names a formal arrangement carrying obligations rather than friendship or ordinary social contact.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A person's safety in Arabia came from who would answer for them. Holding a tie with a rising power was the standard hedge, done openly and without shame. What this passage addresses is not treachery in the dramatic sense. It is the ordinary caution of a world where standing had to be borrowed from somewhere else.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for announcing good news here is used elsewhere in the Quran for the promise of a child and the promise of the Garden. Turning it around here is one of several places where the Quran uses a word against its usual sense. Early scholars treat the effect as deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The question asked is a diagnosis rather than a charge, since it names what people were actually after. The answer does not tell them to stop wanting standing. It says the whole of it lies elsewhere. That treats the failure as a wrong address rather than an appetite to be crushed. It is the same move the surah makes with wealth and with reward.

crossReferences.why: Restates the instruction directly to believers a few verses later, in the form of a question.
Says whoever desires honour should know that all honour belongs to God entirely.
Records a claim that the mightier will expel the weaker, and answers that might belongs to God.

studies.applyIt: Ask where you go to feel that you count: a group, a title, an association you mention when introducing yourself. Not in order to give it up. Just name it accurately once. The method here is to identify the source you draw standing from, and naming it is most of what changes.
studies.explainEasier: God says to tell those who play both sides that a painful punishment is waiting. They look for standing by siding with people outside the faith. All standing really belongs to God.

studies.title: Until They Change The Subject
studies.meaning: You are sitting with people and the talk turns to mockery of God's revelations. The verse recalls an instruction already given in the Book: do not stay seated there until the talk moves to something else. The condition is precise, since it is the sitting that is addressed and not the speaking. The reason given is that staying makes you like them. Early scholars note that the exit is temporary, tied to the subject rather than to the company.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, pointing back to an instruction given earlier. Early scholars identify it with a passage revealed in Mecca on the same situation. Restating it here applies it to a different setting. In the city such talk happened among neighbours rather than strangers, which made leaving costlier and far more visible than before.

keyTerms.note: The verb for sitting, used earlier in this surah of those who stayed behind. It addresses physical presence rather than taking part, which is what makes this instruction unusual.
A verb for stepping into water and stirring it up. Applied to speech it describes talk that goes in without care, which is how the Quran regularly names idle or mocking conversation.
A word for a likeness or an equivalent. The claim is not that you become guilty of what they said, but that you occupy the same position, which is a claim about presence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gatherings in Medina were where a person's world was run: business, marriage deals, news. Leaving one openly was a public act with costs. The people speaking were often relatives or trading partners. The instruction is hard in exactly the way its first hearers would have felt. That is why the exit lasts only as long as the subject does.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction here is described as already revealed. Early scholars identify the earlier passage as a Meccan one on the same situation. So this is one of the places where the Quran refers back to itself by content. It treats an earlier revelation as a text the audience could be expected to recall.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Presence is treated as taking part, which is a strong claim. Nothing needs to be said or agreed to, since staying seated is itself a position. The remedy is kept in proportion and temporary, tied to a subject rather than to people. That keeps it from becoming a general retreat from anyone whose speech you happen to dislike.

crossReferences.why: Gives the earlier instruction, to turn away from those who wade into ridicule of revelation.
Describes the servants of the Merciful as passing by idle talk with dignity intact.
Names what does have good in private conversation, a few verses earlier in this surah.

studies.applyIt: Next time a conversation turns to something you would rather not be part of, do not argue and do not stay. Get up, refill something, take a call, come back when it has moved on. The instruction here concerns position rather than protest, and it is easier to follow than most people expect.
studies.explainEasier: God already told the believers this in the Book. If people start making fun of God's words, do not sit there with them. Wait until they talk about something else, or you become like them.

studies.title: Those Who Lie In Wait
studies.meaning: The verse shows a behaviour by quoting it twice. When the community wins, the claim is: were we not with you. When the other side gains, the claim is: did we not side with you and defend you from the believers. Both are put as questions, which is what makes them claims on somebody. Then judgement is deferred to the Day of Resurrection, and the verse closes by saying no way will ever be granted over the believers.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the section on those whose loyalty was divided. Early scholars describe people who stayed close to the community without joining it. They placed themselves to claim credit whichever way a fight went. The reports describe this as a known pattern in the city rather than one incident. The passage records both halves of it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for waiting for something to happen to someone. It describes patience with a purpose, watching to see how a situation resolves before deciding where to stand.
From the verb to open. Victory in Arabic is named as an opening rather than as a conquest, which is why one word covers a decisive success and the unlocking of something closed.
A rare verb meaning to take control of something and dominate it. Its use inside a boast makes the claim awkward, since it concedes rather more than the speaker intends.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Between two rival powers, a small party's best play was to be owed something by both. Claims of past help were the coin of that world. They were pressed loudly the moment they came due. Everyone in Medina had watched such claims being made, often within days of a clear result.
studies.didYouKnow: Both claims here are put as questions rather than as statements, which in Arabic makes them harder to refuse. A question invites the hearer to supply the agreement. Early scholars note that this construction is what makes the two sentences a strategy rather than merely a lie.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a final judgement against a present muddle. Both claims may be hard to disprove now, so the matter is put off rather than settled. Then the ending does something else. It promises that no way will be given over the believers, which early scholars discuss carefully as a statement about the final outcome.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same position from inside, wavering with neither one party nor the other.
Describes those who wait for misfortune to turn against the believers, and what awaits them.
Names those who hold others back and come to the fighting only very reluctantly.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you have positioned yourself so as to be able to claim credit either way. Everyone does this at work, in families, in arguments among friends. Pick one such position and commit to it out loud this week, before you know how it turns out. That is the whole of what the verse describes.
studies.explainEasier: Some people waited to see who would win. When the believers won, they said they had been with them all along. When the other side gained, they said they had protected them. God will settle it.

studies.title: Standing Up Lazily
studies.meaning: An attempt at deception is described and answered in the same breath, with one verb used of both sides. Early scholars discuss this carefully. They read it as the Quran matching a word to itself, not as saying God deceives. Then the description turns concrete: standing for prayer without energy, performing for an audience, remembering God only a little. The whole reading comes through the way a body stands.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the section on those whose loyalty was divided. Early scholars note that the verse moves from an abstract claim about deception to a behaviour you can watch. They read the description as one the community could check for itself. The setting is a city where prayer was held together and attendance was visible to everybody present.

keyTerms.note: A form implying attempt and exchange. Early scholars stress that its use of God is a matching of the word to itself, a known Arabic device, rather than any attribution of deception.
A plural adjective for sluggishness. It describes the manner of standing rather than the fact of it, so the failure named is visible in how a body actually carries itself.
From the verb to see, in a reciprocal form. The audience is built into the word, so the act is described as performed toward people rather than merely observed by them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Prayer in Medina was done together, in rows, several times a day. Absence was noticed and so was manner. In a congregation of neighbours, how a man stood was as plain as whether he came at all. Everyone could tell the difference between someone present and someone merely attending.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the same verb for the attempt at deception and for God's answer to it. Arabic uses that construction to mark a matching reply rather than an identical act. Early scholars across the tradition explain the device carefully. It turns up wherever a response is described in the language of the offence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse locates an inner condition in a physical detail. Nothing is inferred from doctrine or from speech, and the evidence offered is the way a person stands. That implies inner states have outward form. The claim has two edges, since it means a practice done listlessly is reporting something rather than merely being imperfect.

crossReferences.why: Names those heedless in their prayer, who perform it in order to be seen by people.
Says their spending is not accepted, and that they come to prayer only reluctantly.
Describes remembrance in every posture, which this description stands directly against.

studies.applyIt: Watch how you stand for prayer this week rather than what you say in it. Not in order to judge yourself. The test here is physical, and posture is unusually honest: it reports what you actually brought before you have had time to decide what you meant to bring.
studies.explainEasier: These people think they are fooling God, but He is the one dealing with them. When they get up to pray, they stand there without energy. They are doing it so other people will see.

studies.title: Wavering Between The Two
studies.meaning: One word carries the first of these verses, an intensive form for something driven back and forth. Then it is spelled out: not toward these, not toward those. The next verse turns to believers with an instruction and a question, and the question is the sharper of the two. It asks whether they want to hand God a clear case against themselves, which makes the matter one of evidence rather than of loyalty.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, continuing the passage on divided loyalty and then turning to address the community directly. Early scholars note the shift. A description of others becomes an instruction to the hearers. So these verses are read as a warning against becoming what has just been described. The setting is a city where such ties were open to almost anyone.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from a root about swinging or dangling. It pictures something moved by an outside force rather than choosing, like a bucket swinging inside a well shaft.
A word for authority and for the proof that establishes it. The question asks whether they wish to supply the evidence themselves, which turns the matter into one of testimony.
The plural of the word for a close ally, carrying formal obligations in that society. The instruction concerns alliance rather than acquaintance, as the surah's usage elsewhere makes clear.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A well bucket swung on its rope when it was neither at the water nor at the rim. The word used here comes from that motion. Everyone drew water daily, so the image would have landed at once: something hanging and moving, useful in neither spot, and going wherever the rope was pulled.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing this wavering occurs only once in the whole Quran. It is built from a doubled root, a form Arabic uses for repeated back-and-forth motion. Its sound carries the meaning. That is why translators reach for words like wavering, vacillating or dangling, none of which quite catches it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The second of these verses turns the whole question into one of evidence.
