Rather than saying such alliance is disloyal, it asks whether a person wants to hand over a clear case against himself. That puts the hearer in the place of a witness testifying about his own life. It is a distinctive way of giving an instruction, aimed at the will rather than the conscience.

crossReferences.why: Traces the sequence of reversals that ends in exactly this suspended position.
Names the same behaviour a few verses earlier and asks what is really being sought in it.
Addresses the same matter of alliance, with an exception for those under real threat.

studies.applyIt: Identify one area where you have carefully avoided committing, so that you can move either way later. Notice what that flexibility costs you in energy, since holding two options open takes more than either would. Then close one this week. The image here is of something that never comes to rest.
studies.explainEasier: These people swing between two sides. They are not with one group and not with the other. God tells the believers not to take people outside the faith as their allies instead of other believers.

studies.title: Except Those Who Turn Back
studies.meaning: The lowest level of the Fire is named, using a word for a step going down rather than a rank. Then the whole thing is opened by an exception. Four things are listed: repenting, setting things right, holding fast to God, and making your religion sincerely His. Early scholars note that this exception comes straight after the severest statement in the section. The door opens at the point of greatest weight.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the long section on divided loyalty. Early scholars read the exception as part of the same revelation, not as something that came later. They note that this surah keeps following a hard statement with an opening. The people described had lived in the city all along. So the way out named was open to just those the passage was about.

keyTerms.note: A word for a step going down, the opposite of the term used for the rising degrees promised earlier in this surah. The vocabulary of ranks is mirrored downward here.
From a root meaning to grasp something for protection, used of clinging to a rope. It describes an active grip rather than a belief, which is why it sits among verbs of doing.
From a root meaning to clear something of what is mixed into it, as metal is refined. Applied to religion it names the removal of other motives rather than the adding of anything new.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Refining metal was a familiar process. You heated something until what was mixed into it separated and could be drawn off. The word for sincerity comes from that. Its first hearers would have understood it as a taking away rather than an adding. Nothing is added to make a thing pure. Other things are taken out of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the lowest level of the Fire is a term for a step going down. It mirrors the word for the rising degrees used earlier in this surah. The Quran builds both directions from the vocabulary of stairs. One image of steps runs upward and downward through the chapter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The four conditions move from inward to outward and back: turning, repairing, holding on, and cleaning the motive. Repentance alone is not the whole of it. Repair is named second, which keeps the turn from being purely private. The passage then places such people with the believers. That restores a standing rather than merely lifting a penalty.

crossReferences.why: Describes the pattern this exception releases people from, and its final settled direction.
States the terms of repentance earlier in this surah, in a more general form.
Uses the same verb for holding fast, there of holding to the rope of God together.

studies.applyIt: Take the four things named here in order and apply them to one thing you regret. Turn from it, and repair what you can. Take hold of something steadier, then remove whatever other motive is still attached. The second and fourth are the ones people skip, and they are usually where the work actually is.
studies.explainEasier: Those who play both sides end up at the very bottom of the Fire. But there is a way out. If they turn back, fix what they broke, hold on to God and mean it, they join the believers.

studies.title: What Would God Gain
studies.meaning: The passage opens with a question, and it is not an empty one. It asks what purpose punishment would serve for someone who is grateful and believes. Then come two short instructions, one about speech and one about pardon, and each closes on a name of God that matches it. God is called appreciative, then hearing, then pardoning and able. So each instruction rests on something about God rather than on a rule.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the section on those whose loyalty was divided and turning to a wider address. Early scholars read the opening question as softening the severity of the passage before it. The allowance for someone wronged to speak openly is tied in some reports to disputes among neighbours. No single occasion is agreed on.

keyTerms.note: The word for a grateful person, applied here to God. Early scholars read it as meaning that God acknowledges and multiplies what is small, since God receives nothing at all from anyone.
A noun for raising the voice or making something public. What is addressed is the broadcasting of harsh speech rather than the feeling behind it, which is why the exception concerns a grievance.
Two names paired deliberately. Pardon from someone unable to act is not pardon at all, so the second name is what gives the first its weight inside the sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A grievance in a small city had two routes. You could speak it in public and force the matter open, or absorb it and let the relationship go on. Both were costly. The allowance given here for a wronged person to speak admits that silence was not always available, and that some injuries had no other remedy.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for gratitude is applied to God in this passage, and the classical scholars discuss that carefully. Since God gains nothing, they explain the name as describing how small acts are received and multiplied. They note that the Quran uses several human words this way, while insisting the meaning is not the same.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The opening question moves punishment from something owed to something with a point. And it finds no point in it for a person who is thankful and believes. That changes the subject. What follows is not described as satisfying anything in God. These three verses then set a high bar for speech while letting the wronged speak, and close by naming pardon as the better way.

crossReferences.why: Permits an equivalent response, then names pardon and reconciliation as what God rewards.
States that gratitude brings increase, the other side of this passage's opening question.
Asks those with standing to pardon and overlook, since they want God's forgiveness themselves.

studies.applyIt: Take a grievance you have been telling people about. This passage does not say you were wrong to speak, and it plainly allows it. But it names pardon as the better option and attaches a name of God to that. Try one week of not raising it, and see what it costs you and what it does not.
studies.explainEasier: God asks what He would gain by punishing someone who is thankful and believes. He does not like people shouting bad words in public, unless they have been wronged. And pardoning someone is better than paying them back.

studies.title: We Believe In Some
studies.meaning: A position is described exactly and then named. Some accept part of what was sent and reject the rest, splitting God from His messengers. They look for a route somewhere between accepting and refusing. Early scholars note that the concern here is the middle path itself, described as a chosen position rather than as hesitation. Then the verdict comes, with the word for truly closing off any bargaining.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This opens a section addressed to communities that hold earlier scripture. Early scholars place it among arguments in the city about which messengers were to be accepted. Several scriptural groups lived side by side there, each holding a settled view of the others. No single occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for splitting something into parts. Its object here is God and His messengers, so what is described is a division of things the passage treats as inseparable.
The ordinary word for a road. Describing the middle position as a path chosen makes it deliberate, which is why the verse that follows can treat it as a settled stance.
A word covering truth and reality together. Attached to the verdict, it closes the gap between what a position calls itself and what it actually amounts to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Communities in Medina held long-settled views about which prophets belonged to their line and which did not. These were part of a family's identity, not an idea they had argued out. Accepting a new claim meant moving a great deal around. The middle path described here was the natural way through, which is just why the passage addresses it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for separating between messengers appears in this passage, and then again in the very next verse with a negation on it. So one word describes both the condemned position and the approved one within two sentences. The Quran often builds such a pair, defining a thing and its opposite by a single term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is treated as one thing sent in many parts. So picking among the messengers is called rejecting the source, not half-accepting it. That is a claim about unity. It also turns down the middle path in particular, which is rare. A middle path is usually read as caution, not as a stance that needs a verdict.

crossReferences.why: States the approved position immediately after, using the same verb with a negation attached.
Describes believers as making no distinction between any one of God's messengers.
Lists the prophets by name and says we make no distinction between any of them.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you have quietly built a position out of the parts you found agreeable. Everyone does this with traditions, with advice, with medicine. Name one thing you have set aside because it was awkward rather than because you looked at it. Then look at it once, properly, this week.
studies.explainEasier: Some people say they believe in some of God's messengers and not in others. They want a road halfway between believing and refusing. The Quran says that is refusing, plainly.

studies.title: No Distinction Between Them
studies.meaning: Here is the matching statement, built from the same verb as the verse before it with a negation added. Those who believe in God and His messengers, and draw no line between any of them, are promised their recompense. Early scholars note the shift in number, since the promise is stated for a group while the wage is owed to each one. And the closing names are forgiveness and mercy, rather than any name of justice.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, completing the pair that began with the description of a selective belief. Early scholars read the two verses as one construction. They note that this surah often states a position and then its opposite in verses side by side. The setting is a city where several scriptural communities lived alongside each other with settled views about one another.

keyTerms.note: The same intensive verb used in the verse before, now negated. Placing them together defines the approved position entirely by contrast with the one just described.
A word for a single individual, used in negative constructions to mean not even one. Its presence rules out drawing a line anywhere, however small the distinction being claimed.
The plural of the ordinary word for a wage. Its use keeps the promise inside the language of what is owed rather than of what is freely given as a favour.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Loyalty to a line of prophets was inherited much as loyalty to a tribe was, and it carried similar social weight. Being told to draw no line among them cut across an inheritance people had been raised inside. The instruction was not abstract. It asked for a rearranging of how a family understood itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states this principle of making no distinction among messengers in several places, and in two of them it appears as words spoken by the believers themselves. It is not an instruction given to them there. The community is shown taking up the position rather than only being told to hold it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage closes on forgiveness and mercy rather than on any name about reward, which early scholars find telling. A statement about right belief ends by naming the qualities that matter when someone falls short. That suggests the position described is not being treated as a test passed. It is an orientation that will still need covering.

crossReferences.why: Describes the position this verse answers, selecting among messengers and seeking a path between.
Puts this same statement into the mouths of the believers, as words they say themselves.
Lists the prophets and closes with submission to God and no distinction among any of them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a tradition you inherited and the parts of it you were taught to hold at arm's length. Not doctrine, just the figures and sources your family or community quietly set aside. Read something from one of them this week, on its own terms. Do that before you decide anything about it.
studies.explainEasier: People who believe in God and in all of His messengers will be given their full reward. They do not pick and choose among them. God is forgiving and He is kind.

studies.title: Show Us God Plainly
studies.meaning: A demand is put: bring down a book from the sky. The verse answers by pointing to a larger demand made long before, and that comparison is the whole argument. Early scholars note that the passage does not refuse the request directly. It places it inside a history. Two episodes follow, the demand to see God plainly and the making of the calf, and both close with something unexpected: a pardon, and an authority given.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the section addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. Early scholars report that a demand was put to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). It was for a written text delivered from the sky, in the manner described in earlier scripture. The reports differ over who made it and agree on its substance. The verse answers by recalling episodes from the account of Moses.

keyTerms.note: The same root used a few verses earlier of speaking aloud. Here it means seeing with the eyes rather than being told, so the demand is for direct sight with nothing in between.
A word for a lightning strike and for the stupor it causes. It names both the event and its effect, which is why early scholars discuss whether it describes death or a loss of consciousness.
From the root meaning to erase a trace. Its placement after the calf, the gravest episode named, is what makes the sentence turn, since pardon rather than punishment closes the account.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A written page carried great weight in a world that mostly spoke, just because it was rare. Groups with scripture were known as people of the Book. The text itself was part of their standing. Asking for a book sent down from the sky was a demand for the one thing that could settle a public quarrel.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to the account of Moses more often than to any other story. Its retellings vary in detail from one place to another, according to the argument being made. Here two separate episodes are packed into a single verse. The point being made is a comparison rather than a story.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A demand for a sign is answered by noting what happened when larger signs were given. That is an argument about evidence and belief. The calf came after clear proofs, so proof is shown not to produce belief on its own. And the account closes with pardon and with authority given, which keeps the history from being only a charge sheet.

crossReferences.why: Narrates the same demand to see God plainly, and what followed immediately from it.
Gives the episode of the calf at greater length, including the turning that followed it.
Says a written text sent down in their hands would still have been called plain magic.

studies.applyIt: Notice what evidence you have told yourself would settle a question you keep reopening. Then ask whether the last piece of evidence that arrived settled anything. This passage argues that the demand usually outlives the answer. That is worth testing against your own history first.
studies.explainEasier: Some people asked for a book to come down from the sky. Long ago others asked Moses for something bigger. They wanted to see God with their own eyes. Then they worshipped a calf, and God still pardoned them.

studies.title: The Mountain Raised Above
studies.meaning: Three moments stand side by side, each attached to a pledge. The mountain was raised over them. They were told to enter a gate humbly, and they were told about the Sabbath. Early scholars discuss the first at length and record differing readings of what the raising describes. What binds the three is the closing word, a covenant called thick and heavy, using the same phrase this surah applied earlier to a marriage.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, continuing the address to communities holding earlier scripture. Early scholars read the verse as a compressed recollection of episodes told at greater length elsewhere in the Quran. They are gathered here because each one involves a pledge. The passage sits between an answer to a demand for a sign and a list of covenant failures, so its subject is what was undertaken.

keyTerms.note: A word the Quran uses specifically of the mountain of Moses. Early scholars record differing readings of what its raising over them describes, and they preserve the range rather than settling it.
A plural participle describing the manner of entering. It names a posture rather than an action performed once inside, so the instruction concerns how a threshold is crossed.
The same phrase this surah used earlier of a marriage. Its reuse here for a community's pledge places a household agreement and a covenant with God inside one vocabulary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A pledge in Arabia was sworn in public, often with a physical act attached: hands clasped, a stone touched, a formula repeated before witnesses. Its binding force came from having been seen. The episodes recalled here each attach a pledge to a place or an act. To that audience, this would have read as the proper shape of a covenant.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a solid covenant occurs only a few times in the Quran. It is used of the pledge taken from the prophets, of a marriage, and here of a community's undertaking. Early scholars note that three very different bonds are described by one term. That is the sort of link a long surah builds deliberately.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage gathers orders of different kinds under one idea. Something was taken on. Entering a gate, keeping a day, and making a covenant at a mountain are not similar acts. What makes them one subject is the pledge tied to each. That treats the moral life as a set of standing promises, not a list of separate rules.

crossReferences.why: Narrates the raising of the mountain and the covenant taken there at greater length.
Gives the instruction about entering the gate, and reports what was said instead.
Uses the same phrase for a solid covenant, there of the pledge inside a marriage.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list of what you have actually undertaken: promises you gave, roles you accepted, things you said you would be. Not aspirations, undertakings. Most people find the list shorter and heavier than they expected, and simply having it written down changes which of them get kept.
studies.explainEasier: God raised the mountain above them when they made their promise. He told them to go through the gate humbly and to keep the Sabbath. And He took a solemn pledge from them.

studies.title: Our Hearts Are Covered
studies.meaning: The verse lists a series of covenant failures. One item is a phrase they said about themselves: our hearts are wrapped. The reply turns that claim around, saying it is God who sealed them. Early scholars read the exchange as being about the cause rather than about the condition itself. A second charge follows, a grave falsehood spoken against Mary, which the Quran names without ever repeating it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, within the address to communities holding earlier scripture. Early scholars explain the phrase about wrapped hearts as an idiom in use at the time, claiming that a message could not get through. The passage lists specific failures rather than making a general charge. It ends with the note that a few among them do believe.

keyTerms.note: A plural adjective from a root meaning a covering or a sheath. The claim describes hearts as already enclosed, turning an unwillingness to hear into a condition nobody could be blamed for.
The verb for pressing a seal into clay or wax. It describes a closure that is fixed rather than temporary, and early scholars read it as following repeated refusal rather than as an original state.
From a root meaning to leave someone stunned. The same word appeared earlier in this surah, of a husband reclaiming a dowry and of blaming an innocent person for a fault.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A sword kept in a sheath was described with the same word used here of the heart. The image was ordinary rather than poetic: something useful but covered, out of reach until drawn. Claiming that your heart was sheathed used a picture people handled daily. That is part of why the reply engages the image rather than brushing it aside.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran does not repeat the falsehood spoken against Mary. It names it as a great slander and moves on. Early scholars note that restraint. They observe that the Quran elsewhere gives a long passage to the account of Mary, so the refusal to restate the charge here is a choice rather than a gap.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exchange about hearts turns on who did the covering. A claim of being unable is met not by denial but by moving its cause. That keeps responsibility while granting the condition. The list also stays specific, naming acts rather than a people. It closes with an exception for the few, which early scholars always stress when reading it.

crossReferences.why: Records the same claim about wrapped hearts, and gives the same answer to it.
Gives the account of Mary at length, including the defence that was made of her.
Continues the list with the next claim, this one concerning the Messiah himself.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you say you cannot change something about yourself. Sometimes that is accurate. But listen to the sentence you use, and ask whether it describes a condition or excuses one. The passage does not deny that hearts can close. It disputes only the account of how they got that way.
studies.explainEasier: They broke their promise, turned down God's signs, and killed prophets. They said their hearts were covered up and nothing could get in. God says He sealed their hearts because they kept refusing.

studies.title: It Was Made To Appear
studies.meaning: A claim is quoted and then denied twice, once at the start of the sentence and again at its end. What the Quran states is that he was neither killed nor crucified, and that the matter was made to appear otherwise. The classical scholars offer several accounts of how, and they set them side by side without agreeing. The verse describes those who differ about him as in doubt, following guesswork rather than knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This sits inside a passage listing claims made about earlier prophets. The people of Medina lived among groups with settled views about Jesus, and Christian groups across the region held the crucifixion at the heart of their faith. Early scholars read the verse as answering a claim to have carried out the killing. The tradition has always read it as denying that outcome.

keyTerms.note: A title the Quran uses of Jesus throughout, never as a description it disputes. It appears here inside the quoted claim and is left standing rather than corrected in any way.
A passive from the root for likeness and ambiguity. The grammar leaves the subject unnamed, which is why early scholars offer several readings and none can claim the wording itself.
A word for an opinion held without certainty. It stands against knowledge in the same sentence, so the charge concerns the basis of a claim rather than the sincerity of those making it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Christian communities were settled across Arabia and beyond it, in Najran, in Syria and in Abyssinia. The community in Medina had direct contact with them. A group from Najran later came to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to talk. Claims about Jesus were not distant theology in that setting. They were the subject of conversations people actually had.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names Jesus as the Messiah repeatedly, and describes his birth, his signs and his message at length. This verse calls him the Messenger of God inside the very claim it is denying. What is denied is the outcome asserted, and the titles standing inside the quoted sentence are left untouched.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies an outcome and then declines to say how. That is why the classical commentaries record several accounts rather than one. What it states plainly comes in the next verse: he was raised to God. Christians have understood the matter differently. The difference is a real one, and this verse itself describes it as something people dispute.

crossReferences.why: States what the Quran affirms positively, that God raised him up to Himself.
Records God taking him and raising him, in another passage on the same subject.
Places peace on him at his birth, at his death, and on the day he is raised alive.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you hold a firm position on something you have never examined, simply because the people around you hold it. The charge in this verse concerns the basis of a claim rather than its content. Pick one such position of your own and find out, this week, what it actually rests on.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said they had killed Jesus. The Quran says they did not kill him and did not put him on a cross. It only looked that way to them. Those who argue about it are guessing.

studies.title: Raised Up To Himself
studies.meaning: What the passage states is put in four words: rather, God raised him to Himself. Nothing further is described, and early scholars note the restraint. Then the next verse makes a statement about belief coming before a death. The tradition keeps genuinely different readings of whose death is meant. Some take it as his, and some as each person at their own end.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, completing the passage about claims made concerning Jesus. Early scholars read these two verses as the positive counterpart to the denial before them. The second has been discussed at length in the tradition, since its pronouns can be read more than one way. The classical commentaries pass on the options without choosing between them.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for raising something up, used of rank as well as of position. The Quran leaves the manner unspecified, which is why early scholars discuss it without claiming the verse settles it.
A possessive pronoun that can attach to either party in the sentence. That ambiguity is the source of the tradition's two readings, and the commentaries record both rather than resolving it.
From the root for presence. A witness testifies to what he was there for, so the word implies a relationship to those being testified about rather than the role of a judge over them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the tool of justice in a world without records. A witness was chosen for standing rather than for being neutral. Being testified about by somebody who knew you was the most serious kind of reckoning available. That is the picture the second verse draws on, and its first hearers would have felt the weight at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two verses holds a pronoun that can attach to two different subjects. The classical commentaries record both readings side by side across the centuries. It is one of the clearest cases of the tradition passing on a real ambiguity in the grammar. They did not settle it into one account.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The statement is short where the denial before it was emphatic, and that shapes what the passage claims to know. The closing names, mighty and wise, are attached to a raising rather than to a punishment. So the event is described as an exercise of power under judgement. The witness named next brings the matter back to answering for things.

crossReferences.why: States the denial this verse answers, and the two are read together throughout the tradition.
Describes God taking him and raising him, and placing his followers above those who refused.
Shows him questioned about what he told people, answering that God was the witness over them.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much more confidently you speak about things you were told than about things you saw. This passage is unusually careful about that difference. It affirms little and denies firmly. Try marking the difference once this week, out loud, when you pass something on: what you know, and what you heard.
studies.explainEasier: God raised Jesus up to Himself. Everyone who was given the earlier books will believe in him before they die. On the last day he will stand as a witness about them.

studies.title: Good Things Withheld
studies.meaning: A consequence is described as following from conduct. Because of wrongdoing, and because of turning many away from God's path, things once permitted were withheld. Early scholars note that the limit is presented as a response rather than as an arbitrary load. What was withheld is described only as good things, with no list given. The Quran gives more detail on this elsewhere.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, continuing the section addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. Early scholars connect the limit to food rules described in earlier revelation, and discuss which of them are meant. The passage forms part of a longer list of consequences, each attached to a named conduct. That is how the classical commentaries read it.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for what is pure and pleasant, used across the Quran of permitted food. Its use makes the restriction a loss of something good rather than the removal of something harmful.
A verbal noun covering both turning aside yourself and blocking others. The construction attaches the consequence to obstruction of other people rather than only to their own conduct.
An adjective of quantity closing the clause. Early scholars read it as attaching either to the number of people turned away or to the frequency of the turning, and they record both.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food rules were among the clearest marks setting one group apart from another there, clearer even than belief. What a household would and would not eat decided who could share a meal with whom. Shared meals were how alliances and marriages were built. A limit on good food reached deep into daily life.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere states that limits of this kind came as a consequence and did not belong to the original guidance. It describes a later message as lifting some of them. The idea that a limit can be a response to conduct rather than a permanent feature runs through several passages.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Presenting a limit as a consequence changes what it is. It is neither random nor built in. It is a response. So the moral history of a community is described as shaping what stays open to it. The passage also puts weight on blocking others, treating the effect on other people's access as separate from your own conduct.

crossReferences.why: Names specific restrictions and says they were a recompense for wrongdoing committed.
States that food was lawful before, apart from what one community restricted for itself.
Describes a messenger who lifts burdens and removes the shackles that were upon them.

studies.applyIt: Think about a limit in your own life that arrived as a consequence: a limit on your time, your money, your freedom, brought on by something you did. Rather than resenting it, name the conduct it followed from. That naming is the whole of what this passage does. It usually changes the resentment.
studies.explainEasier: Because of the wrong they did, God took away some good foods that had been allowed for them. They had also turned many people away from God's path. The limit came from what they did.

studies.title: Taking What Was Closed Off
studies.meaning: Two charges about money close the list, and they belong together. One is taking increase on a loan when it had been closed off to them. The other is eating people's wealth with no real basis. Early scholars note that the two are named together because the second explains the first. What makes the increase an offence in this account is that it takes from someone with nothing underneath it. Then the words about punishment narrow to the faithless among them.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the list of consequences addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. Early scholars note that the community in Medina was itself being taught about lending in the same period. So the charge is made where the subject was live for everyone. The closing words limit the statement rather than widening it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to grow or to swell. The word names the increase itself rather than the transaction, so the Quran describes the thing that expands rather than the arrangement producing it.
From a root meaning to be void or come to nothing. The same phrase appeared earlier in this surah, of wealth taken between believers with no real basis under it.
A partitive phrase, meaning some of them rather than all. Its placement before the punishment restricts the statement, which early scholars consistently note when reading the passage.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Lending in that economy was often between neighbours and against a harvest not yet in. A loan that grew while a debtor's crop failed could take a grove that had been in a family for generations. Everyone had watched it happen. That is why the practice is treated across the Quran as a matter of what happens to people.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for increase on a loan comes from a root meaning growth. The same root gives Arabic its ordinary words for raising a child and for a hill. The language names the practice by what it does, which is to swell, rather than by any judgement attached to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the two charges together defines the first by the second. What is objected to is not increase as such. It is wealth moving from one person to another with nothing real underneath the movement. That grounds the matter in a relationship rather than in a mechanism. And the closing words keep the statement from describing everyone.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about consuming wealth without ground, there addressed to believers.
Addresses the same practice at length, and describes what a lender is left with.
Contrasts what is given to increase through people's wealth with what is given seeking God.

studies.applyIt: Look at your income and find anything that arrives without a matching thing having been done or given. Not in order to condemn it, simply to see it clearly. The standard in this passage is whether something real sits under a transfer of wealth. That question is worth asking of your own arrangements.
studies.explainEasier: They took extra money on loans after being told not to. They also took other people's wealth in ways that were not fair. A painful punishment is waiting for those among them who refuse.

studies.title: Firmly Rooted In Knowledge
studies.meaning: After a long list of failures, the passage turns and names an exception with unusual warmth. Those firmly rooted in knowledge among them, and the believers, are described as accepting what was revealed to this Prophet and what came before him. Then four practices are listed and a great reward promised. Early scholars note that the exception is not grudging. It is fuller and more specific than the charge before it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the address to communities holding earlier scripture. Early scholars report that people from those communities had accepted the message. They read this ayah as naming them. The reports differ on who is meant, but agree that the exception describes real people rather than a category, which shapes how the passage is read.

keyTerms.note: A participle from a verb used of mountains set firmly into the earth. Knowledge is described as depth of footing rather than as quantity, which is why the image is one of stability.
A participle from the verb to make something stand upright. Used of prayer it means keeping a practice standing rather than merely performing it whenever the occasion arises.
The ordinary word for a wage, with an adjective of magnitude. The phrase recurs through this surah, and its appearance here places this group inside the same promise given to believers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Learned communities in Medina held their knowledge in memory and in books. It passed from teacher to student across many years. A man called deeply rooted in knowledge was a known figure with standing in his own group. For such a man to accept a new message cost more than it cost anyone else.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for those firmly rooted in knowledge appears twice in the Quran. The other place is a passage about the reading of ambiguous verses. In both, it names people whose depth of learning is tied to how they meet something difficult, not to how much they can recite.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exception comes at the end of a list of failures and is given more detail than the failures were. That changes the weight of the passage. It also joins knowledge to acceptance rather than setting them against each other. Depth of learning is described as what makes recognition possible. The four practices named are ordinary ones, so the exception rests on nothing exceptional.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for those firmly rooted in knowledge, facing verses that are ambiguous.
Names an upright group among the same communities, standing in prayer through the night.
Describes those whose eyes overflow when they recognise the truth in what was sent down.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you expect a person's learning to make them harder to reach rather than easier. This ayah ties depth of knowledge to being able to see something new. Ask one person who knows more than you about something what changed their mind most recently. Then listen to the whole answer.
studies.explainEasier: Some of them know their own books deeply, and they believe. They accept what was sent to this Prophet and what came before. They pray, they give to the poor, and God will give them a great reward.

studies.title: As We Inspired Noah
studies.meaning: A single sentence sets up continuity by listing names. What comes to this Prophet is described in the same terms as what came to Noah and those after him. Then a series of names follows, ending with a book given to David. Early scholars note the order, which is not chronological throughout, and read the list as gathering rather than sequencing. The claim is made by placement rather than by argument.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering a demand for a written text and a run of disputes about which messengers to accept. Early scholars read the list as the response to those disputes. Rather than defending one claim, the passage sets it inside a series. The names chosen span several communities' traditions, which is part of how the argument works in that setting.

keyTerms.note: A verb for communicating something swiftly and privately, used of a signal or a gesture as well as of revelation. It names the manner rather than the content of what was given.
A plural word for the branches descending from a common ancestor. Its inclusion in a list of individuals widens the sentence from named prophets to whole lines of them.
From a root meaning to write or inscribe firmly. The Quran uses it of what was given to David, and the word names a written thing specifically inside a list of inspirations.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Genealogy was recited aloud and learned by heart. In Arabia a list of names was a known form of argument, not a decoration. To back a claim, a speaker recited the line it belonged to. This ayah uses exactly that form, so its first hearers would have known the shape of the argument before weighing its content.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names twenty-five prophets in all. Several of the lists that gather them, this one included, put the names in an order that is not chronological. Early scholars discuss the ordering in each case. They generally read it as thematic or rhythmic rather than as a claim about sequence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is made by structure rather than by claim. Placing a new claim inside a list of accepted ones shifts the burden. It asks the hearer to say why this one should be treated differently. The passage also describes revelation as one kind of event that keeps happening. That is the premise the ayat before it rest on.

crossReferences.why: Gives a longer list of prophets, and states that they were guided and chosen.
Lists many of the same names and says we make no distinction between any of them.
Describes the selective belief this list is set against, accepting some and rejecting others.

studies.applyIt: Take something you find hard to accept and set it beside the things you already accept without trouble. Ask honestly what makes the new one different, in plain terms. This ayah's whole method is that comparison. The answer is often about what is familiar rather than about evidence.
studies.explainEasier: God says he sent his message to this Prophet the same way he sent it to Noah and the prophets after him. He names many of them, one after another. And he gave David the Psalms.

studies.title: Messengers Not Told To You
studies.meaning: The list of names is closed with a statement that changes its scope: there were also messengers whose accounts were never given. So the list was never a census. Then one figure is singled out by the manner of address rather than by rank, with the verb for speaking repeated as its own noun, an Arabic intensive. The second ayah gives the purpose of sending them at all, which is stated as the removal of an argument.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes the passage that answered demands about which messengers to accept. Early scholars read the note about untold accounts as answering a move in that argument. Otherwise a group could test a new claim against a fixed and known list. The passage then widens from named men to the purpose of prophecy itself.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to follow a track, which also gives the word for a story. A narrative in Arabic is pictured as following footprints rather than as composing something.
A verbal noun repeating the verb before it, an Arabic construction used for emphasis. It rules out any reading in which the speaking would be figurative rather than real.
A word for a proof advanced in dispute, from a root about aiming for something. The purpose of sending messengers is stated as removing a case people could otherwise make.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A claim in Arabia was tested against what people already knew. A genealogy or a list of names was how such knowledge was held. Saying that the list is incomplete removed the ability to check a claim by looking it up in memory. That was the standard method in a society without archives.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names twenty-five prophets and states here that others were sent whose accounts were not given. Early scholars have generally declined to guess at numbers. The tradition's usual answer to the question of how many there were is that only God knows.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The purpose of prophecy is given as the removal of an excuse, which is a striking way to state it. Messengers are described as closing off a case people could otherwise bring. So revelation is framed as a matter of fairness in judgement, not only as guidance. And the incomplete list keeps any community from claiming it holds the whole record.

crossReferences.why: States again that messengers were sent whose accounts were not related to you.
Says God does not punish until a messenger has been sent, the same principle stated directly.
Narrates the occasion of speaking with Moses, and what was asked and answered there.

studies.applyIt: Notice how confidently you dismiss things that fall outside the account you were given. This ayah tells its first audience that their record was incomplete by design. Hold one such gap open this week rather than filling it, and see whether anything you were certain of loosens slightly.
studies.explainEasier: God told this Prophet about some of the messengers, but not about all of them. He spoke to Moses directly. Messengers came with good news and with warnings, so that nobody could say they were never told.

studies.title: The Angels Bear Witness
studies.meaning: Testimony is offered where agreement has not been reached. God is described as bearing witness to what was sent down, and a clause is added about the manner of sending: it was sent with His knowledge. Then a second witness is named, the angels, and the sentence closes by saying God suffices as a witness. Early scholars note that a witness is not an argument, which is why the ayah opens with a word for contrast.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the section addressed to communities holding earlier scripture, after a long exchange of claims. Early scholars read the opening particle as marking a turn. The argument is not carried on but set aside in favour of testimony. The passage arrives at a point where the disagreement had been stated fully on both sides.

keyTerms.note: From the root for presence. A witness testifies to what he was there for, so the verb makes the claim rest on presence at the event rather than on reasoning about it.
A phrase early scholars read in more than one way: that it was sent containing His knowledge, or sent by it. Both readings are recorded, and the grammar sustains each of them.
A verb meaning to be enough, used across this surah in closing clauses. Its effect is to end an argument by declaring that nothing further needs to be added to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Witnesses were the base of every claim in that society. Their number and standing decided outcomes. A dispute that could not be settled by argument was settled by who would stand and speak. Ending a long disagreement by naming witnesses used the exact method people expected, at a scale they could not contest.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying that God suffices as a witness appears several times across the Quran. It always comes at the close of a passage, never at its opening. Early scholars note the placement. It works as a seal on an argument already made, not as a premise offered at the start.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Moving from argument to testimony changes what is asked of the hearer. An argument invites a counter-argument. A witness invites either acceptance or the charge that the witness cannot be trusted. Naming the angels alongside makes the testimony plural. The closing clause then declares the first witness enough on its own.

crossReferences.why: Answers a denial of messengership by naming God as sufficient witness between the parties.
Asks what thing is greatest in testimony, and answers that God is witness between us.
States that God is sufficient as a witness, earlier in this same surah.

studies.applyIt: Notice how long you keep arguing after the point where nothing new is being said. Both sides have usually stated everything by then. Try ending one such exchange this week by simply saying what you believe and stopping, without requiring the other person to concede anything.
studies.explainEasier: God himself says that what came to this Prophet is from him. He sent it down knowing exactly what it was. The angels say the same. But God alone is enough as a witness.

studies.title: Except The Road To Hell
studies.meaning: Three short ayat that narrow as they go. The first names refusal together with turning others away, and calls the result a straying that has gone far. The second adds wrongdoing and states that neither forgiveness nor guidance to a road will come. The third then supplies the one road that remains, which is a grim piece of wordplay: guidance is withheld, and a route is named anyway.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the long argument with those who had refused the message while working to turn others from it. Early scholars note that the passage names two things together throughout: refusal and blocking. They read the pairing as the reason for its severity. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: A verb covering both turning aside oneself and obstructing others. Its presence alongside refusal is what distinguishes the people described from those who simply did not accept.
A different word from the one used for a path elsewhere in this surah, and it recurs in the next ayah. The repetition is what makes the third ayah land as it does.
An adjective for what costs no effort. Closing a severe passage with it removes any suggestion of struggle, which is the same move made earlier in this surah about the Fire.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Roads in that landscape were few and known by name, and a traveller who lost one had no alternative to find. Being told there was no road was a complete statement about a journey. Naming a road and then specifying which one carried the same weight as a guide pointing at the only track and saying where it ended.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a road appears in two ayat in a row here. First it is what is withheld. Then it is what is supplied anyway. Arabic wordplay of this kind, repeating a term to reverse its force, runs through the Quran, and early scholars point it out in passages of warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is careful to name two things rather than one. Refusal on its own is described elsewhere in the Quran, and much wider openings are left there. Here blocking others is added. The severity follows that addition. So weight falls on the effect a person has on other people's access. That is treated as a matter apart from their own position.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for a straying that has gone far, earlier in this surah.
Adds punishment upon punishment for those who refused and turned others from God's path.
Names those who refused and obstructed and then died refusing, and what follows for them.

studies.applyIt: Consider the difference these ayat draw. It is one thing to hold back from something yourself, and another to make it harder for the people around you. Ask whether anyone finds a good thing harder because of how you speak about it, and adjust that one thing this week.
studies.explainEasier: Some people turn away from God and also stop others from reaching him. They have gone a long way off the road. God will not forgive them or show them any road, except the one that leads to the Fire.

studies.title: Better For You
studies.meaning: The address widens for the first time in a long stretch. It moves from particular communities to people in general. The Messenger has come with the truth, and belief is urged in two words that read as an assessment rather than a command: better for you. The other option is then met with the statement of ownership used across the surah's closing sections. Refusal changes nothing about what is held.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's long argument and turning outward. Early scholars note the shift in address, from those given earlier scripture to all people. They read the ayah as the summary the whole section has been building toward. The statement about the heavens and the earth comes back here as it does several times in these later passages.

keyTerms.note: The widest form of address in the Quran, used of humanity rather than of believers or of a named community. Its appearance here marks the end of a long stretch of particular argument.
A word covering truth, reality and a rightful claim together. Saying he came with it rather than about it makes the truth something carried rather than something asserted.
A comparative with the beneficiary named. It states an assessment rather than an instruction, which is why the sentence reads as advice offered rather than as a demand made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca and Medina sat on routes that carried people from Yemen, Syria, Abyssinia and Persia. A market town on such a route held a truly mixed crowd. An address to people in general was not empty talk there. A speaker in a market could expect several groups to be within hearing.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah is the first in the Quran's order to open with an address to all people rather than to believers. It returns to that address here, near its close. Early scholars note the framing. The chapter's opening and its final section both widen the audience in the same way.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting the appeal as an assessment rather than a command changes the relation it assumes. The hearer is treated as someone weighing a gain. He is not treated as someone under an order. That fits an address to people who have not yet accepted any authority. And the clause about ownership makes clear that the gain named runs one way only.

crossReferences.why: Opens the surah with the same wide address to humanity, before any particular community.
Repeats the address a few ayat later, naming a proof and a clear light instead.
Says whoever is guided is guided for himself, and whoever strays does so against himself.

studies.applyIt: Notice how differently you take advice framed as a command and the same advice framed as a gain for you. Try giving one piece of advice this week in the second form. Then watch how much of the resistance you usually meet was caused by the framing.
studies.explainEasier: God speaks to all people here. The Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord. Believing is better for you. If you refuse, everything in the sky and on the earth still belongs to God.

studies.title: Do Not Go To Excess
studies.meaning: The ayah speaks to those who hold earlier scripture. It warns against going too far in religion, not against religion itself. Then it gives Jesus three titles the Quran uses of him. He is a messenger of God. He is God's word, delivered to Mary. He is a spirit from Him. After that comes a statement that God is one. The ayah closes by saying God is far above having a son. Christians read these matters differently, and that is what the passage speaks to.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, near the end of the surah. Early scholars place it among exchanges with Christian communities of the region. Some tie it to a delegation that came to discuss such questions. The reports differ over which occasion is meant. What the classical scholars agree on is this. The ayah takes up claims made about Jesus, not his standing as a prophet.

keyTerms.note: A verb for passing a proper limit, used of a price rising too high. The fault named is excess, not devotion. The instruction is about measure, not about direction.
A title the Quran gives Jesus. Early scholars read it alongside the word of command by which he was created. They record the discussion rather than settling it on one sense.
A phrase the early scholars handle with care. They usually read the preposition as marking origin, not a part of God. The Quran uses the same wording elsewhere for things God grants.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Christian communities in Najran, Syria and Abyssinia were large. Their own debates about doctrine were live and unsettled across the region that century. Traders and travellers carried those debates into Arabian markets. So questions about how Jesus should be described were familiar to the Quran's first hearers. They were not remote.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah gives Jesus three titles and denies another claim at the same time. It says yes and no inside one sentence. Early scholars also note how it opens. It addresses its audience with a respectful form, naming them by their scripture rather than by their disagreement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is against excess, not against reverence. That places the disagreement exactly. Titles are given first. Then a limit is drawn on what may be said about God. The ayah roots that limit in ownership. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God. So nothing needs to be added to Him in the way of family.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same instruction against excess in religion, in almost the same words.
States the same conclusion after the account of Jesus, that God takes no son.
Compares the creation of Jesus with that of Adam, both by a word of command.

studies.applyIt: Notice where your admiration for someone has quietly outgrown what you would say about them in plain words. It happens with teachers, parents, leaders and writers. The instruction here is about measure, not about affection. Saying the plain version once usually brings the measure back. It rarely costs the affection.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people who follow earlier books not to go too far. Jesus was a messenger. He was God's word, given to Mary. God is one God. He does not have a son.

studies.title: Never Too Proud To Serve
studies.meaning: One verb carries the ayah. It means to hold yourself above something out of pride. The Messiah is described as never doing that about being a servant. The angels brought near are named beside him. The argument works upward. If those closest to God do not think service is beneath them, the question of who might is already answered. The closing clause then gathers everyone up regardless.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It follows the passage on excess in describing Jesus. Early scholars read the two together. This ayah answers the same question from another direction. Instead of disputing a title, it describes what the figure in question is reported to have accepted. The angels are added because they too were the subject of claims in the region.

keyTerms.note: A rare verb built from a root about turning the face aside. It names refusal out of pride, not refusal for any other reason. That is what the ayah measures.
The ordinary word for one who serves. The Quran uses it of prophets at their highest moments. Here it makes servanthood a mark of nearness rather than of low rank.
A passive form from the verb to bring close. The nearness is granted, not achieved. That is why the word can sit beside a statement about not holding service beneath you.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Service in Arabia was a matter of standing. A free man guarded that line with care. To be called someone's servant was an insult, unless the master was extraordinary. Then it became a boast. That is the register the ayah works in. Attachment to a great house was a claim to honour, not an admission of low rank.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran calls its own Prophet a servant of God at the highest moments in the book. The night journey is one. The sending down of the revelation is another. The title is saved for those points, not for ordinary ones. That is the pattern this ayah leans on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a claim about status by showing what status looks like from inside. Those nearest are the least likely to hold service beneath them. That turns the usual link between rank and deference upside down. Pride becomes a mark of distance, not of height. The argument rests on disposition rather than on doctrine.

crossReferences.why: Says everyone in the heavens and earth comes to the Merciful only as a servant.
Describes the angels as honoured servants who do not speak ahead of Him.
Names the Prophet as a servant at the very moment of the night journey.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the tasks you consider beneath you: the cleaning, the setting up, the message you think somebody junior should send. Do one of them this week without arranging for anyone to notice. The ayah's argument is that distance from that reluctance is what nearness actually looks like.
studies.explainEasier: Even Jesus was never too proud to serve God. Neither are the angels closest to God. Anyone who is too proud to worship Him will still be brought back to Him in the end.

studies.title: Paid In Full, And More
studies.meaning: Two outcomes are given in one sentence, and the asymmetry is deliberate. The first group is paid its wages in full and then increased from God's bounty, so the account is settled and then exceeded. The second, described by the pride named in the ayah before, is met with punishment and with the absence of any protector or helper. The two halves are built in matching grammar so the difference is audible.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes the passage on servanthood and pride that began with the Messiah and the angels. Early scholars read this ayah as the outcome attached to the disposition just described. The subject stays the same across the three ayat. The surah is in its final section, gathering its arguments toward a close.

keyTerms.gloss: He will pay them in full
keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for completing a payment without shortfall. It belongs to the vocabulary of settling a debt, which is why the increase mentioned next is described separately from it.
The ordinary verb for adding more. Its placement after full payment is what makes the sentence generous, since nothing further was owed once the account had been settled.
A verb meaning to make oneself great, from the root for bigness. Paired with the rare verb of the previous ayah, it names the disposition rather than any particular act.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A day labourer in Medina was paid at the end of the work, and whether he was paid in full and on time was a matter people spoke about. A master who added something beyond the agreed wage was remembered for it. The ayah's two verbs describe exactly that sequence, which its first hearers would have recognised at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The reward comes in two stages here: full payment, then increase. That shape recurs across the Quran wherever wages are described. Early scholars note that the second stage is always put down to bounty, not to the accounting. So it is never described as owed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Keeping payment and increase apart holds on to both justice and generosity. Neither one swallows the other. What was earned is settled exactly. What is added comes from another source entirely. The other half of the sentence names the absence of a protector. That phrase runs across this surah for the position of someone standing entirely alone.

crossReferences.why: Names the disposition whose two outcomes this ayah sets out in matching construction.
Uses the same pairing, full payment of wages followed by an increase from His bounty.
States earlier in this surah that no protector or helper is found besides God.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time somebody gave you more than was agreed, and how differently that landed from being paid exactly what was owed. Do that once this week for a person who works for you or with you. The distinction this ayah draws is small in size and large in effect.
studies.explainEasier: People who believe and do good will get everything they earned, and more on top. People who are too proud will be punished. When that happens, no one but God can help them or keep them safe.

studies.title: A Proof And A Light
studies.meaning: The wide address returns. Two things are named as having arrived: a proof from your Lord, and a clear light sent down. Early scholars discuss what each one refers to and usually read them together. One term is drawn from argument, the other from sight. The second ayah then says what follows for those who believe and take hold. It ends on a straight path that leads to Him, not merely to a destination.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's closing section. Early scholars note that the address to humanity appears twice within a few ayat here. It frames the end of the chapter as it framed the opening. The passage comes after a long argument. It sums up by naming what has been given, not by restating any of the disputes.

keyTerms.note: A word for decisive evidence, from a root connected with brightness. Arabic ties proof to light at the level of the root, which is why the two terms in this ayah sit together naturally.
Light paired with an adjective meaning both clear in itself and clarifying. The doubling makes the light not only visible but the means by which other things become visible too.
From a root meaning to grasp something for protection, used of clinging to a rope. It names an action rather than a state, which is why it stands beside believing rather than inside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel at night in open country was done by starlight. A lamp carried through a settlement showed where a person was going. It also showed who was moving at that hour. Light was scarce, so it was practical rather than decorative. To call something a clear light was to name the difference between moving and waiting.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for a decisive proof comes from a root about brightness and shining. The language ties evidence to light at the level of the root. So the two nouns in this ayah sit closer together in Arabic than the English words proof and light suggest.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Pairing a proof with a light separates two things that are often confused. One settles an argument. The other lets you see. The second ayah adds a third element, taking hold. So belief is described as needing a grip, not only agreement. The path named at the close leads to God rather than to a place.

crossReferences.why: Describes a light and a clear Book as having come from God to the same audience.
Uses the same verb for holding fast, there of holding to the rope of God together.
Opens the same wide address a few ayat earlier, naming truth rather than light.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between being convinced of something and being able to see by it. Most people have beliefs of the first kind and very few of the second. Take one thing you are convinced of and use it this week to decide something, which is the only way the second kind is ever formed.
studies.explainEasier: God says clear proof has come to people, and a light they can see by. Anyone who believes in God and holds on to Him will be brought into His mercy. He will show them a straight road.

studies.title: The Case Left Open
studies.meaning: The surah closes by answering the one inheritance case it had left unfinished. That is an estate with neither parent nor child. The ayah names the shares the siblings take in it. Then a short clause gives the reason for the whole passage. God makes this clear so that you do not go astray. Early scholars note that the surah's last word before the closing name is about straying. It is the same word the surah has used throughout.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It is reported as among the last passages of the surah to come down. Early scholars pass on that a question about this case was raised again and again, and answered here. Several accounts describe it as the answer to an illness, during which a man asked how his estate would be divided. The reports differ in detail while agreeing on the substance.

keyTerms.gloss: an estate with no direct heirs
keyTerms.note: The rare term left partly open earlier in this surah. Early scholars discuss its exact scope at length and record the difficulty. They generally read it as an estate with neither parent nor child.
A verb for coming to an end, used of a person dying and of things being destroyed. Its plainness is notable in a passage otherwise built from precise legal vocabulary.
The verb for losing one's road, used repeatedly across this surah. Its appearance in the reason given for the passage ties inheritance to the same image used of belief.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man with no children and no surviving parents left an estate families really fought over. Custom offered no settled answer. Everyone with a claim had a case. Such disputes could run for years and split a household for good. That is why a question about this case was asked again and again, not once.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah closes the surah by returning to the subject its opening ayat began with. The chapter ends where it started, on the property of those left behind. The unfinished case named earlier in the surah is completed only in the final ayah. That is an unusually deliberate piece of building.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reason given for the detail is that people should not go astray. That is the same word this surah uses of belief and of conduct. It ties exact shares to the moral life directly. Without a clear division, families lose their way. The passage treats that as the same kind of straying as any other. Clarity is offered as a mercy, not as a limit.

crossReferences.why: Raises this same case earlier in the surah and leaves part of it unresolved there.
Sets out the shares for children and parents that this ayah completes for siblings.
States the principle these shares implement, that men and women both hold a fixed portion.

studies.applyIt: If you have never written down what should happen to what you leave, start this week. Do one small piece of it: a list, a note, a conversation with one person. The reason given here is that clarity keeps people from losing their way. That losing usually happens between people who loved each other.
studies.explainEasier: This answers a question about who inherits when someone dies with no parents and no children. A sister gets half. Two sisters get two thirds. God explains it so people do not get it wrong.
